Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus, bishop and martyr, and the impersonation of the catholic church of the middle of the third century, sprang from a noble and wealthy heathen family of Carthage, where he was born about the year 200, or earlier. His deacon and biographer, Pontius, considers his earlier life not worthy of notice in comparison with his subsequent greatness in the church. Jerome tells us, that he stood in high repute as a teacher of rhetoric.(370) He was, at all events, a man of commanding literary, rhetorical, and legal culture, and of eminent administrative ability which afterwards proved of great service to him in the episcopal office. He lived in worldly splendor to mature age, nor was he free from the common vices of heathenism, as we must infer from his own confessions. But the story, that he practised arts of magic arises perhaps from some confusion, and is at any rate unattested. Yet, after he became a Christian he believed, like Tertullian and others, in visions and dreams, and had some only a short time before his martyrdom. A worthy presbyter, Caecilius, who lived in Cyprian’s house, and afterwards at his death committed his wife and children to him, first made him acquainted with the doctrines of the Christian religion, and moved him to read the Bible. After long resistance Cyprian forsook the world, entered the class of catechumens, sold his estates for the benefit of the poor,(371) took a vow of chastity, and in 245 or 246 received baptism, adopting, out of gratitude to his spiritual father, the name of Caecilius. He himself, in a tract soon afterwards written to a friend,(372) gives us the following oratorical description of his conversion: While I languished in darkness and deep night, tossing upon the sea of a troubled world, ignorant of my destination, and far from truth and light, I thought it, according to my then habits, altogether a difficult and hard thing that a man could be born anew, and that, being quickened to new life by the bath of saving water, he might put off the past, and, while preserving the identity of the body, might transform the man in mind and heart. How, said I, is such a change possible? How can one at once divest himself of all that was either innate or acquired and grown upon him?... Whence does he learn frugality, who was accustomed to sumptuous feasts? And how shall he who shone in costly apparel, in gold and purple, come down to common and simple dress? He who has lived in honor and station, cannot bear to be private and obscure .... But when, by the aid of the regenerating water,(373) the stain of my former life was washed away, a serene and pure light poured from above into my purified breast. So soon as I drank the spirit from above and was transformed by a second birth into a new man, then the wavering mind became wonderfully firm; what had been closed opened; the dark became light; strength came for that which had seemed difficult; what I had thought impossible became practicable." Cyprian now devoted himself zealously, in ascetic retirement, to the study of the Scriptures and the church teachers, especially Tertullian, whom be called for daily with the words: "Hand me the master!"(374) The influence of Tertullian on his theological formation is unmistakable, and appears at once, for example, on comparing the tracts of the two on prayer and on patience, or the work of the one on the vanity of idols with the apology of the other. It is therefore rather strange that in his own writings we find no acknowledgment of his indebtedness, and, as far as I recollect, no express allusion whatever to Tertullian and the Montanists. But he could derive no aid and comfort from him in his conflict with schism. Such a man could not long remain concealed. Only two years after his baptism, in spite of his earnest remonstrance, Cyprian was raised to the bishopric of Carthage by the acclamations of the people, and was thus at the same time placed at the head of the whole North African clergy. This election of a neophyte was contrary to the letter of the ecclesiastical laws (comp. 1 Tim. 3:6), and led afterwards to the schism of the party of Novatus. But the result proved, that here, as in the similar elevation of Ambrose, Augustin, and other eminent bishops of the ancient church, the voice of the people was the voice of God. For the space of ten years, ending with his triumphant martyrdom, Cyprian administered the episcopal office in Carthage with exemplary energy, wisdom, and fidelity, and that in a most stormy time, amidst persecutions from without and schismatic agitations within. The persecution under Valerian brought his active labors to a close. He was sent into exile for eleven months, then tried before the Proconsul, and condemned to be beheaded. When the sentence was pronounced, he said: "Thanks be to God," knelt in prayer, tied the bandage over his eyes with his own hand, gave to the executioner a gold piece, and died with the dignity and composure of a hero. His friends removed and buried his body by night. Two chapels were erected on the spots of his death and burial. The anniversary of his death was long observed; and five sermons of Augustin still remain in memory of Cyprian’s martyrdom, Sept. 14, 258. Character and Position. As Origen was the ablest scholar, and Tertullian the strongest writer, so Cyprian was the greatest bishop, of the third century. He was born to be a prince in the church. In executive talent, he even surpassed all the Roman bishops of his time; and he bore himself towards them, also, as "frater" and "collega," in the spirit of full equality. Augustin calls him by, eminence, "the catholic bishop and catholic martyr;" and Vincentius of Lirinum, "the light of all saints, all martyrs, and all bishops." His stamp of character was more that of Peter than either of Paul or John. His peculiar importance falls not so much in the field of theology, where he lacks originality and depth, as in church organization and discipline. While Tertullian dealt mainly with heretics, Cyprian directed his polemics against schismatics, among whom he had to condemn, though he never does in fact, his venerated teacher, who died a Montanist. Yet his own conduct was not perfectly consistent with his position; for in the controversy on heretical baptism he himself exhibited his master’s spirit of opposition to Rome. He set a limit to his own exclusive catholic principle of tradition by the truly Protestant maxims: "Consuetudo sine veritate vetustas erroris est, and, Non est de consuetudine praescribendum, sed ratione vincendum." In him the idea of the old catholic hierarchy and episcopal autocracy, both in its affinity and in its conflict with the idea of the papacy, was personally embodied, so to speak, and became flesh and blood. The unity of the church, as the vehicle and medium of all salvation, was the thought of his life and the passion of his heart. But he contended with the same zeal for an independent episcopate as for a Roman primacy; and the authority of his name has been therefore as often employed against the papacy as in its favor. On both sides he was the faithful organ of the churchly spirit of the age. It were great injustice to attribute his high churchly principle to pride and ambition, though temptations to this spirit unquestionably beset a prominent position like his. Such principles are, entirely compatible with sincere personal humility before God. It was the deep conviction of the divine authority, and the heavy responsibility of the episcopate, which lay it the bottom both of his first "nolo episcopari, " and of subsequent hierarchical feeling. He was as conscientious in discharging the duties, as he was jealous in maintaining the rights, of his office. Notwithstanding his high conception of the dignity of a bishop, he took counsel of his presbyters in everything, and respected the rights of his people. He knew how to combine strictness and moderation, dignity and gentleness, and to inspire love and confidence as well as esteem and veneration. He took upon himself, like a father, the care of the widows and orphans, the poor and sick. During the great pestilence of 252 he showed the most self-sacrificing fidelity to his flock, and love for his enemies. He forsook his congregation, indeed, in the Decian persecution, but only, as he expressly assured them, in pursuance of a divine admonition, and in order to direct them during his fourteen months of exile by pastoral epistles. His conduct exposed him to the charge of cowardice. In the Valerian persecution he completely washed away the stain of that flight with the blood of his calm and cheerful martyrdom. He exercised first rigid discipline, but at a later period—not in perfect consistency—he moderated his disciplinary principles in prudent accommodation to the exigencies of the times. With Tertullian he prohibited all display of female dress, which only deformed the work of the Creator; and he warmly opposed all participation in heathen amusements,—even refusing a converted play-actor permission to give instruction in declamation and pantomime. He lived in a simple, ascetic way, under a sense of the perishableness of all earthly things, and in view of the solemn eternity, in which alone also the questions and strifes of the church militant would be perfectly settled. "Only above," says he in his tract De Mortalitate, which be composed during the pestilence, "only above are true peace, sure repose, constant, firm, and eternal security; there is our dwelling, there our home. Who would not fain hasten to reach it? There a great multitude of beloved awaits us; the numerous host of fathers, brethren, and children. There is a glorious choir of apostles there the number of exulting prophets; there the countless multitude of martyrs, crowned with victory after warfare and suffering; there triumphing virgins; there the merciful enjoying their reward. Thither let us hasten with longing desire; let us wish to be soon with them, soon with Christ. After the earthly comes the heavenly; after the small follows the great after perishableness, eternity." His writings. As an author, Cyprian is far less original, fertile and vigorous than Tertullian, but is clearer, more moderate, and more elegant and rhetorical in his style. He wrote independently only on the doctrines of the church, the priesthood, and sacrifice. (1.) His most important works relate to practical questions on church government and discipline. Among these is his tract on the Unity of the Church (A. D. 251), that "magna charta" of the old catholic high-church spirit, the commanding importance of which we have already considered. Then eighty-one Epistles,(375) some very long, to various bishops, to the clergy and the churches of Africa and of Rome, to the confessors, to the lapsed, &c.; comprising also some letters from others in reply, as from Cornelius of Rome and Firmilian of Caesarea. They give us a very graphic picture of his pastoral labors, and of the whole church life of that day. To the same class belongs also his treatise: De Lapsis (A. D. 250) against loose penitential discipline. (2.) Besides these he wrote a series of moral works, On the Grace of God (246); On the Lord’s Prayer (252); On Mortality (252); against worldly-mindedness and pride of dress in consecrated virgins (De Habitu Virginum); a glowing call to Martyrdom; an exhortation to liberality (De Opere el Eleemosynis, between 254 and 256), with a touch of the "opus operatum" doctrine; and two beautiful tracts written during his controversy with pope Stephanus: De Bono Patienti, and De Zelo et Livore (about 256), in which he exhorts the excited minds to patience and moderation. (3.) Least important are his two apologetic works, the product of his Christian pupilage. One is directed against heathenism (de Idolorum Vanitate), and is borrowed in great part, often verbally, from Tertullian and Minucius Felix. The other, against Judaism (Testimonia adversus Judaeos), also contains no new thoughts, but furnishes a careful collection of Scriptural proofs of the Messiahship and divinity of Jesus. Novatian, the second Roman anti-Pope (Hippolytus being probably the first), orthodox in doctrine, but schismatic in discipline, and in both respects closely resembling Hippolytus and Tertullian, flourished in the middle of the third century and became the founder of a sect called after his name.(376) He was a man of unblemished, though austere character, considerable biblical and philosophical learning, speculative talent, and eloquence.(377) He is moreover, next to Victor and Minucius Felix, the first Roman divine who used the Latin Language, and used it with skill. We may infer that at his time the Latin had become or was fast becoming the ruling language of the Roman church, especially in correspondence with North Africa and the West; yet both Novatian and his rival Cornelius addressed the Eastern bishops in Greek. The epitaphs of five Roman bishops of the third century, Urbanus, Anteros, Fabianus, Lucius, and Eutychianus (between 223 and 283), in the cemetery of Callistus are Greek, but the epitaph of Cornelius (251–253) who probably belonged to the noble Roman family of that name, is Latin ("Cornelius Martyr E. R. X.")(378) At, that time the Roman congregation numbered forty presbyters, seven deacons, seven sub-deacons, forty-two acolytes, besides exorcists, readers and janitors, and an "innumerable multitude of the people," which may have amounted perhaps to about 50,000 members.(379) We know nothing of the time and place of the birth and death of Novatian. He was probably an Italian. The later account of his Phrygian origin deserves no credit, and may have arisen from the fact that he had many followers in Phrygia, where they united with the Montanists. He was converted in adult age, and received only clinical baptism by sprinkling on the sick bed without subsequent episcopal confirmation, but was nevertheless ordained to the priesthood and rose to the highest rank in the Roman clergy. He conducted the official correspondence of the Roman see during the vacancy from the martyrdom of Fabian, January 21, 250, till the election of Cornelius, March, 251. In his letter to Cyprian, written in the name of "the presbyters and deacons abiding at Rome,"(380) he refers the question of the restoration of the lapsed to a future council, but shows his own preference for a strict discipline, as most necessary in peace and in persecution, and as "the rudder of safety in the tempest."(381) He may have aspired to the papal chair to which he seemed to have the best claim. But after the Decian persecution had ceased his rival Cornelius, unknown before, was elected by a majority of the clergy and favored the lenient discipline towards the Fallen which his predecessors Callistus and Zephyrinus had exercised, and against which Hippolytus had so strongly protested twenty or thirty years before. Novatian was elected anti-Pope by a minority and consecrated by three Italian bishops.(382) He was excommunicated by a Roman council, and Cornelius denounced him in official letters as "a deceitful, cunning and savage beast." Both parties appealed to foreign churches. Fabian of Antioch sympathized with Novatian, but Dionysius of Alexandria, and especially Cyprian who in the mean time had relaxed his former rigor and who hated schism like the very pest, supported Cornelius, and the lax and more charitable system of discipline, together with worldly conformity triumphed in the Catholic church. Nevertheless the Novatian schism spread East and West and maintained its severe discipline and orthodox creed in spite of imperial persecution down to the sixth century. Novatian died a martyr according to the tradition of his followers. The controversy turned on the extent of the power of the Keys and the claims of justice to the purity of the church and of mercy towards the fallen. The charitable view prevailed by the aid of the principle that out of the church there is no salvation. Novatian was a fruitful author. Jerome ascribes to him works On the Passover; On the Sabbath; On Circumcision; On the Priest (De Sacerdote); On Prayer; On the Jewish Meats; On Perseverance;(383) On Attilus (a martyr of Pergamus); and "On the Trinity." Two of these books are preserved. The most important is his Liber de Trinitate (31 chs.), composed a.d. 256. It has sometimes been ascribed to Tertullian or Cyprian. Jerome calls it a "great work," and an extract from an unknown work of Tertullian on the same subject. Novatian agrees essentially with Tertullian’s subordination trinitarianism. He ably vindicates the divinity of Christ and of the Holy Spirit, strives to reconcile the divine threeness with unity, and refutes the Monarchians, especially the Sabellians by biblical and philosophical arguments. In his Epistola de Cibus Judaicis (7 chapters) written to his flock from a place of retirement during persecution, he tries to prove by allegorical interpretation, that the Mosaic laws on food are no longer binding upon Christians, and that Christ has substituted temperance and abstinence for the prohibition of unclean animals, with the exception of meat offered to idols, which is forbidden by the Apostolic council (Acts 15). § 201. Commodian was probably a clergyman in North Africa.(384) He was converted from heathenism by the study of the Scriptures, especially of the Old Testament.(385) He wrote about the middle of the third century two works in the style of vulgar African latinity, in uncouth versification and barbarian hexameter, without regard to quantity and hiatus. They are poetically and theologically worthless, but not unimportant for the history of practical Christianity, and reveal under a rude dress with many superstitious notions, an humble and fervent Christian heart. Commodian was a Patripassian in christology and a Chiliast in eschatology. Hence he is assigned by Pope Gelasius to the apocryphal writers. His vulgar African latinity is a landmark in the history of the Latin language and poetry in the transition to the Romance literature of the middle ages. The first poem is entitled "Instructions for the Christian Life," written about a.d. 240 or earlier.(386) It is intended to convert heathens and Jews, and gives also exhortations to catechumens, believers, and penitents. The poem has over twelve hundred verses and is divided into eighty strophes, each of which is an acrostic, the initial letters of the lines composing the title or subject of the section. The first 45 strophes are apologetic, and aimed at the heathen, the remaining 35 are parenetic and addressed to Christians. The first part exhorts unbelievers to repent in view of the impending end of the world, and gives prominence to chiliastic ideas about Antichrist, the return of the Twelve Tribes, the first resurrection, the millennium, and the last judgment. The second part exhorts catechumens and various classes of Christians. The last acrostic which again reminds the reader of the end of the world, is entitled "Nomen Gazaei,"(387) and, if read backwards, gives the name of the author: Commodianus mendicus Christi.(388) The second work which was only brought to light in 1852, is an "Apologetic Poem against Jews and Gentiles," and was written about 249. It exhorts them (like the first part of the "Instructions" to repent without delay in view of the approaching end of the world. It is likewise written in uncouth hexameters and discusses in 47 sections the doctrine of God, of man, and of the Redeemer (vers. 89–275); the meaning of the names of Son and Father in the economy of salvation (276–573); the obstacles to the progress of Christianity(574–611); it warns Jews and Gentiles to forsake their religion (612–783), and gives a description of the last things (784–1053). The most interesting part of this second poem is the conclusion. It contains a fuller description of Antichrist than the first poem. The author expects that the end of the world will soon come with the seventh persecution; the Goths will conquer Rome and redeem the Christians; but then Nero will appear as the heathen Antichrist, reconquer Rome, and rage against the Christians three years and a-half; he will be conquered in turn by the Jewish and real Antichrist from the east, who after the defeat of Nero and the burning of Rome will return to Judaea, perform false miracles, and be worshipped by the Jews. At last Christ appears, that is God himself (from the Monarchian standpoint of the author), with the lost Twelve Tribes as his army, which had lived beyond Persia in happy simplicity and virtue; under astounding phenomena of nature he will conquer Antichrist and his host, convert all nations and take possession of the holy city of Jerusalem. The concluding description of the judgment is preserved only in broken fragments. The idea of a double Antichrist is derived from the two beasts of the Apocalypse, and combines the Jewish conception of the Antimessiah, and the heathen Nero-legend. But the remarkable feature is that the second Antichrist is represented as a Jew and as defeating the heathen Nero, as he will be defeated by Christ. Arnobius, a successful teacher of rhetoric with many pupils (Lactantius being one of them), was first an enemy, then an advocate of Christianity. He lived in Sicca, an important city on the Numidian border to the Southwest of Carthage, in the latter part of the third and the beginning of the fourth century . He was converted to Christ in adult age, like his more distinguished fellow-Africans, Tertullian and Cyprian. "O blindness," he says, in describing the great change, "only a short time ago I was worshipping images just taken from the forge, gods shaped upon the anvil and by the hammer .... When I saw a stone made smooth and smeared with oil, I prayed to it and addressed it as if a living power dwelt in it, and implored blessings from the senseless stock. And I offered grievious insult even to the gods, whom I took to be such, in that I considered them wood, stone, and bone, or fancied that they dwelt in the stuff of such things. Now that I have been led by so great a teacher into the way of truth, I know what all that is, I think worthily of the Worthy, offer no insult to the Godhead, and give every one his due .... Is Christ, then, not to be regarded as God? And is He who in other respects may be deemed the very greatest, not to be honored with divine worship, from whom we have received while alive so great gifts, and from whom, when the day comes we expect greater gifts?"(390) The contrast was very startling indeed, if we remember that Sicca bore the epithet "Veneria," as the seat of the vile worship of the goddess of lust in whose temple the maidens sacrificed their chastity, like the Corinthian priestesses of Aphrodite. He is therefore especially severe in his exposure of the sexual immoralities of the heathen gods, among whom Jupiter himself takes the lead in all forms of vice.(391) We know nothing of his subsequent life and death. Jerome, the only ancient writer who mentions him, adds some doubtful particulars, namely that he was converted by visions or dreams, that he was first refused admission to the Church by the bishop of Sicca, and hastily wrote his apology in proof of his sincerity. But this book, though written soon after his conversion, is rather the result of an inward impulse and strong conviction than outward occasion. We have from him an Apology of Christianity in seven books of unequal length, addressed to the Gentiles. It was written a.d. 303,(392) at the outbreak of the Diocletian persecution; for he alludes to the tortures, the burning of the sacred Scriptures and the destruction of the meeting houses, which were the prominent features of that persecution.(393) It is preserved in only one manuscript (of the ninth or tenth century), which contains also the "Octavius" of Minucius Felix.(394) The first two books are apologetic, the other five chiefly polemic. Arnobius shows great familiarity with Greek and Roman mythology and literature, and quotes freely from Homer, Plato, Cicero, and Varro. He ably refutes the objections to Christianity, beginning with the popular charge that it brought the wrath of the gods and the many public calamities upon the Roman empire. He exposes at length the absurdities and immoralities of the heathen mythology. He regards the gods as real, but evil beings. The positive part is meagre and unsatisfactory. Arnobius seems as ignorant about the Bible as Minucius Felix. He never quotes the Old Testament, and the New Testament only once.(395) He knows nothing of the history of the Jews, and the Mosaic worship, and confounds the Pharisees and Sadducees. Yet be is tolerably familiar, whether from the Gospels or from tradition, with the history of Christ. He often refers in growing language to his incarnation, crucifixion, and exaltation. He represents him as the supreme teacher who revealed God to man, the giver of eternal life, yea, as God, though born a man, as God on high, God in his inmost nature, as the Saviour God, and the object of worship.(396) Only his followers can be saved, but he offers salvation even to his enemies. His divine mission is proved by his miracles, and these are attested by their unique character, their simplicity, publicity and beneficence. He healed at once a hundred or more afflicted with various diseases, he stilled the raging tempest, he walked over the sea with unwet foot, he astonished the very waves, he fed five thousand with five loaves, and filled twelve baskets with the fragments that remained, he called the dead from the tomb. He revealed himself after the resurrection "in open day to countless numbers of men;" "he appears even now to righteous men of unpolluted mind who love him, not in any dreams, but in a form of pure simplicity."(397) His doctrine of God is Scriptural, and strikingly contrasts with the absurd mythology. God is the author and ruler of all things, unborn, infinite, spiritual, omnipresent, without passion, dwelling in light, the giver of all good, the sender of the Saviour. As to man, Arnobius asserts his free will, but also his ignorance and sin, and denies his immortality. The soul outlives the body but depends solely on God for the gift of eternal duration. The wicked go to the fire of Gehenna, and will ultimately be consumed or annihilated. He teaches the resurrection of the flesh, but in obscure terms. Arnobius does not come up to the standard of Catholic orthodoxy, even of the ante-Nicene age. Considering his apparent ignorance of the Bible, and his late conversion, we need not be surprised at this. Jerome now praises, now censures him, as unequal, prolix, and confused in style, method, and doctrine. Pope Gelasius in the fifth century banished his book to the apocryphal index, and since that time it was almost forgotten, till it was brought to light again in the sixteenth century. Modern critics agree in the verdict that he is more successful in the refutation of error than in the defense of truth. But the honesty, courage, and enthusiasm of the convert for his new faith are as obvious as the defects of his theology. If be did not know or clearly understand the doctrines of the Bible, be seized its moral tone.(398) "We have learned," he says, "from Christ’s teaching and his laws, that evil ought not to be requited with evil (comp. Matt. 5:39), that it is better to suffer wrong than to inflict it, that we should rather shed our own blood than stain our hands and our conscience with that of another. An ungrateful world is now for a long period enjoying the benefit of Christ; for by his influence the rage of savage ferocity has been softened, and restrained from the blood of a fellow-creature. If all would lend an ear to his salutary and peaceful laws, the world would turn the use of steel to occupations of peace, and live in blessed harmony, maintaining inviolate the sanctity of treaties."(399) He indignantly asks the heathen, "Why have our writings deserved to be given to the flames, and our meetings to be cruelly broken up? In them prayer is offered to the supreme God, peace and pardon are invoked upon all in authority, upon soldiers, kings, friends, enemies, upon those still in life, and those released from the bondage of the flesh. In them all that is said tends to make men humane, gentle, modest, virtuous, chaste, generous in dealing with their substance, and inseparably united to all that are embraced in our brotherhood."(400) He uttered his testimony boldly in the face of the last and most cruel persecution, and it is not unlikely that he himself was one of its victims. Victorinus, probably of Greek extraction, was first a rhetorician by profession, and became bishop of Petavium, or Petabio,(401) in ancient Panonia (Petau, in the present Austrian Styria). He died a martyr in the Diocletian persecution (303). We have only fragments of his writings, and they are not of much importance, except for the age to which they belong. Jerome says that he understood Greek better than Latin, and that his works are excellent for the sense, but mean as to the style. He counts him among the Chiliasts, and ascribes to him commentaries on Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Isaiah, Ezekiel, Habakkuk, Canticles, the Apocalypse, a book Against all Heresies, "et multa alia." Several poems are also credited to him, but without good reason.(402) The fragment on the Creation of the World is a series of notes on the account of creation, probably a part of the commentary on Genesis mentioned by Jerome. The days are taken liberally. The creation of angels and archangels preceded the creation of man, as light was made before the sky and the earth. The seven days typify seven millennia; the seventh is the millennial sabbath, when Christ will reign on earth with his elect. It is the same chiliastic notion which we found in the Epistle of Barnabas, with the same opposition to Jewish sabbatarianism. Victorinus compares the seven days with the seven eyes of the Lord (Zech. 4:10), the seven heavens (comp. Ps. 33:6), the seven spirits that dwelt in Christ (Isa. 11:2, 3), and the seven stages of his humanity: his nativity, infancy, boyhood, youth, young-manhood, mature age, death. This is a fair specimen of these allegorical plays of a pious imagination. The scholia on the Apocalypse of John are not without interest for the history of the interpretation of this mysterious book.(403) But they are not free from later interpolations of the fifth or sixth century. The author assigns the Apocalypse to the reign of Domitian (herein agreeing with Irenaeus), and combines the historical and allegorical methods of interpretation. He also regards the visions in part as synchronous rather than successive. He comments only on the more difficult passages.(404) We select the most striking points. The woman in ch. 12 is the ancient church of the prophets and apostles; the dragon is the devil. The woman sitting on the seven hills (in ch. 17), is the city of Rome. The beast from the abyss is the Roman empire; Domitian is counted as the sixth, Nerva as the seventh, and Nero revived as the eighth Roman King.(405) The number 666 (13:18) means in Greek Teitan(406) (this is the explanation preferred by Irenaeus), in Latin Diclux. Both names signify Antichrist, according to the numerical value of the Greek and Roman letters. But Diclux has this meaning by contrast, for Antichrist, "although he is cut off from the supernal light, yet transforms himself into an angel of light, daring to call himself light."(407) To this curious explanation is added, evidently by a much later hand, an application of the mystic number to the Vandal king Genseric (genshvriko") who in the fifth century laid waste the Catholic church of North Africa and sacked the city of Rome. The exposition of ch. 20:1–6 is not so strongly chiliastic, as the corresponding passage in the Commentary on Genesis, and hence some have denied the identity of authorship. The first resurrection is explained spiritually with reference to Col. 3:1, and the author leaves it optional to understand the thousand years as endless or as limited. Then he goes on to allegorize about the numbers: ten signifies the decalogue, and hundred the crown of virginity; for he who keeps the vow of virginity completely, and fulfils the precepts of the decalogue, and destroys the impure thoughts within the retirement of his own heart, is the true priest of Christ, and reigns with him; and "truly in his case the devil is bound." At the close of the notes on ch. 22, the author rejects the crude and sensual chiliasm of the heretic Cerinthus. "For the kingdom of Christ," he says, "is now eternal in the saints, although the glory of the saints shall be manifested after the resurrection."(408) This looks like a later addition, and intimates the change which Constantine’s reign produced in the mind of the church as regards the millennium. At the close of our period we meet with three representative divines, in close connection with the first Christian emperor who effected the politico-ecclesiastical revolution known as the union of church and state. Their public life and labors belong to the next period, but must at least be briefly foreshadowed here. Eusebius, the historian, Lactantius, the rhetorician, and Hosius, the statesman, form the connecting links between the ante-Nicene and Nicene ages; their long lives—two died octogenarians, Hosius a centenarian—are almost equally divided between the two; and they reflect the lights and shades of both.(410) Eusebius was bishop of Caesarea and a man of extensive and useful learning, and a liberal theologian; Lactantius, a professor of eloquence in Nicomedia, and a man of elegant culture; Hosius, bishop of Cordova and a man of counsel and action.(411) They thus respectively represented the Holy Land, Asia Minor, and Spain; we may add Italy and North Africa, for Lactantius was probably a native Italian and a pupil of Arnobius of Sicca, and Hosius acted to some extent for the whole western church in Eastern Councils. With him Spain first emerges from the twilight of legend to the daylight of church history; it was the border land of the west which Paul perhaps had visited, which had given the philosopher Seneca and the emperor Trajan to heathen Rome, and was to furnish in Theodosius the Great the strong defender of the Nicene faith. Eusebius, Lactantius, and Hosius were witnesses of the cruelties of the Diocletian persecution, and hailed the reign of imperial patronage. They carried the moral forces of the age of martyrdom into the age of victory. Eusebius with his literary industry saved for us the invaluable monuments of the first three centuries down to the Nicene Council; Lactantius bequeathed to posterity, in Ciceronian Latin, an exposition and vindication of the Christian religion against the waning idolatry of Greece and Rome, and the tragic memories of the imperial persecutors; Hosius was the presiding genius of the synods of Elvira (306), Nicaea (325), and Sardica (347), the friend of Athanasius in the defense of orthodoxy and in exile. All three were intimately associated with Constantine the Great, Eusebius as his friend and eulogist, Lactantius as the tutor of his eldest son, Hosius as his trusted counsellor who probably suggested to him the idea of convening the first œcumenical synod; he was we may say for a few years his ecclesiastical prime minister. They were, each in his way, the emperor’s chief advisers and helpers in that great change which gave to the religion of the cross the moral control over the vast empire of Rome. The victory was well deserved by three hundred years of unjust persecution and heroic endurance, but it was fraught with trials and temptations no less dangerous to the purity and peace of the church than fire and sword. The Phoenix was a favorite symbol of renovation and resurrection, and even of Christ himself, among the early Christians, and appears frequently on coins, medals, rings, cups, and tombstones. But in this point they were no more superstitious than the most intelligent heathen contemporaries. Herodotus heard the marvelous story of the burial of the parent bird by the offspring from Egyptian priests, II. 73. Ovid and other Latin poets refer to it, and Claudian devotes a poem to it. Tacitus (Ann. VI. 28), Pliny ) H. Nat. X. 2), and Dion Cassius LVIII. 27) record that the Phoenix actually reappeared in Egypt, a.d. 34, after In interval of 250 years. According to Pliny the bird was also brought to Rome by a decree of Claudius, and exhibited in the comitium, in the year of the city 800 (A. D. 47). This, of course, was a fraud, but many, and among them probably Clement, who may have seen the wonderful bird from Egypt at the time, took it for genuine. But an inspired writer like Paul would never have made use of such a heathen fable as an argument for a Christian truth. "It is now known," says Lightfoot."that the story owes its origin to the symbolic and pictorial representations of astronomy. The appearance of the phoenix is the recurrence of a period marked by the heliacal rising of some prominent star or constellation." From the title "Verissimus, " which Marcus Aurelius ceased to bear after his adoption by Antonine in 138, and from the absence of the title "Caesar" which he received in 139, the older critics have inferred that it must have been written shortly after the death of Hadrian (137), and Eusebius, in the Chronicon, assigns it to 141. The early date is strengthened by the fact that in the Dialogue, which was written after the Apologies, the Bar-Cochba war (132-135) is represented as still going on, or at all events as recent (fugw;n to;n nu'n genovmenon povlemon, ex bello nostra aetate profugus, ch. I; Comp. ch. 9). But, on the other hand, Marcus Aurelius was not really associated as co-regent with Antonine till 147, and in the book itself Tustin seems to imply two regents. Lucius Verus, moreover, was born 130, and could not well be addressed in his eighth year as "philosopher; " Eusebius, however, reads "Son of the philosopher Caesar; " and the term filovsofo" was used in a very wide sense. Of more weight is the fact that the first Apology was written after the Syntagma against Marcion, who flourished in Rome between 139-145, though this chronology, too, is not quite certain. Justin says that he was writing 150 years after the birth of the Saviour; if this is not simply a round number, it helps to fix the date. He has prepared the light that none can approach unto, but he has also prepared the vast and eternal gloom of perpetual night." At the close be favors an exception in case of impending death of the penitent lapsed, to whom cautious help should be administered, "that neither ungodly men should praise our smooth facility, nor truly penitent men accuse our severity as cruel." This letter relieves Novatian of the reproach of being chiefly influenced in his schism by personal motives, as Pope Cornelius (Euseb. VI. 43), and Roman historians maintain (also Harnack, in Herzog X. 661). (382; original 1565): "Ex exigna et vilissima Italiae parte." See Jaffé Regesta Pontif. Rom. p. 7. Cornelius, in his letter to Fabian (Euseb. In the last section of his second poem lie calls himself Gazaeus. Ebert understands this geographically, from the city of Gaza in Syria. But in this case he would have written in Greek or in Syriac. The older interpretation is preferable, from Gaza (gavza), treasure, or gazophylacium (gazofulavkion)treasury, which indicates either his possession of the treasure of saving truth or his dependence for support on the treasury of the church. II. 215 sqq. It begins with this noble sentence: "I was a confessor of the faith long before your grandfather Maximian persecuted the church. If you persecute me, I am ready to suffer all rather than to shed innocent blood and to betray the truth." Unfortunately, in his extreme old age he yielded under the infliction of physical violence, and subscribed an Arian creed, but bitterly repented before his death. Athanasius expressly says (l. c. 45), that "at the approach of death, as it were by his last testament, he abjured the Arian heresy, and gave strict charge that no one should receive it." It is a disputed point whether he died at Sirmium in 357, or was permitted to return to Spain, and died there about 359 or 360. Iacobus Beurer) 对若干段落之解释与校订的意见；并收游斯丁门徒塔提安 (Tatian) 的若干作品。亨利库斯·斯特法努斯印行，1592年。斯蒂芬斯 (Stephens) 的抄本至今仍藏于莱顿大学图书馆。博伊勒的抄本已经遗失，但很可能抄自斯特拉斯堡抄本 (Strassburg Codex)，因为斯蒂芬斯在附录中、叙尔堡 (Sylburg) 在注释中所刊出的博伊勒抄本异读，都与该抄本一致。↩︎ “Epistulae ad Diognetum unum tantummodo exemplar antiquius ad nostram usque pervenit memoriam: codicem dico loannis Reuchlini quondam, postea Argentoratensem, qui misero illo incendio die nono ante Calendas Septembres anni MDCCCLXX cum tot aliis libris pretiosis in ciner es dilapsus est.”即：“《致丢格那妥书》只有一个较古老的抄本流传到我们这一代；我所说的，就是原属约翰内斯·罗伊希林 (Ioannes Reuchlin)、后来归斯特拉斯堡所有的抄本。它在1870年8月24日那场惨痛的火灾中，与许多其他珍贵书籍一同化为灰烬。”冯·格布哈特 (Von Gebhardt) 与哈纳克 (Harnack)，第205页。他们在第208页断言，斯蒂芬斯和博伊勒的抄本都抄自斯特拉斯堡抄本。奥托 (Otto) 在《绪论》Prol. 第3页说有“tres codices, Argentoratensis, apographon Stephani, apoqraphon Beureri”，即三个抄本：斯特拉斯堡本、斯蒂芬斯抄本和博伊勒抄本。↩︎ 比较《致丢格那妥书》Ep. ad Diog., 第1章与马可·奥勒留 (Marcus Aurelius)《沉思录》Medit., IX. 3（这是他唯一一次提及基督教，已引于第329页）。马可·奥勒留在《沉思录》Medit., I. 6中怀着感激追念他的老师丢格那妥 (Diognetus)。丢格那妥并不是罕见的名字；不过，本书信的收信人是一位社会地位显赫的人，κράτιστος*（honorable，尊贵的）这一称呼便表明了这一点。奥托和埃瓦尔德 (Ewald) 认定两者是同一人。凯姆 (Keim) 和德雷泽克 (Dräseke，第141页) 承认本书信中的丢格那妥属于宫廷，但认为他的年代较晚。↩︎ 埃瓦尔德 (Ewald) 在《以色列民族史》Geschichte des Volkes Israel, 第VII卷，第150页，将它列为所有未收入新约的早期基督教书信之首，并说它完美地结合了“希腊雄辩的丰赡与技巧，以及最纯粹的爱真理之心；措辞的从容优雅，以及基督徒那令人振奋的庄严认真”。本生 (Bunsen) 说：“无可争议，除圣经之外，这是健全的基督徒情感、高贵的勇气和刚健雄辩最优美的丰碑。”塞米施 (Semisch，在赫尔措格百科全书中) 称它为“ein Kleinod des christl. Joh)，第972–982页（第2版）；以及布莱克 (Bleek)，《启示录讲义》(Vorlesungen über die Apok.)，第34页及下页。吕克 (Lücke) 和布莱克都认为这部注释出自维克托里努斯 (Victorinus)，但含有后人插入的文字。布莱克认为，其原本的千禧年主义色彩更为鲜明。↩︎ 正如卡西奥多鲁斯 (Cassiodorus) 所说：“Difficillima quaedam loca breviter tractavit.”（他简要地论述了某些极难的段落。）↩︎ 对17:10、11的这一解释，是建立在尼禄 (Nero) 将作为敌基督重返世间的期待之上；后来安德烈 (Andreas) 和阿瑞塔斯 (Arethas) 有充分理由将其弃置，但近代支持尼禄假说的人又使之复兴，只是对皇帝的计数方式不同。参见第I卷，第864页及后的讨论。↩︎ T=300；E=5；I=10；T=300；A=1；N=50；合计666。去掉末尾的 n，便得到 Teita=616，这是爱任纽 (Irenaeus) 所提及的13:18的另一异读。提图斯 (Titus) 毁灭了耶路撒冷，但他是在不自觉中应验了基督的预言；他并未逼迫教会，而且是罗马皇帝中最贤明者之一。↩︎ D=500；I=1；C=100；L=50；V=5；X=10；合计=666。“Id est quod Graece sonat τειτάν* id quod Latine dicitur diclux, quo nomine per antiphrasin expresso intelligimus antichrstum, qui cum a luce superna abscissus sit et ea privatus, transfigurat tamen se in angelum lucis audens sese dicere lucem. Item invenimus in quodom codice, Graeco ἄντεμος*。”（也就是说，希腊文所称的这个名字，在拉丁文中称为 diclux；我们将这个以反语表达的名字理解为敌基督。他虽与天上的光隔绝，并被剥夺了这光，却仍装作光明的天使，胆敢自称为光。我们还在某一希腊文抄本中发现了另一个名字。）最后这个名字或许是 Ἄντειμος* 的讹写；后者见于默西亚 (Moesia) 的钱币，用来称呼一个统治王朝；也可能意在描述一种品性：honori contrarius（与尊荣相反）。参见米涅，V. 339，以及吕克，第978页。↩︎ “Nam regnum Christi nunc est sempiternum in sanctis, cum fuerit gloria post resurrectionem manifestata sanctorum.”（因为基督的国如今在圣徒中是永远的，待圣徒复活之后，荣耀便要显明。）（米涅 V. 344。）↩︎ 比较§188，第612页及后。↩︎ 优西比乌卒于公元340年；拉克坦提乌 (Lactantius) 卒于320至330年之间；何西乌 (Hosius) 卒于357至360年之间。↩︎ 何西乌没有留下著作。我们所拥有的唯一出自他手笔的文献，是他致阿里乌派皇帝君士坦提乌 (Constantius) 的信，由亚他那修 (Athanasius) 保存下来（《阿里乌派史》〔Hist. Arian.〕，44）。参见盖恩斯 (Gains)，前引书，II. 215及后。此信以这句高尚的话开头：“早在你的祖父马克西米安 (Maximian) 逼迫教会以前很久，我就已是信仰的宣认者。你若逼迫我，我宁愿忍受一切，也不愿流无辜人的血，背叛真理。”不幸的是，他在极其衰老之年，因遭受身体上的暴力而屈服，签署了一份阿里乌派信经，但临终前深深痛悔。亚他那修明确说（前引书，45）：“在死亡临近时，他仿佛以最后遗嘱的形式，弃绝了阿里乌派异端，并严命任何人都不可接受它。”他究竟于357年死在西尔米乌姆 (Sirmium)，还是获准返回西班牙，并于约359年或360年在那里去世，仍有争议。我们只知道，他活了一百多岁，担任主教六十多年。亚他那修，前引书；苏尔皮基乌斯·塞韦鲁斯 (Sulpicius Severus)，《历史》(Hist.)，II. 55。↩︎

title: 《基督教会史》·第二卷·第十二章 大公神学在与异端的冲突中的发展
text: Translated from Philip Schaff's History of The Christian Church 第十二章 大公神学在与异端的冲突中的发展 目录 § 137. 大公正统信仰 § 138. 圣经与正典 § 139. 大公教会的传统 § 140. 信仰准则与《使徒信经》 § 141. 《使徒信经》的异文 § 142. 上帝与创造 § 143. 人与堕落 § 144. 基督与道成肉身 § 145. 基督的神性 § 146. 基督的人性 § 147. 基督里面神性与人性的关系 § 148. 圣灵 § 149. 三位一体 § 150. 反三位一体论者。第一类：阿洛吉派、狄奥多图、阿尔特蒙、撒摩撒他的保罗 § 151. 第二类反三位一体论者：普拉克西亚、诺埃图、卡利斯图、贝吕鲁 § 152. 撒伯流主义 § 153. 救赎 § 154. 其他教义 § 155. 末世论：不朽与复活 § 156. 死亡与复活之间 § 157. 审判之后：将来的刑罚 § 158. 千年国论 § 137. 大公正统信仰 I. 史料：尼西亚会议以前诸教父的教义与论战著作，尤其是殉道者游斯丁 (Justin Martyr)、爱任纽 (Irenaeus)、希坡吕托斯 (Hippolytus)、德尔图良 (Tertullian)、居普良 (Cyprian)、亚历山大的革利免 (Clement of Alex.) 和奥利金 (Origen) 的著作。 文献：佩特拉维乌斯 (Petravius)、明舍尔 (Münscher)、尼安德 (Neander)、吉斯勒 (Giesler)、鲍尔 (Baur)、哈根巴赫 (Hagenbach)、谢德 (Shedd)、尼奇 (Nitzsch)、哈纳克 (Harnack) 的教义史著作中的相关章节（哈纳克的第一卷出版于1886年；第2版，1888年）。 约斯·施瓦内 (Jos. Schwane，罗马天主教)：《尼西亚会议以前的教义史》(Dogmengeschichte der vornicänischen Zeit.)。明斯特 (Münster)，1862年。 埃德姆·德·普雷桑塞 (Edm. De Pressensé)：《异端与基督教教义》(Heresy and Christian Doctrine,)，安妮·哈伍德 (Annie Harwood) 译。伦敦 (Lond.)，1873年。 专题文献见下文。另参第十三章所列文献。 上一章所述广泛流传的谬误，向教会发起了一场强大的思想挑战；教会终于得胜而出，正如她的主所应许的，圣灵要引导她进入一切真理。面对异端分子主观、无根而又变动不居的臆测、梦想和虚构，教会以神圣启示中充实而坚固的实在与之抗衡。基督教神学的成长，固然出于信仰对知识的要求，仿佛是一种内在的必然；但异端，尤其是诺斯替主义 (Gnosticism)，却从外面给了它强大的推动，如同一场使田地肥沃的雷雨。教会从起初就在信仰的经验和圣经中拥有真理，并以一丝不苟的忠实，将圣经世代相传。但如今的任务，是以理论的形式阐发基督教真理的实质1，从各方面加以巩固，并清楚地呈现在理智面前。因此，基督教的论战神学与教义神学，亦即教会对救恩教义的逻辑理解，便在这场与异端的冲突中发展起来；正如护教文献与殉道，是在犹太人和异教徒的逼迫之下产生的一样。 从此以后，大公信仰与异端、正统与异说、教会的信仰与持异议的个人意见之间的区别，便日益显著。凡与圣经和教会信仰相合的教义，都被接纳为大公的，也就是普世的，并排除其他教义的。2凡在实质上偏离这一标准的，每一种由这个或那个人任意构成的观念，每一种对基督教启示教义的歪曲或败坏，以及每一种背离教会共同信念的主张，都被视为异端。3 几乎所有教父都起来反对当时的异端，运用圣经中的论据、教会的传统以及理性的论证，证明这些异端内在的矛盾与荒谬。 但在这样做的时候，他们虽然在精神和目的上是一致的，却采取了两条迥然不同的道路；这取决于希腊与罗马民族特性的差别、心智结构的特点，以及上帝护理的安排。希腊神学，尤其是以革利免和奥利金为代表的亚历山大神学，主要是理念性和思辨性的，所探讨的是上帝、道成肉身、三位一体以及基督论等客观教义；它力求以真正的知识，即建立在基督教信仰 (pistis) 之上的正统哲学，来取代虚假的灵知 (gnosis)。它的逻各斯 (Logos) 教义深受柏拉图式思辨的影响。拉丁神学，尤其是以德尔图良和居普良为最杰出代表的北非神学，则更为务实而注重实践，关切人性与救恩的教义，也更直接地敌视诺斯替主义和哲学。与此相关的是，希腊教父最初是哲学家，而拉丁教父多为法学家和政治家；前者通过思辨的道路达到基督教信仰，后者则本着实践道德的精神归信。同样具有特色的是，希腊教会主要以使徒约翰这位卓越的默想型“神学家”为根基；拉丁教会则以教会务实的领袖彼得为根基。亚历山大的革利免和奥利金常常游离到朦胧而近乎诺斯替主义的思辨之中，几乎要把基督教观念的真实内涵化解成稀薄的唯灵论；德尔图良却毫不妥协地反对诺斯替主义及其所依据的异教哲学。他问道：“雅典与耶路撒冷、学园与教会、异端分子与基督徒，有什么相交呢？”然而，这种差别只是相对的。亚历山大学派虽然具有种种唯灵论倾向，却仍拘守一种惊人的字面解释；而德尔图良尽管厌恶哲学，却致力于深刻的思辨观念，这些观念到奥古斯丁 (Augustin) 那里才得到充分发展。 爱任纽出身于东方教会，使用希腊语，却在西方工作；他在教会这两个分支之间，处于某种居间调和的地位。总的说来，可以把他视为尼西亚会议以前教会正统信仰最为温和而健全的代表。他反对诺斯替主义，与德尔图良同样坚决，却没有忽视这一体系所流露出的思辨需要。他在177至192年间写成的反驳灵知的著作4，是第二世纪最重要的论战著作。在第一卷中，爱任纽详尽介绍了瓦伦廷派 (Valentinian) 的灵知体系；第二卷开始用哲学与逻辑的方法予以反驳；第三卷则以大公传统和圣经抗衡这一体系，维护关于上帝独一、世界受造、逻各斯道成肉身的正统教义，反对幻影说 (Docetism) 对基督真实人性的否认，以及伊便尼派 (Ebionites) 对他真实神性的否认；第四卷进一步巩固这些教义，并针对马吉安学派 (school of Marcion) 的反律法主义，论证新旧约的一致性；第五卷也是最后一卷，阐述他关于末世论的见解，尤其是身体复活这一极为诺斯替唯灵论所厌恶的教义，最后论及敌基督、世界的终结、中间状态和千禧年。 他的门徒希坡吕托斯在《哲学论辩》(Philosophumena) 中，就早期异端在许多方面给了我们更为详尽的记述，并追溯它们在异教哲学体系中的根源，但对于教会大公教义的阐释，却不及他深入。 这些论战文献的主要努力，自然是在正面阐发并确立基督教真理；这同时也是对相反谬误最有效的驳斥。其目的，尤其在于确定信仰准则、上帝道成肉身，以及基督真实的神性与真实的人性等教义。在这一努力中，教会的心智不断受到上帝圣言和使徒传统的引导，以不致迷误的直觉，航行于险峻的礁崖之间。然而，在对这些要点的系统理解和表述上，仍有不少不确定和模糊之处。而且在这个风雨飘摇的时代，尚无大公会议，能够以全教会的声音裁定教义争论。三位一体和基督位格的教义，直到下一个时期，即尼西亚时期，才臻于成熟，并获得最终的信经界定。 关于异端的附注 异端一词源于 αἵρεσις*，原意或为捕获（来自 αἱρέω*），或为选取、选择（来自 αἱρέομαι*），后来又附加了任意反对公共意见与权威的意思。在新约中，它指一种所选择的生活方式、一个学派、宗派或党派，未必含有贬义；它被用来称法利赛人、撒都该人，甚至用来将基督徒称为犹太教的一个宗派（《使徒行传》5:17；15:5；24:5、14；26:5；28:22）；其次，它表示意见分歧所引起的不和（《加拉太书》5:20；《哥林多前书》11:19）；最后，它表示谬误（《彼得后书》2:1，αἱρέσεις ἀπωλείας*，即毁灭性的异端，或走向灭亡的宗派）。这最后一处最接近教会所下的定义。异端分子（αἱρετικὸς ἄνθρωπος*）一词只出现过一次，见《提多书》3:10，其意思是好结党的人、宗派分子、党人，而不主要是持谬见者。 君士坦丁大帝 (Constantine the Great) 仍把基督教会称为一个宗派，ἡ αἵρεσις ἡ καθολική, ἡ ἁγιωτάτη αἵρεσις*（见他致叙拉古主教克雷斯图斯 [Chrestus, bishop of Syracuse] 的信，载优西比乌 [Eusebius]《教会史》[H. E.] X卷，第5章，§ 21、22，海尼兴 [Heinichen] 版，第I卷，第491页）。但在他以后，教会与宗派便成了对立的概念：前者只用于那唯一居统治地位的团体，后者则用于持异议的少数派。 教父通常以异端指与大公教义相反的错误教导，以分裂指与大公教会治理相反的纪律破坏。古代的异端研究者——他们虽诚实虔敬，却大多缺乏批判眼光，轻信而偏执，是狭隘正统信仰的狂热维护者——将异端的范围扩展到基督教之外，又把所有变体和差异分别计数，从而不合理地增加了异端的数目。布雷西亚 (Brescia)，又名布里克西亚 (Brixia) 的主教菲拉斯特里乌斯或菲拉斯特鲁斯 (Philastrius or Philastrus，卒于387年)，在《论异端》(Liber de Haeresibus,) 中列举了28种犹太异端和128种基督教异端；塞浦路斯的埃皮法尼乌斯 (Epiphanius of Cyprus，卒于403年) 在《药箱》(Πανάριον*) 中总共列出80种异端，其中20种在基督以前，60种在基督以后；奥古斯丁（卒于430年）列出88种基督教异端，包括伯拉纠主义 (Pelagianism)；《预定论者》(Proedestinatus) 列出90种，包括伯拉纠主义和聂斯托利主义 (Nestorianism)。（教皇庇护九世 [Pius IX] 在1864年的《谬误表》[Syllabus of Errors] 中，谴责了80种现代异端。）奥古斯丁说，要给异端下定义，是“完全不可能的，或者无论如何也是极其困难的”；他又明智地补充说，构成异端的，与其说是谬误本身，不如说是人坚持谬误时所抱的精神。谬误有无辜的，也有应当归罪的。此外，许多人比他们所信的信条或不持信条的立场更好，也有许多人比他们所信的信条更坏，无论那信条多么正统。我们的主最严厉的话，正是针对法利赛人假冒为善的正统信仰。随着时间推移，异端被界定为：在真理已由教会以权威方式加以界定并宣告之后，仍故意而执拗地坚持与之相反的宗教谬误；或曰，“pertinax defensio dogmatis ecclesiae universalis judicio condemnati”，即“顽固地维护那经普世教会裁决所谴责的教义”。对神学上尚无定论的问题所作的思辨，并不是异端。奥利金在他自己的时代并不是异端分子，却在死后很久才遭到定罪。 在基督教世界目前分裂的状况下，正统与异端各有不同的种类。正统是符合公认的信经或公开教义的准则；异端则是故意偏离这些准则。希腊教会将罗马教会关于教皇制度、圣灵双重发出、童贞女马利亚无原罪始胎以及教皇无误的教义斥为异端，因为这些教义违反前七次大公会议的教导。罗马教会在特伦托会议 (Council of Trent) 上，将新教宗教改革的一切特有教义都加以咒诅。另一方面，福音派新教徒则把希腊教会和罗马教会那些不合圣经的传统视为异端。新教各教会之间又有较小的教义分歧；各教会持守这些不同见解时，其排他或宽容的程度，因其偏离罗马天主教会的程度而异。例如，路德 (Luther) 不肯容忍茨温利 (Zwingli) 对圣餐的看法，而茨温利却愿意不顾这一分歧，与他以弟兄相交。路德宗的《协同信条》(Formula of Concord) 和加尔文派的多特会议 (Synod of Dort)，曾拒绝并谴责一些教义，而如今在正统的福音派教会中，持守这些教义却不受惩处。正统的危险在于走向排他而缺乏爱心的偏执，使真理变得狭隘；自由主义的危险则在于走向松弛与漠不关心，抹煞真理与谬误之间永恒的区别。 使徒受超乎人类智慧的引导，并赋有超乎教会的权柄，因此对一切在根本上偏离所启示之救恩真理的行为，都作了严厉的判断。保罗咒诅那些犹太化的教师，因为他们把割礼作为取得真正教会成员资格的条件（《加拉太书》1:8）；他又讥讽地称他们为“犬类”、行“妄自行割”的人（《腓立比书》3:2，βλέπετε τοὺς κύνας ... τῆς κατατομῆς*）。他警告以弗所的长老，他离开以后，将有“凶暴的豺狼”（λύκοι βαρεῖς*）进入他们中间（《使徒行传》20:29）；又把当时兴起、冒称为知识的灵知（ψευδώνυμος* γνῶσις*）之种种思辨，称为“鬼魔的道理”（διδασκαλίαι δαιμονίων*，《提摩太前书》4:1；比较6:3–20；《提摩太后书》3:1及下文；4:3及下文）。约翰也同样恳切而严厉地警告人，要防备一切否认道成肉身这一事实的假教师，并称他们为敌基督（《约翰一书》4:3；《约翰二书》7）；《彼得后书》和《犹大书》则以最阴暗的色彩描绘异端分子。 因此，尼西亚会议以前的教父极端憎恶当时的诺斯替派异端分子，称他们为撒但的仆役、人形的野兽、致命毒药的贩卖者、强盗和海盗，我们也就不必惊讶了。坡旅甲 (Polycarp，《致腓立比人书》[Ad Phil.] 第7章)、伊格那修 (Ignatius，《致士每拿人书》[Ad Smyrn.] 第4章)、殉道者游斯丁 (Justin M.，《护教篇》[Apol.] I，第26章)、爱任纽 (Irenaeus，《驳异端》[Adv. Haer.] III，第3、4章)、希波吕托斯 (Hippolytus)、德尔图良 (Tertullian)，甚至亚历山大的革利免 (Clement of Alexandria) 和奥利金 (Origen)，在对异端毫不妥协的敌对态度上，与尼西亚时期及其后各时期的教父，基本上持相同立场。他们把异端看作魔鬼撒在主田里的稗子（《马太福音》13:3–6及下文）。因此，德尔图良推论说：“最初传下来的，出于主而且真实；后来引进的，则是外来的而且虚假”（《论异端的抗辩》[Praescr.] 第31章：“Ex ipso ordine manifestatur, id esse dominicum et verum quod sit prius traditum, id autem extraneum et falsum quod sit posterius inmissum”）。异端与宗派固然是免不了的（《哥林多前书》11:19），但“那绊倒人的有祸了”（《马太福音》18:7）。德尔图良说（同上，第30章）：“主被出卖，固然是必要的；但那卖主的人有祸了。” 教父论战的另一特点，是把异端归因于卑劣的动机，如骄傲、野心受挫、肉欲和贪财。他们不考虑心智禀赋的不同、教育的影响以及其他原因。不过，也有少数高尚的例外。奥利金和奥古斯丁 (Augustin) 承认，至少有些传播谬误的教师是诚实而认真的。 我们必须注意尼西亚会议以前与其后的异端，以及惩治异端的方式，在两个重要方面的区别。 尼西亚会议以前的主要异端，无疑是对基督教真理的根本歪曲，不容有任何妥协。伊便尼派 (Ebionism)、诺斯替主义 (Gnosticism) 和摩尼教 (Manichaeism)，在本质上都是反基督教的。教会若容忍这种异教道理与荒谬之说的混杂物，就必危及自身的存在。但对于孟他努派 (Montanists)、诺瓦atian派 (Novatians)、多纳徒派 (Donatists)、十四日派 (Quartodecimanians)，以及其他在教义或纪律的次要问题上意见不同的宗派，教会的判断则较为温和，也承认他们的洗礼。 尼西亚会议以前，教会对异端的惩罚纯属教会性质，包括责备、罢职和逐出教会，并不影响其公民地位。 但教会与国家一开始联合，民政官员便在教会的赞同下，仿照摩西律法，增设没收财产、流放和处死等世俗刑罚，却违反了基督和使徒的精神与榜样。君士坦丁 (Constantine) 于公元316年颁布若干针对多纳徒派的敕令，开了先例。瓦伦提尼安一世 (Valentinian I.) 禁止摩尼教徒公开礼拜（371年）。第二次大公会议击败阿里乌派 (Arians) 之后，狄奥多西大帝 (Theodosius the Great) 在381至394年间颁布十五道敕令，以法律惩罚强制推行信仰一致。霍诺里乌斯 (Honorius，408年)、阿卡狄乌斯 (Arcadius)、小狄奥多西 (the younger Theodosius) 和查士丁尼 (Justinian，529年) 都沿袭了这一道路。根据这些帝国法令，异端分子，即公开反对帝国国教的人，被剥夺担任一切公职、公开礼拜、接受或遗赠财产以及订立有效契约的权利；他们受到罚款、放逐、体罚，甚至死刑。见《狄奥多西法典》(Theos. Code) 第XVI卷，第V题，De Haereticis（论异端分子）。最早因异端罪而被执行斩刑的，是普里西利安 (Priscillian) 及其六名持摩尼教观点的追随者（385年）。米兰的安布罗斯 (Ambrose of Milan) 和图尔的马丁 (Martin of Tours) 出于较为仁厚的情怀，抗议这一行为，却归于徒然。甚至伟大而良善的圣奥古斯丁，尽管自己曾作过九年的异端分子，仍因错误解释《路加福音》14:23的 Cogite eos intrare（勉强人进来），而为宗教逼迫的原则辩护（第93封书信，ad Vinc.；第185封书信，ad Bonif.；《订正录》[Retract.] II，第5章）。倘若他预见到讨伐阿尔比派 (Albigenses) 的十字军，以及西班牙宗教裁判所的种种惨事，他必会撤回这一危险的意见。神权式或伊拉斯都派 (Erastian) 的国教理论——无论属于希腊大公教会、罗马天主教会，还是新教——都把一切冒犯教会的行为视为冒犯国家的行为，并且要求按照当时对正统的热心和对异端的憎恨程度，施以轻重不等的惩罚。然而，上帝至高的护理使一切恶事生出善果，对异端分子的血腥逼迫——教会史中最黑暗的篇章之一——竟结出了宗教自由的甘美果实。见第III卷，第138–146页。 § 138. 圣经与正典 罗伊斯 (Reuss)、韦斯科特 (Westcott，第6版，1889年)、赞恩 (Zahn，1888年) 关于正典的著作。霍尔茨曼 (Holtzmann)：《正典与传统》(Kanon u. 这里立刻产生一个问题，即圣书的数目与编排，也就是正典的问题；正典既有别于那些蒙光照却未受默示的教会教师的著作，也有别于最初四个世纪中为异端的利益或为满足无谓的好奇心，假托某位使徒或其他杰出人物之名而写成、刊行的大量伪经作品（福音书、行传、书信和启示录），其中有些至今尚存。不过，这些伪经并非全都出自伊便尼派和诺斯替派；有些不过是企图用虚构的故事，填补耶稣和使徒历史中的空白，或采用 vaticinia post eventum（事后编造的预言），借着当时普遍容许的虔诚欺诈，来荣耀基督教。 旧约正典由犹太人传给教会，并有基督和使徒的认可。犹太人的次经收在《七十士译本》中，又由此进入基督教的各译本。新约正典仿照旧约的模式，在最初四个世纪中，在同一位圣灵的引导下逐渐形成；各卷使徒著作也正是受这位圣灵的感动而写成的。其最初的痕迹见于《彼得后书》3:15，那里预设已有一部保罗书信集，6 并将之与“别的经书”并列。7 诚然，使徒教父和早期护教士为了证明基督教出于上帝，通常诉诸旧约、使徒口头的宣讲、基督教各教会活泼的信仰、殉道者得胜的死，以及持续发生的神迹。然而，他们的著作也引用了使徒最重要的著作，虽通常不注明作者姓名，或至少也有所引述，足以使这些著作的悠久年代和教会权威超乎一切合理的怀疑。8 第二世纪中叶，诺斯替派的马吉安 (Marcion) 所立的异端正典，由一部删残的《路加福音》和保罗的十封书信组成；这无疑意味着当时已有一部正统的正典，因为异端总以真理的存在为前提，而它本身不过是真理的歪曲形象。 新约的主要书卷，即四福音书、《使徒行传》、保罗的十三封书信、《彼得前书》和《约翰一书》——优西比乌 (Eusebius) 称之为“公认书卷”(Homologumena)——在第二世纪中叶以后，已在教会中普遍使用，并被承认为使徒所作、受基督之灵的默示，因此具有权威，属于正典。这一点由殉道者游斯丁 (Justin Martyr)、他提安 (Tatian)、安提阿的提阿非罗 (Theophilus of 至于其余七卷，即优西比乌所称的“有争议书卷”(Antilegomena)，也就是《希伯来书》、10《启示录》、11《彼得后书》《约翰二书》《约翰三书》《雅各书》和《犹大书》，教会的传统直到优西比乌所处的第四世纪初，仍在接受与拒绝之间摇摆不定。不过，现存两部年代可追溯至优西比乌和君士坦丁 (Constantine) 时代的最古老希腊文新约抄本中，一部——《西奈抄本》(Codex Sinaiticus)——包含全部二十七卷；另一部——《梵蒂冈抄本》(Codex Vaticanus)——原来可能也同样完整，尽管《希伯来书》最后几章（自11:14起）、教牧书信、《腓利门书》和《启示录》现已遗失。有争议书卷还有第二类，优西比乌称之为“伪作”(νόθα*)，包括使徒以后时期的几部著作，即《巴拿巴公函》、罗马的革利免《致哥林多人第一书》、坡旅甲 (Polycarp)《致腓立比人书》、《黑马牧人书》(Shepherd of Hermas)、现已失传的《彼得启示录》和《希伯来人福音》；这些著作至少曾在某些教会中诵读，但后来普遍被排除在正典之外。其中有些甚至收入最古老的圣经抄本，如《西奈抄本》中的《巴拿巴书》和《黑马牧人书》的一部分（二者均为希腊文原文），以及《亚历山大抄本》(Codex Alexandrinus) 中罗马的革利免《第一书》。 新约正典首次得到明确界定，并采用此后普遍沿用的形式，是在非洲举行的两次教会会议上：393年的希坡 (Hippo) 会议和397年的迦太基 (Carthage) 会议。奥古斯丁出席了这两次会议；他对当时一切神学问题都有举足轻重的影响。至少到那时，全教会对于正典书卷的数目必定已经近乎一致，甚至似乎无须再由大公会议予以认可。无论如何，东方教会在这件事上完全独立于北非教会。老底嘉 (Laodicea) 会议（363年）列出了我们现有新约各卷的名单，只缺《启示录》。包含这份名单的最后一条教规，很可能是后来增补的；然而，尼西亚及后尼西亚时期各大教父散见于各处的见证，证实所有这些书卷早已在教会中使用，只对《启示录》尚有若干疑问。这些教父包括亚他那修 (Athanasius，卒于373年)、耶路撒冷的区利罗 (Cyril of Jerusalem，卒于386年)、拿先斯的贵格利 (Gregory of Nazianzum，卒于389年)、萨拉米斯的埃皮法尼乌 (Epiphanius of Salamis，卒于403年)、金口约翰 (Chrysostom，卒于407年) 等。12 Novum Testamentum（新约）13 这一名称，以及 Novum Instrumentum（具有法律效力之意的法律用语），最早见于德尔图良，后来普遍使用，取代了更准确的名称“新盟约”(New Covenant)。这些书卷通常分为两部分：“福音书”14 和“使徒书”；第二部分的书信又分为大公书信（或普通书信）和保罗书信。如此确定的大公教会正典，直到宗教改革时期都未受触动；那时，次经和有争议书卷的问题才重新提出，圣经批判学也随之诞生。然而，近代最彻底的研究，未能动摇教会对新约的信仰，将来也绝不能动摇。 关于使徒著作的起源和性质，教父们把犹太人用于旧约的那种略带机械性与神秘力量色彩的默示理论，应用于新约；他们认为，各卷书都是在圣灵非凡的帮助之下写成的，因此得以免于错误（照奥利金的看法，甚至免于记忆的差错）。但这并不被认为排除了作者本身的活动和个性。例如，爱任纽认为保罗具有独特的文体，并将其归因于他那热切心灵中奔涌的思想。然而，亚历山大学派却把默示的观念扩展到了令人疑虑的程度。亚历山大的革利免称柏拉图 (Plato) 的著作受了默示，因为其中含有真理；他又认为，历史中一切美与善，都是无限者的一缕气息，是神圣的逻各斯 (Logos) 从人类灵魂的琴弦上奏出的一个音符。 圣经既是上帝启示的受默示之工具所产生的作品，便被承认为无谬的知识来源，以及基督徒信仰与行为绝无错误的准则，并被用来反驳异端，而未在新旧两约之间作批判性的区分。爱任纽称福音为真理的柱石和根基。德尔图良要求每一项教义都须有圣经的凭据，并宣称异端无法立足于纯粹的圣经基础之上。在奥利金看来，凡不能由圣经的见证加以证实的，都不值得相信。 起初，圣经的解释纯粹着眼于实际，目的在于直接造就信徒。与诺斯替派 (Gnostics) 的争论，要求采用一种更具学术性的方法。正统派与异端都仿效拉比派和亚历山大犹太教，大量采用寓意和神秘的解释，且不时迷失于纯粹的幻想和最荒诞的臆测之中。除少数例外（金口约翰和哲罗姆）之外，教父们一般几乎没有语法与历史释经的观念。 奥利金最早结合犹太柏拉图主义者斐罗 (Philo) 的寓意法，提出一套正式的解释理论，并将其贯彻于一长系列释经著作之中；这些著作以勤勉和才思见长，却鲜有扎实的成果。他认为圣经是一个活的有机体，由三种要素构成，分别对应柏拉图心理学所说的人的身体、魂和灵。因此，他赋予圣经三重意义：(1) 属身体的、字面的或历史的意义，直接来自字词的含义，但仅仅是遮蔽更高观念的帷幕；(2) 属魂的或道德的意义，使第一层意义富有生气，用以造就一般信徒；(3) 属灵的、神秘的和理念的意义，专供那些立于哲学知识高地的人领会。在运用这一理论时，他表现出与斐罗相同的倾向，即以属灵化的解释消解圣经的字面意义，尤其是在明白的历史意义似乎不够高尚之处，如大卫犯罪的历史；他并不只是阐明圣经的意义，反而把种种外来的观念和不相干的幻想塞进其中。但这种寓意化的解释迎合了当时的趣味，加上他丰富的才思和令人折服的学识，奥利金便成了早期教会释经方面的权威，直到他的正统性受到怀疑。他也是圣经文本批判的先驱，他的《六栏本》(Hexapla) 是编纂多语对照圣经的首次尝试。 尽管释经中的无数臆测和细节上的分歧，足以驳倒特伦托会议 (Tridentine) 所虚构的“教父一致同意”(unanimis consensus patrum)，教父们从圣经引出最重要的信条时，在方法上仍有某种一致性。他们在解释中都遵循同一教义原则，即某种“信仰类比”(analogia fidei)。这就把我们引向传统的问题。 关于正典的附注 I. 优西比乌的陈述 E. III. 25，海尼兴 (Heinichen) 版，第I卷，第130页及后；参较其第III卷，第87页及后的注释）。 公认书卷 (Homologumena)，即普遍承认的书卷 (ὁμολογούμενα*)：新约二十七卷中的二十二卷，即四福音书、《使徒行传》、保罗的十四封书信（包括《希伯来书》）、《彼得前书》《约翰一书》和《启示录》。他说：“论述至此，我们应当将前面（III. 24）所提到的新约著作列出一份简明的目录 (Ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι τὰς δηλωθείσας τῆς καινῆς διαθήκης γραφάς*)。首先，我们必须列入神圣的四部福音书（或四重组合，τετρακτύν*），其次是《使徒行传》(ἡ τῶν πράξεων τῶν ἀποστόλων γραφή*)。在此之后，必须算上保罗的书信，再其次，必须确认为真作（κυρωτέον*，是 κυρόω* 的动词形容词，意为认可）的，是流传为约翰第一封的那封书信 (τὴν φερομένην Ἰωάννου προτέραν*)，同样还有彼得的书信 (καὶ ὁμοίως τὴν Πέτρου ἐπιστολήν*)。除这些书之外，若认为适当 (εἴγε φανείη*)，我们还须列入《约翰启示录》(τὴν ἀποκάλυψιν Ἰωάννου*)；关于此书的不同意见，我们将在适当之处陈述。这些都列在普遍接受的书卷之中 (ἐν ὁμολογουμένοις*)。” 优西比乌在第III卷第3章中说，保罗的“十四封书信”(τοῦ δὲ Παύλου πρόδηλοι καὶ σαφεῖς αἱ δεκατέσσαρες*) 普遍受到接受，但又补充说：“有人拒绝《希伯来书》，说此书受到争议，因为它不是保罗的书信之一。” 关于《启示录》，优西比乌的态度游移不定，取决于他是在陈述教会公认的信念，还是自己的私人意见。他先把它列在公认书卷之中，随后又在同一段（III. 25）中把它列入伪作；但两处都加上了限定语（εἰ φανείη*），把此事留给读者判断。他很少引用此书，通常称之为《约翰启示录》，但在一处（III. 39）暗示，此书可能出自“第二位约翰”；这必定是指有别于使徒的那位所谓“长老约翰”。这种意见很受施莱尔马赫 (Schleiermacher) 批判学派的赞同。由于其神秘的性质，直到今日，《启示录》对少数人而言仍是新约中最受喜爱的书卷，对多数人而言却是最不受喜爱的。它所得的见证与其他任何一卷同样充分，而且最激进的近代批评家（鲍尔、勒南）也承认，此书由使徒所作，写于耶路撒冷毁灭以前。 有争议书卷 (Antilegomena)，即受到争议的书卷，但“教会中大多数人仍然熟悉”这些书 (ἀντιλεγόμενα, γνώριμα δ’ ὅμως τοῖς πολλοῖς*，III. 25)。共有五卷（或七卷），即雅各的一封书信、犹大的一封书信、《彼得后书》《约翰二书》和《约翰三书》（“无论这两封究竟属于福音书作者，还是另一位约翰”）。 我们可以把《希伯来书》和《启示录》也加在其中（尽管优西比乌没有明说）：前者因为未被普遍承认为保罗所作，后者则因其中被认为含有千禧年论 (chiliasm)，而这种学说为优西比乌和亚历山大学派所反感。 伪作 (νόθα*)，如《保罗行传》《彼得启示录》《牧人书》（黑马）、《巴拿巴书》、所谓《使徒教训》，以及《希伯来人福音》，“那些接受了基督的希伯来人，特别喜爱此书”。 如前所述，他又前后不一地把《约翰启示录》加在其中：“正如我所说，有人拒绝此书 (ἥν τινες ἀθετοῦσιν*)，另有人则把它列在普遍接受的书卷之中 (τοῖς ὁμολογουμένοις*)。”他本应将其列入有争议书卷。 可以说，这些 νόθα* 相当于旧约的次经，虔敬而有益，却不属于正典。 Nicaea) 并未像人们可能预期的那样确定正典，但圣经被毫无争议地视为正统信仰确实而不可动摇的根基。小亚细亚 (Asia Minor) 的冈格拉会议 (Synod of Gangra，约在四世纪中叶) 在最后一条教规（第20或21条）中说：“简而言之，我们愿教会遵守借着神圣经书和使徒传统传给我们的事。”参赫费勒 (Hefele)，《大公会议史》(Conciliengesch.)，I. 789。 第一个明确规定正典书卷数目的会议，是小亚细亚弗吕家 (Phrygia) 的老底嘉会议 (Council of Laodicea，召开于公元343至381年之间，可能约在363年)。其最后一条教规（第60或59条）先列举旧约正典书卷，然后按以下次序列出新约全部书卷，但《启示录》除外： “新约的书卷如下：四福音书，即《马太福音》《马可福音》《路加福音》《约翰福音》；《使徒行传》；七封大公书信，即雅各一封、彼得两封、约翰三封、犹大一封；保罗的十四封书信，即致罗马人一封、致哥林多人两封、致加拉太人一封、致以弗所人一封、致腓立比人一封、致歌罗西人一封、致帖撒罗尼迦人两封、致希伯来人一封、致提摩太两封、致提多一封、致腓利门一封。” 若干抄本和译本没有这份目录，它很可能是后来从耶路撒冷的区利罗 (Cyril of Jerusalem) 的著作中插入的。施皮特勒 (Spittler)、赫布斯特 (Herbst) 和韦斯科特 (Westcott) 否认这份目录出自老底嘉会议，施勒克 (Schrökh) 和赫费勒则为此说辩护。它与《使徒教规》第85条的目录相似，后者同样没有《启示录》，但加入了革利免的两封书信和伪托的《使徒宪章》。 T.)，第2版，第382页及后。 在西方教会，第三次迦太基地方会议 (Council of Carthage，公元397年召开) 列出了新旧两约正典书卷的完整目录，规定教会中应当把这些书卷作为神圣经书诵读，其他一概排除。新约书卷按以下次序列出：“福音书四卷，《使徒行传》一卷，使徒保罗的书信十三封，同一位〔使徒〕致希伯来人的书信一封，使徒彼得的书信两封，约翰的书信三封，雅各的书信一封，犹大的书信一封，《约翰启示录》一卷。”这一教规此前已于公元393年由非洲的希波雷吉乌斯会议 (Synod of Hippo regius) 采纳；当时仍任长老的奥古斯丁 (Augustin) 在会上发表了《论信仰与信经》(De Fide et Symbolo) 的讲论。该会议的记录已佚，但其决议为第三次迦太基会议重新采纳；后者只有四十三位非洲主教参加，不能声称具有普遍的权威。（见韦斯科特，第391页；查特里斯 (Charteris)，第20页；赫费勒，修订版，II. 53、68。） 奥古斯丁（两次会议均有出席）和哲罗姆 (Jerome，曾应罗马教皇达马苏斯 (Damasus) 的请求翻译拉丁文圣经)，对于拉丁教会正典的确定发挥了决定性的影响。 特伦托会议 (Council of Trent，1546年) 确认了传统观点，并咒诅持异议者。韦斯科特博士说（第426页及下页）：“这项祸害深远的法令，由五十三位高级教士批准；其中没有一个德国人，没有一个以历史学识著称的学者，也没有一个人曾作过专门研究，足以审查这个只能凭古代见证才能判明真相的问题。” 对希腊教会和罗马教会而言，正典问题已经定案，尽管从未有一个代表整个教会的、严格意义上的大公会议对此作出裁决。但新教要求享有尼西亚会议以前时期的自由，以及重新考察圣经每一卷书之起源与历史的权利。没有这种自由，释经神学就不可能有真正的进步。 § 139. 大公教会的传统 爱任纽 (Irenaeus)：《驳异端》(Adv. 教父们，尤其是爱任纽和德尔图良，除了诉诸圣经，也同样满怀信心地援引“信仰准则”；15即教会共同的信仰，由自基督及其使徒以来直至他们当时绵延不绝的主教传承，以口头方式传递下来，尤其仍鲜活地存留于最初的使徒教会中，如耶路撒冷、安提阿、以弗所和罗马的教会。因此，传统与原始的主教制度紧密相连。后者是前者的载体，两者都被视为抵挡异端的堡垒。 爱任纽以大公教会公开而纯正的传统，对抗诺斯替派 (Gnostics) 的秘密传统，并指向众教会，尤其是罗马教会，视其为教义合一的可见中心。他说，凡愿认识真理的人，都能在整个教会中看见使徒的传统；我们也能逐一数出使徒所按立的主教，以及直至我们这时代的继任者，他们既未教导，也不知道任何这类异端。随后，他以罗马教会从利奴 (Linus) 到埃柳特里乌斯 (Eleutherus) 的头十二位主教为例，作为纯正使徒教义的见证人。他或许能够设想没有圣经的基督教，却无法想象没有活的传统的基督教；为支持这一见解，他提到那些没有纸墨——“sine charta et atramento”——却有福音写在心中的蛮族部落。 德尔图良在他著名的抗辩论证中，找到了对付一切异端的万能解毒剂。这一论证从一开始就剥夺异端者诉诸圣经的一切权利，理由是：圣经产生于基督的教会，赐给了教会，唯有在教会之内、借着教会，才能得到正确的理解。他在这里也提醒人注意那有形可见的传承；它将大公教会与任意妄为、变幻不定的异端宗派区别开来。在所有主要会众中，尤其是在使徒最初建立的群体中，这传承都从一位主教到另一位主教，毫无间断地上溯至使徒本身，由使徒上溯至基督，再由基督上溯至上帝。他在论抗辩的著作中说：“来吧，你若要在关乎自己救恩的事上作更有益的探究，就去遍访使徒的众教会吧。在那里，使徒本人的座位仍居于主持的地位，他们亲笔的真确书信仍被公开诵读，发出他们各人的声音，显出他们各人的面容。如果亚该亚 (Achaia) 离你最近，你就有哥林多；如果你离马其顿 (Macedonia) 不远，你就有腓立比，有帖撒罗尼迦；如果你能到亚细亚 (Asia)，你就有以弗所；如果你住在意大利附近，你就有罗马，我们〔非洲教会〕也从那里而来。使徒以自己的鲜血，将全部教义倾注其中的教会，是何等有福啊！”等等。 要衡量这一论证的分量，我们必须记住，这些教父距离使徒时期仍然相当近，最古老教会的主教传承，可以凭两三代人尚存的记忆加以证实。事实上，爱任纽年轻时就认识圣约翰的门徒坡旅甲 (Polycarp)。但也正因如此，我们必须谨防过分高估这一见证，并用它来支持那些起源较晚、没有圣经根据的传统。 我们也不能设想，这些教父曾想过要让个人判断盲目而奴性地服从教会权威，服从使徒所建母会之主教的裁决。正是这位爱任纽，曾坦率地反对罗马主教维克多 (Victor)。德尔图良虽然在基本信仰上仍持守正统，却从他后来的孟他努派 (Montanistic) 立场出发，在若干问题上与大公教会争辩，并提出了真正的新教原则：尤其在宗教事务上，所当顾念的不是习俗，而是真理；尽管他起初只就童女蒙头这一惯行的习俗提出这原则。16他的学生居普良几乎将“合乎圣经的”与“大公教会的”视为可互换的用语，却仍郑重抗议罗马关于异端洗礼有效性的理论；在这场争论中，他与德尔图良完全一致，宣称没有真理的习俗，不过是历久而受尊崇的错误。17亚历山大学派自由地培植了种种独特见解，后来这些见解被斥为异端；尽管 παράδοσις ἀποστολική* 在他们那里占有显著地位，这一用语及类似表述在他们的语言中却具有不同含义，有时仅仅指圣经。例如，革利免在那段著名的话中说：“正如有人受了喀耳刻 (Circe) 的魔法，从人变为兽；照样，一个人若起来反对教会传统，转而投向人随意臆造的立场，就不再属于上帝，也不再忠于主了。” 这种使徒传统在教义实质上与圣经一致；虽然就形式而言，它来自使徒的口头宣讲，但就内容而言，它实际上与使徒的著作完全相同。从这一角度看，早期教父在信仰问题上同时赋予圣经和传统最高权威，所显出的矛盾便消解了。使徒亲口传讲、随后写入著作，而教会又以言语和文字世代忠实传递下来的，乃是同一个福音。18 § 140. 信仰准则与《使徒信经》 鲁菲努斯 起初并没有一种对所有信徒都有约束力的固定信仰公式。各主要教会虽同以洗礼公式为基础，却各按自己的需要，以一种近乎独立会众的方式制定信经；也可能以一份从使徒时代传下来的简短原型为范本。因此，在尼西亚以前的作者中，我们见到多种这样的信仰准则，确切地说，是关于这些准则的零星记述；有长有短，有陈述式，也有问答式。例如里昂的爱任纽 (Irenaeus of Lyons，180年)、迦太基的德尔图良 Antioch，300年)、凯撒利亚的优西比乌 (Eusebius of Caesarea，325年)、安居拉的马尔凯鲁 (Marcellus of Ancyra，340年)、耶路撒冷的区利罗 (Cyril of Jerusalem，350年)、塞浦路斯的伊皮法纽 (Epiphanius of Cyprus，374年)、阿奎莱亚的鲁菲努斯 (Rufinus of Aquileja，390年)，以及《使徒宪章》中的记载。19然而，尽管形式和篇幅各异，实质上却是一致的，故德尔图良可以说，信仰准则 (regula fidei) 是“una omnino, sola immobilis et irreformabilis”（完全为一，唯一不动摇、不可更改）。它们都是同一主题的变奏。要说明这种多样性与统一性，我们可以参看新英格兰清教徒各教会众多的正统会众信经；它们都以《威斯敏斯特准则》为基础。 东方的公式一般比西方的更长、变化更多，也更富形而上学色彩，并含有一些教义术语，用以反对东方盛行的异端教说。它们最终都被《尼西亚信经》（325、381及451年）取代；这信经被赋予大公会议的权威，至今仍是希腊教会的根本信经。严格说来，它是基督教世界唯一的大公信经，因为西方也采纳了它，虽然增添了一个后来成为分隔之墙的条款（Filioque，“及子”）。我们将在下一卷再论及它。 西方的各种公式——北非、高卢、意大利的公式——较短而简单，变化较少，显示出更为统一的类型。它们都汇入了罗马信经；这信经成为拉丁教会及其衍生教会的根本信经，直到今日仍是如此。 这份罗马信经，更以《使徒信经》(Apostles’ Creed) 这一受尊崇的名称为人所知。长期以来，人们相信（罗马教会中许多人至今仍相信），它是使徒们在离开耶路撒冷、分赴各地以前编成的，用来概括他们的教训（每位使徒在更高的默示下，各贡献十二条中的一条）。20这一兴起于四世纪的传统，21已被尼西亚以前诸信经以及《使徒信经》本身的种种异文所否定。使徒们若曾编写这样一份文献，人们必会谨慎地将其原封不动地传承下来。以使徒为名的这份信经，无疑是逐渐形成的。我们现有它的两种形式。 见于古老手稿的较早形式，22要短得多，可能追溯至三世纪，甚至二世纪。它可能是从东方传入的，也可能形成于罗马；它在实质上与安居拉的马尔凯鲁约于340年写给教皇尤利乌斯一世 (Julius I) 的信中、为证明自己正统而附上的希腊文信经相同，23也与埃塞尔斯坦王 (King Aethelstan)《诗篇集》所载的信经相同。24直到三世纪，希腊语一直是罗马教会及其文献的主导语言。25 罗马信经的较长形式，即现今的通行文本，直到六或七世纪才出现。其中有几个重要条款，是早期形式所没有的，如“他降在阴间”，26ecclesiam（教会）之后的修饰语“大公的”，27“圣徒相通”，28以及“永生”。29这些增文采自各行省的版本（高卢与北非），并被纳入较早的形式。 因此，《使徒信经》按其现有形式而言，属于使徒以后的时期；但就其内容和精神而言，却真正是使徒性的。它体现了尼西亚以前教会的信仰，是次一级默示的产物，正如《荣耀归于至高上帝颂》(Gloria in Excelsis) 和《赞美上帝颂》(Te deum) 一样；这两首颂歌体现了同一时代的敬虔，也同样无法追溯至某一位或某几位作者。它遵循父、子、圣灵三一上帝启示的历史次序，始于创造，终于复活和永生。它以基督为我们信仰的中心条款，环绕着他而展开。它陈述活生生的事实，而非抽象的教条；它使用百姓的语言，而非神学院的语言。它只限于根本真理，简单、简短，却又全面，极其适合教理教导和礼仪之用。无论正统基督教世界不同时代和不同支派彼此有多大差异，它至今仍是将他们联结起来的活纽带；更长、更完备的信经，无论在各自的位置上如何必要，也永远不能取代它。它既有古老的权威，又有常青青春的甘露，这一点胜过使徒以后时期的任何其他文献。它是西方唯一严格意义上的大公信经，正如《尼西亚信经》是东方唯一的大公信经一样。30它是信经中的信经，正如主祷文是祷告中的祷告。 Wilh. Möller)：《希腊教会直至奥利金时期的宇宙论史》(Geschichte der Kosmologie in der griechischen Kirche bis auf Origenes.)。哈雷 (Halle)，1860年，第112–188、474–560页。这部博学著作的大部分篇幅，论述的是诺斯替派 (Gnostics) 的宇宙论。 在阐述教会的各项教义时，我们必须始终记住：基督教进入世界，并不是作为一个逻辑体系，而是作为一个神人相合的事实；《新约》不仅是供学者使用的神学教科书，更是从始至终供一切信徒使用的生命之书。救恩的教义当然蕴含在这些救恩的事实之中，但所采取的是具体、鲜活、常新而通俗的形式。从上帝的话语和基督徒的经验中，以合乎逻辑、系统严谨的方式展开这些教义，乃是留给神学家的工作。因此，在我们所考察的这一时期，即使最杰出的教师对于重要信条的认识仍十分模糊而有缺欠，我们也不必惊讶；这些教师在自己心中感受到这些信条的实际力量，并将其深印在别人心上，其热忱丝毫不逊于他们最正统的继承者。基督教的中心，是基督神人二性的位格和神人二性的工作。从这一中心发出的变革，贯穿了当时宗教观念的整个领域，从最初的原则直到最终的结果，肯定先前宗教中的真实成分，摒弃其中的虚假。 最初几个世纪的信经，尤其《使徒信经》和《尼西亚信经》，几乎都以宣认信仰上帝为开端：他是全能的父，是天地及一切有形无形之物的创造者。爱任纽 (Irenaeus) 在驳斥诺斯替异端时，首先便维护这项在《圣经》第一章就已确立的根本教义。倘若主自己宣告的不是创造者，而是另一位上帝，他连主也不会相信。他拒绝任何以先验（a priori）方式构造上帝观念的做法，将自己对上帝的认识完全建立在启示和基督徒的经验上。 我们先从一切宗教赖以成立的一般上帝观念说起。这一观念因上帝在基督里的显现而得到净化，变得更属灵，也更有生气。我们尤其可以从德尔图良 (Tertullian) 的见解中看出这一进展：他认为人的灵魂有一种不可抗拒的倾向，趋向上帝，且趋向那独一的真上帝。他说：“上帝绝不会隐藏，上帝绝不会令世人失望；只要人愿意，他总能被认识、被感知、被看见。上帝使我们本身的一切，以及我们置身其中的一切，都成为他的见证。这样，他借着为众人所认识，证明自己是上帝，是独一的上帝；因为若有另一位，就必须先加以证明。对上帝的意识，是灵魂原初所禀赋的；在埃及、叙利亚和本都，这意识都相同，并无别样；因为一切灵魂都称犹太人的上帝为自己的上帝。”但自然界也为上帝作见证。它是他手中的工作，本身是好的；并非如诺斯替派所教导的，是物质或魔鬼的产物，本质上是恶的。按照爱任纽的看法，除非上帝启示自己，否则他是完全隐藏、不可理解的。但他已在创造和救赎中将自己显明，因此不可能向任何人完全隐而不露。 在证明上帝存在的各种论证中，我们发现宇宙论和自然神学方法的萌芽已见于这一时期。在理解上帝本性的方式上，我们看到这样的差别：亚历山大学派 (Alexandrians) 力求避免一切将上帝拟人化、赋予他人类情感的观念，强调上帝的非物质性与属灵性，几乎达到抽象化的地步；德尔图良却甚至将形体性归于上帝。不过，他认为唯有不存在者才是绝对无形体的，因此，他所谓的形体性，可能仅仅意在表示至高者的实体性和具体的位格性。33 关于上帝独一的教义，即上帝是永恒、全能、无所不在、公义、圣洁的万有创造者和维系者，基督教会从犹太教承继而来，并加以捍卫，以抵御异教徒荒谬的多神论，尤其抵御诺斯替派的二元论；后者假定物质与上帝同为永恒，并将世界的创造归于居间的造物主 (Demiurge)。这种二元论不过是多神论的另一种形式，它排除了绝对性，也随之排除了一切恰当的上帝观念。 关于创造：爱任纽 (Irenaeus) 和德尔图良 (Tertullian) 最坚决地拒绝异教和诺斯替主义 (Gnosticism) 的物活论 (hylozoism) 与造物主论 (demiurgism)，并按照《创世记》教导说，上帝创造了包括物质在内的世界；当然，不是用任何材料造的，而是从无中创造的，或者从正面说，是出于他自由而全能的旨意，借着他的话语创造的。34 上帝这自由的旨意，这出于爱的旨意，是一切存在的至高原因和终极根据，绝对不受任何条件限制，却规定一切条件，因而排除了一切物理强力或流溢的观念。每一个受造物既出于良善圣洁的上帝，就其本质而言，本身都是好的。35 因此，恶并不是一种原初而具有实体的存在，而是本性的败坏，所以能够借着救赎的大能加以消灭。没有正确的创造论，就不可能有真正的救赎论；诺斯替派的一切体系都表明了这一点。 俄利根 (Origen) 关于永恒创造的见解颇为独特。他所想到的，与其说是新世界无穷无尽地相继出现，不如说是原初世界不断发生新的变化，从起初就彰显上帝的全能、智慧和良善。与此相联系的，是他那柏拉图式的灵魂先存观。他从上帝与世界之间密切关系的观念出发，将世界表述为上帝必然的启示。若主张曾有一个时候，上帝没有彰显那些构成他自身存在的本质属性，那便是不敬虔而荒谬的。他从未闲置无为，也从未静止不动。上帝的存在与他的良善和爱是同一的，他的旨意也与他的本性是同一的。他按着自己的本性必须创造，也愿意创造。因此，必然之事同时也是自由的行动。每一个世界都有开端和终结，二者都包含在上帝的护理之中。但在第一个世界以前又是什么呢？俄利根将时间的观念与世界的观念联系起来，却不能超越时间无穷相继的观念。上帝的永恒超乎时间，却又充满一切时间。俄利根以逻各斯 (Logos) 的永恒受生作为从上帝到世界的中介；逻各斯是父本体的真像，上帝借着他先创造属灵的世界，然后创造物质的世界。而他的受生本身也是一个持续的过程；上帝始终（ἀεί*）生他的儿子，从未有过没有儿子的时候，正如子也从不离开父一样。36 § 143. 人与堕落 人是按上帝的形象受造的，原本纯洁圣善，后来因自己的罪责和撒但的引诱而堕落，而撒但自己也从原初的地位堕落了——这是教会普遍的信仰。然而，罪的范围和堕落的后果，直到第五世纪的伯拉纠争论 (Pelagian controversy) 才得到充分讨论。关于人类灵魂起源的形而上学问题，情形也是如此。不过，三种理论的萌芽已经出现。 德尔图良是灵魂遗传说 (traducianism) 的创立者，37 此说认为灵魂与身体都通过生育过程由父母传来。38 它假定上帝从无创造（de nihilo）的工作在第六日已经完成，亚当的灵魂受赋予一种能力，能够繁衍出各个个体的灵魂，正如植物界最初受造的种子具有繁衍同类的能力一样。西方神学家大多追随德尔图良而持此说，因为它最容易解释原罪如何借着生育而传播；39 但它将起源于心灵的罪物质化了。亚当在吃禁果之前，就已经因怀疑和悖逆而在内心堕落了。 亚里士多德式的灵魂创造说 (creationism) 将每一个体灵魂的起源追溯到上帝的直接作为，并假定灵魂后来因与身体接触而败坏；然而，这一理论破坏了灵魂与身体的有机统一，并将罪归源于物质部分。东方神学家以及西方的哲罗姆 (Jerome) 都倡导此说。奥古斯丁 (Augustin) 在这两种理论之间摇摆不定，而教会从未对此问题作出裁决。 第三种理论是先存说 (pre-existence)，俄利根曾加以教导，在他以前，柏拉图 (Plato) 和斐洛 (Philo) 也曾持此说。它假定每一个人在历史开始以前就已存在并且堕落，借此解释原罪与个人的罪责；但除了在观念的意义上，它既无圣经的支持，也无人类意识的支持，因此在查士丁尼 (Justinian) 统治时期，被列为俄利根派的异端之一而遭定罪。尽管如此，它仍不时作为一种孤立的思辨见解而复兴。40 基督教信仰的事业要求人们一方面申明人需要救赎，以反对伊壁鸠鲁派 (Epicureans) 的轻浮和斯多亚派 (Stoics) 的自足；另一方面申明人能够蒙救赎，以反对诺斯替派和摩尼教派 (Manichaeans) 所持的本性本恶观念，以及各种形式的宿命论。 希腊教父，尤其亚历山大学派的教父，极力维护意志的自由，认为它是人的责任和全部道德本性的基础，也是区分德行与恶行不可或缺的条件。它因堕落而受损、削弱，却并未毁灭。对俄利根而言，选择的自由是其神学体系的主要支柱。爱任纽和希波吕托斯 (Hippolytus) 无法设想人会没有理智与自由这两种不可分离的属性。德尔图良在反驳马吉安 (Marcion) 和赫尔摩根尼 (Hermogenes) 时，也明确断言，自由意志是灵魂固有的属性之一，41 正如灵魂出于上帝、具有不朽性、统治的本能和预知的能力一样。42 然而，另一方面，爱任纽遵循保罗的教导，主张亚当的原罪与全人类的罪性之间存在因果联系，尤其德尔图良主张罪是遗传的，并借生育而传播；这些见解都趋向于奥古斯丁体系。这位最伟大的拉丁教父在与伯拉纠异端的争论中发展了这一体系，它对宗教改革家产生了极为强大的影响，却对东方教会毫无影响，且在实际中也被罗马教会部分地否认了。43 § 144. 基督与道成肉身 文献 狄奥尼修斯·佩塔维乌斯 (Dionys.
