Sabellius is by far the most original, profound, and ingenious of the ante-Nicene Unitarians, and his system the most plausible rival of orthodox trinitarianism. It revives from time to time in various modifications.(147) We know very little of his life. He was probably a Lybian from the Pentapolis. He spent some time in Rome in the beginning of the third century, and was first gained by Callistus to Patripassianism, but when the latter became bishop be was excommunicated.(148) The former fact is doubtful. His doctrine spread in Rome, and especially also in the Pentapolis in Egypt. Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, excommunicated him in 260 or 261(149) at a council in that city, and, in vehement opposition to him declared in almost Arian terms for the hypostatical independence and subordination of the Son in relation to the Father. This led the Sabellians to complain of that bishop to Dionysius of Rome, who held a council in 262, and in a special treatise controverted Sabellianism, as well as subordinatianism and tritheism, with nice orthodox tact.(150) The bishop of Alexandria very cheerfully yielded, and retracted his assertion of the creaturely inferiority of the Son in favor of the orthodox homo-ousios. Thus the strife was for a while allayed, to be renewed with still greater violence by Arius half a century later. The system of Sabellius is known to us only from a few fragments, and some of these not altogether consistent, in Athanasius and other fathers. While the other Monarchians confine their inquiry to the relation of Father and Son, Sabellius embraces the Holy Spirit in his speculation, and reaches a trinity, not a simultaneous trinity of essence, however, but only a successive trinity of revelation. He starts from a distinction of the monad and the triad in the divine nature. His fundamental thought is, that the unity of God, without distinction in itself, unfolds or extends itself(151) in the course of the world’s development in three different forms and periods of revelation(152) and, after the completion of redemption, returns into unity. The Father reveals himself in the giving of the law or the Old Testament economy (not in the creation also, which in his view precedes the trinitarian revelation); the Son, in the incarnation; the Holy Ghost, in inspiration. The revelation of the Son ends with the ascension; the revelation of the Spirit goes on in regeneration and sanctification. He illustrates the trinitarian relation by comparing the Father to the disc of the sun, the Son to its enlightening power, the Spirit to its warming influence. He is said also to have likened the Father to the body, the Son to the soul, the Holy Ghost to the spirit of man; but this is unworthy of his evident speculative discrimination. His view of the Logos,(153) too, is peculiar. The, Logos is not identical with the Son, but is the monad itself in its transition to triad; that is, God conceived as vital motion and creating principle, the speaking God,(154) in distinction from the silent God.(155) Each provswpon is another dialevgesqai and the three provswpa together are only successive evolutions of the Logos or the worldward aspect of the divine nature. As the Logos proceeded from God, so he returns at last into him, and the process of trinitarian development(156) closes. Athanasius traced the doctrine of Sabellius to the Stoic philosophy. The common element is the pantheistic leading view of an expansion and contraction(157) of the divine nature immanent in the world. In the Pythagorean system also, in the Gospel of the Egyptians, and in the pseudo-Clementine Homilies, there are kindred ideas. But the originality of Sabellius cannot be brought into question by these. His theory broke the way for the Nicene church doctrine, by its full coordination of the three persons. He differs from the orthodox standard mainly in denying the trinity of essence and the permanence of the trinity of manifestation; making Father, Son, and Holy Ghost only temporary phenomena, which fulfil their mission and return into the abstract monad. § 153. The work of the triune God, in his self-revelation, is the salvation, or redemption and reconciliation of the world: negatively, the emancipation of humanity from the guilt and power of sin and death; positively, the communication of the righteousness and life of fellowship with God. First, the discord between the Creator and the creature must be adjusted; and then man can be carried onward to his destined perfection. Reconciliation with God is the ultimate aim of every religion. In heathenism it was only darkly guessed and felt after, or anticipated in perverted, fleshly forms. In Judaism it was divinely promised, typically foreshadowed, and historically prepared. In Christianity it is revealed in objective reality, according to the eternal counsel of the love and wisdom of God, through the life, death, and resurrection of Christ, and is being continually applied subjectively to individuals in the church by the Holy Spirit, through the means of grace, on condition of repentance and faith. Christ is, exclusively and absolutely, the Saviour of the world, and the Mediator between God and man. The apostolic scriptures, in the fulness of their inspiration, everywhere bear witness of this salvation wrought through Christ, as a living fact of experience. But it required time for the profound ideas of a Paul and a John to come up clearly to the view of the church; indeed, to this day they remain unfathomed. Here again experience anticipated theology. The church lived from the first on the atoning sacrifice of Christ. The cross ruled all Christian thought and conduct, and fed the spirit of martyrdom. But the primitive church teachers lived more in the thankful enjoyment of redemption than in logical reflection upon it. We perceive in their exhibitions of this blessed mystery the language rather of enthusiastic feeling than of careful definition and acute analysis. Moreover, this doctrine was never, like Christology and the doctrine of the Trinity, a subject of special controversy within the ancient church. The oecumenical symbols touch it only in general terms. The Apostles’ Creed presents it in the article on the forgiveness of sins on the ground of the divine-human life, death, and resurrection of Christ. The Nicene Creed says, a little more definitely, that Christ became man for our salvation,(158) and died for us, and rose again. Nevertheless, all the essential elements of the later church doctrine of redemption may be found, either expressed or implied, before the close of the second century. The negative part of the doctrine, the subjection of the devil, the prince of the kingdom of sin and death, was naturally most dwelt on in the patristic period, on account of the existing conflict of Christianity with heathenism, which was regarded as wholly ruled by Satan and demons. Even in the New Testament, particularly in Col. 2:15, Heb. 2:14, and 1 John 3:8, the victory over the devil is made an integral part of the work of Christ. But this view was carried out in the early church in a very peculiar and, to some extent, mythical way; and in this form continued current, until the satisfaction theory of Anselm gave a new turn to the development of the dogma. Satan is supposed to have acquired, by the disobedience of our first parents, a legal claim (whether just or unjust) upon mankind, and held them bound in the chains of sin and death (Comp. Hebr. 2:14, 15). Christ came to our release. The victory over Satan was conceived now as a legal ransom by the payment of a stipulated price, to wit, the death of Christ; now as a cheat upon him,(159) either intentional and deserved, or due to his own infatuation.(160) The theological development of the doctrine of the work of Christ began with the struggle against Jewish and heathen influences, and at the same time with the development of the doctrine of the person of Christ, which is inseparable from that of his work, and indeed fundamental to it. Ebionism, with its deistic and legal spirit, could not raise its view above the prophetic office of Christ to the priestly and the kingly, but saw in him only a new teacher and legislator. Gnosticism, from the naturalistic and pantheistic position of heathendom, looked upon redemption as a physical and intellectual process, liberating the spirit from the bonds of matter, the supposed principle of evil; reduced the human life and passion of Christ to a vain show; and could ascribe at best only a symbolical virtue to his death. For this reason even Ignatius, Irenaeus, and Tertullian, in their opposition to docetism, insist most earnestly on the reality of the humanity and death of Jesus, as the source of our reconciliation with God.(161) In Justin Martyr appear traces of the doctrine of satisfaction, though in very indefinite terms. He often refers to the Messianic fifty-third chapter of Isaiah..(162) The anonymous author of the Epistle to an unknown heathen, Diognetus, which has sometimes been ascribed to Justin, but is probably of much earlier date, has a beautiful and forcible passage on the mystery of redemption, which shows that the root of the matter was apprehended by faith long before a logical analysis was attempted. "When our wickedness" he says,(163) "had reached its height, and it had been clearly shown that its reward—punishment and death—was impending over us .... God himself took on Him the burden of our iniquities. He gave His own Son as a ransom for us, the holy One for transgressors, the blameless One for the wicked, the righteous One for the unrighteous, the incorruptible One for the corruptible, the immortal One for them that are mortal. For what other thing was capable of covering our sins than His righteousness? By what other one was it possible that we, the wicked and ungodly, could be justified, than by the only Son of God? O sweet exchange! O unsearchable operation! O benefits surpassing all expectation! that the wickedness of many should be hid in a single righteous One, and that the righteousness of One should justify many transgressors!" Irenaeus is the first of all the church teachers to give a careful analysis of the work of redemption, and his view is by far the deepest and soundest we find in the first three centuries. Christ, he teaches, as the second Adam, repeated in himself the entire life of man, from childhood to manhood, from birth to death and hades, and as it were summed up that life and brought it under one head,(164) with the double purpose of restoring humanity from its fall and carrying it to perfection. Redemption comprises the taking away of sin by the perfect obedience of Christ; the destruction of death by victory over the devil; and the communication of a new divine life to man. To accomplish this work, the Redeemer must unite in himself the divine and human natures; for only as God could he do what man could not, and only as man could he do in a legitimate way, what man should. By the voluntary disobedience of Adam the devil gained a power over man, but in an unfair way, by fraud.(165) By the voluntary obedience of Christ that power was wrested from him by lawful means.(166) This took place first in the temptation, in which Christ renewed or recapitulated the struggle of Adam with Satan, but defeated the seducer, and thereby liberated man from his thraldom. But then the whole life of Christ was a continuous victorious conflict with Satan, and a constant obedience to God. This obedience completed itself in the suffering and death on the tree of the cross, and thus blotted out the disobedience which the first Adam had committed on the tree of knowledge. This, however, is only the negative side. To this is added, as already remarked, the communication of a new divine principle of life, and the perfecting of the idea of humanity first effected by Christ. Origen differs from Irenaeus in considering man, in consequence of sin, the lawful property of Satan, and in representing the victory over Satan as an outwitting of the enemy, who had no claim to the sinless soul of Jesus, and therefore could not keep it in death. The ransom was paid, not to God, but to Satan, who thereby lost his right to man. Here Origen touches on mythical Gnosticism. He contemplates the death of Christ, however, from other points of view also, as an atoning sacrifice of love offered to God for the sins of the world; as the highest proof of perfect obedience to God; and as an example of patience. He singularly extends the virtue of this redemption to the whole spirit world, to fallen angels as well as men, in connection with his hypothesis of a final restoration. The only one of the fathers who accompanies him in this is Gregory of Nyssa. Athanasius, in his early youth, at the beginning of the next period, wrote the first systematic treatise on redemption and answer to the question "Cur Deus homo?"(167) But it was left for the Latin church, after the epoch-making treatise of Anselm, to develop this important doctrine in its various aspects. § 154. Other Doctrines. The doctrine of the subjective appropriation of salvation, including faith, justification, and sanctification, was as yet far less perfectly formed than the objective dogmas; and in the nature of the case, must follow the latter. If any one expects to find in this period, or in any of the church fathers, Augustin himself not excepted, the Protestant doctrine of justification by faith alone, as the "articulus stantis aut cadentis ecclesiae" be will be greatly disappointed. The incarnation of the Logos, his true divinity and true humanity, stand almost unmistakably in the foreground, as the fundamental truths. Paul’s doctrine of justification, except perhaps in Clement of Rome, who joins it with the doctrine of James, is left very much out of view, and awaits the age of the Reformation to be more thoroughly established and understood. The fathers lay chief stress on sanctification and good works, and show the already existing germs of the Roman Catholic doctrine of the meritoriousness and even the supererogatory meritoriousness of Christian virtue. It was left to modern evangelical theology to develop more fully the doctrines of soteriology and subjective Christianity. Christianity—and human life itself, with its countless problems and mysteries—has no meaning without the certainty of a future world of rewards and punishments, for which the present life serves as a preparatory school. Christ represents himself as "the Resurrection and the Life," and promises "eternal life" to all who believe in Him. On his resurrection the church is built, and without it the church could never have come into existence. The resurrection of the body and the life everlasting are among the fundamental articles of the early baptismal creeds. The doctrine of the future life, though last in the logical order of systematic theology, was among the first in the consciousness of the Christians, and an unfailing source of comfort and strength in times of trial and persecution. It stood in close connection with the expectation of the Lord’s glorious reappearance. It is the subject of Paul’s first Epistles, those to the Thessalonians, and is prominently discussed in the fifteenth chapter of First Corinthians. He declares the Christians "the most pitiable," because the most deluded and uselessly self-sacrificing, "of all men," if their hope in Christ were confined to this life. The ante-Nicene church was a stranger in the midst of a hostile world, and longed for the unfading crown which awaited the faithful confessor and martyr beyond the grave. Such a mighty revolution as the conversion of the heathen emperor was not dreamed of even as a remote possibility, except perhaps by the far-sighted Origen. Among the five causes to which Gibbon traces the rapid progress of the Christian religion he assigns the second place to the doctrine of the immortality of the soul. We know nothing whatever of a future world which lies beyond the boundaries of our observation and experience, except what God has chosen to reveal to us. Left to the instincts and aspirations of nature, which strongly crave after immortality and glory, we can reach at best only probabilities; while the gospel gives us absolute certainty, sealed by the resurrection of Christ. The heathen notions of the future life were vague and confused. The Hindoos, Babylonians, and Egyptians had a lively sense of immortality, but mixed with the idea of endless migrations and transformations. The Buddhists, starting from the idea that existence is want, and want is suffering, make it the chief end of man to escape such migrations, and by various mortifications to prepare for final absorption in Nirwana. The popular belief among the ancient Greeks and Romans was that man passes after death into the Underworld, the Greek Hades, the Roman Orcus. According to Homer, Hades is a dark abode in the interior of the earth, with an entrance at the Western extremity of the Ocean, where the rays of the sun do not penetrate. Charon carries the dead over the stream Acheron, and the three-headed dog Cerberus watches the entrance and allows none to pass out. There the spirits exist in a disembodied state and lead a shadowy dream-life. A vague distinction was made between two regions in Hades, an Elysium (also "the Islands of the Blessed") for the good, and Tartarus for the bad. "Poets and painters," says Gibbon, peopled the infernal regions with so many phantoms and monsters, who dispensed their rewards and punishments with so little equity, that a solemn truth, the most congenial to the human heart, was oppressed and disgraced by the absurd mixture of the wildest fictions. The eleventh book of the Odyssey gives a very dreary and incoherent account of the infernal shades. Pindar and Virgil have embellished the picture; but even those poets, though more correct than their great model, are guilty of very strange inconsistencies."(170) Socrates, Plato, Cicero, Seneca, and Plutarch rose highest among the ancient philosophers in their views of the future life, but they reached only to belief in its probability—not in its certainty. Socrates, after be was condemned to death, said to his judges: "Death is either an eternal sleep, or the transition to a new life; but in neither case is it an evil;"(171) and he drank with playful irony the fatal hemlock. Plato, viewing the human soul as a portion of the eternal, infinite, all-pervading deity, believed in its pre-existence before this present life, and thus had a strong ground of hope for its continuance after death. All the souls (according to his Phaedon and Gorgias, pass into the spirit-world, the righteous into the abodes of bliss, where they live forever in a disembodied state, the wicked into Tartarus for punishment and purification (which notion prepared the way for purgatory). Plutarch, the purest and noblest among the Platonists, thought that immortality was inseparably connected with belief in an all-ruling Providence, and looked with Plato to the life beyond as promising a higher knowledge of, and closer conformity to God, but only for those few who are here purified by virtue and piety. In such rare cases, departure might be called an ascent to the stars, to heaven, to the gods, rather than a descent to Hades. He also, at the death of his daughter, expresses his faith in the blissful state of infants who die in infancy. Cicero, in his Tusculan Questions and treatise De Senectute, reflects in classical language "the ignorance, the errors, and the uncertainty of the ancient philosophers with regard to the immortality of the soul." Though strongly leaning to a positive view, he yet found it no superfluous task to quiet the fear of death in case the soul should perish with the body. The Stoics believed only in a limited immortality, or denied it altogether, and justified suicide when life became unendurable. The great men of Greece and Rome were not influenced by the idea of a future world as a motive of action. During the debate on the punishment of Catiline and his fellow-conspirators, Julius Caesar openly declared in the Roman Senate that death dissolves all the ills of mortality, and is the boundary of existence beyond which there is no more care nor joy, no more punishment for sin, nor any reward for virtue. The younger Cato, the model Stoic, agreed with Caesar; yet before he made an end to his life at Utica, he read Plato’s Phaedon. Seneca once dreamed of immortality, and almost approached the Christian hope of the birth-day of eternity, if we are to trust his rhetoric, but afterwards he awoke from the beautiful dream and committed suicide. The elder Pliny, who found a tragic death under the lava of Vesuvius, speaks of the future life as an invention of man’s vanity and selfishness, and thinks that body and soul have no more sensation after death than before birth; death becomes doubly painful if it is only the beginning of another indefinite existence. Tacitus speaks but once of immortality, and then conditionally; and he believed only in the immortality of fame. Marcus Aurelius, in sad resignation, bids nature, "Give what thou wilt, and take back again what and when thou wilt." These were noble and earnest, Romans. What can be expected from the crown of frivolous men of the world who moved within the limits of matter and sense and made present pleasure and enjoyment the chief end of life? The surviving wife of an Epicurean philosopher erected a monument to him, with the inscription "to the eternal sleep."(172) Not a few heathen epitaphs openly profess the doctrine that death ends all; while, in striking contrast with them, the humble Christian inscriptions in the catacombs express the confident hope of future bliss and glory in the uninterrupted communion of the believer with Christ and God. Yet the scepticism of the educated and half-educated could not extinguish the popular belief in the imperial age. The number of cheerless and hopeless materialistic epitaphs is, after all, very small as compared with the many thousands which reveal no such doubt, or express a belief in some kind of existence beyond the grave.(173) Of a resurrection of the body the Greeks and Romans had no conception, except in the form of shades and spectral outlines, which were supposed to surround the disembodied spirits, and to make them to some degree recognizable. Heathen philosophers, like Celsus, ridiculed the resurrection of the body as useless, absurd, and impossible. The Jewish doctrine is far in advance of heathen notions and conjectures, but presents different phases of development. (a) The Mosaic writings are remarkably silent about the future life, and emphasize the present rather than future consequences of the observance or non-observance of the law (because it had a civil or political as well as spiritual import); and hence the Sadducees accepted them, although they denied the resurrection (perhaps also the immortality of the soul). The Pentateuch contains, however, some remote and significant hints of immortality, as in the tree of life with its symbolic import;(174) in the mysterious translation of Enoch as a reward for his piety;(175) in the prohibition of necromancy;(176) in the patriarchal phrase for dying: "to be gathered to his fathers," or "to his people;"(177) and last, though not least, in the self-designation of Jehovah as "the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob," which implies their immortality, since "God is not the God of the dead, but of the living."(178) What has an eternal meaning for God must itself be eternal. (b) In the later writings of the Old Testament, especially during and after the exile, the doctrine of immortality and resurrection comes out plainly.(179) Daniel’s vision reaches out even to the final resurrection of "many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth to everlasting life," and of "some to shame and everlasting contempt," and prophesies that "they that are wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament, and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars forever and ever."(180) But before Christ, who first revealed true life, the Hebrew Sheol, the general receptacle of departing souls, remained, like the Greek Hades, a dark and dreary abode, and is so described in the Old Testament.(181) Cases like Enoch’s translation and Elijah’s ascent are altogether unique and exceptional, and imply the meaning that death is contrary to man’s original destination, and may be overcome by the power of holiness. (c) The Jewish Apocrypha (the Book of Wisdom, and the Second Book of Maccabees), and later Jewish writings (the Book of Enoch, the Apocalypse of Ezra) show some progress: they distinguish between two regions in Sheol—Paradise or Abraham’s Bosom for the righteous, and Gehinnom or Gehenna for the wicked; they emphasize the resurrection of the body, and the future rewards and punishments. (d) The Talmud adds various fanciful embellishments. It puts Paradise and Gehenna in close proximity, measures their extent, and distinguishes different departments in both corresponding to the degrees of merit and guilt. Paradise is sixty times as large as the world, and Hell sixty times as large as Paradise, for the bad preponderate here and hereafter. According to other rabbinical testimonies, both are well nigh boundless. The Talmudic descriptions of Paradise (as those of the Koran) mix sensual and spiritual delights. The righteous enjoy the vision of the Shechina and feast with the patriarchs, and with Moses and David of the flesh of leviathan, and drink wine from the cup of salvation. Each inhabitant has a house according to his merit. Among the punishments of hell the chief place is assigned to fire, which is renewed every week after the Sabbath. The wicked are boiled like the flesh in the pot, but the bad Israelites are not touched by fire, and are otherwise tormented. The severest punishment is reserved for idolaters, hypocrites, traitors, and apostates. As to the duration of future punishment the school of Shammai held that it was everlasting; while the school of Hillel inclined to the milder view of a possible redemption after repentance and purification. Some Rabbis taught that hell will cease, and that the sun will burn up and annihilate the wicked.(182) The Christian doctrine of the future life differs from the heathen, and to a less extent also from the Jewish, in the following important points: (a) It gives to the belief in a future state the absolute certainty of divine revelation, sealed by the fact of Christ’s resurrection, and thereby imparts to the present life an immeasurable importance, involving endless issues. (b) It connects the resurrection of the body with the immortality of the soul, and thus gives concrete completion to the latter, and saves the whole individuality of man from destruction. (c) It views death as the punishment of sin, and therefore as something terrible, from which nature shrinks. But its terror has been broken, and its sting extracted by Christ. (d) It qualifies the idea of a future state by the doctrine of sin and redemption, and thus makes it to the believer a state of absolute holiness and happiness, to the impenitent sinner a state of absolute misery. Death and immortality are a blessing to the one, but a terror to the other; the former can hail them with joy; the latter has reason to tremble. (e) It gives great prominence to the general judgment, after the resurrection, which determines the ultimate fate of all men according to their works done in this earthly life. But we must distinguish, in this mysterious article, what is of faith, and what is private opinion and speculation. The return of Christ to judgment with its eternal rewards and punishment is the centre of the eschatological faith of the church. The judgment is preceded by the general resurrection, and followed by life everlasting. This faith is expressed in the oecumenical creeds. The Apostles’ Creed: "He shall come to judge the quick and the dead," and "I believe in the resurrection of the body and life everlasting." The Nicene Creed: "He shall come again, with glory, to judge the quick and the dead; whose kingdom shall have no end." "And we look for the resurrection of the dead, and the life of the world to come." The Athanasian Creed, so called, adds to these simple statements a damnatory clause at the beginning, middle, and end, and makes salvation depend on belief in the orthodox catholic doctrine of the Trinity and the Incarnation, as therein stated. But that document is of much later origin, and cannot be traced beyond the sixth century. The liturgies which claim apostolic or post-apostolic origin, give devotional expression to the same essential points in the eucharistic sacrifice. The Clementine liturgy: "Being mindful, therefore, of His passion and death, and resurrection from the dead, and return into the heavens, and His future second appearing, wherein He is to come with glory and power to judge the quick and the dead, and to recompense to every one according to his works." The liturgy of James: "His second glorious and awful appearing, when He shall come with glory to judge the quick and the dead, and render to every one according to his works." The liturgy of Mark: "His second terrible and dreadful coming, in which He will come to judge righteously the quick and the dead, and to render to each man according to his works." All that is beyond these revealed and generally received articles must be left free. The time of the Second Advent, the preceding revelation of Antichrist, the millennium before or after the general judgment, the nature of the disembodied state between death and resurrection, the mode and degree of future punishment, the proportion of the saved and lost, the fate of the heathen and all who die ignorant of Christianity, the locality of heaven and hell, are open questions in eschatology about which wise and good men in the church have always differed, and will differ to the end. The Bible speaks indeed of ascending to heaven and descending to hell, but this is simply the unavoidable popular language, as when it speaks of the rising and setting sun. We do the same, although we know that in the universe of God there is neither above nor below, and that the sun does not move around the earth. The supernatural world may be very far from us, beyond the stars and beyond the boundaries of the visible created world (if it has any boundaries), or very near and round about us. At all events there is an abundance of room for all God’s children. "In my Father’s house are many mansions. I go to prepare a place for you" (John 14:2). This suffices for faith. § 156. Among the darkest points in eschatology is the middle state, or the condition of the soul between death and resurrection. It is difficult to conceive of a disembodied state of happiness or woe without physical organs for enjoyment and suffering. Justin Martyr held that the souls retain their sensibility after death, otherwise the bad would have the advantage over the good. Origen seems to have assumed some refined, spiritual corporeity which accompanies the soul on its lonely journey, and is the germ of the resurrection body; but the speculative opinions of that profound thinker were looked upon with suspicion, and some of them were ultimately condemned. The idea of the sleep of the soul (psychopannychia) had some advocates, but was expressly rejected by Tertullian.(183) Others held that the soul died with the body, and was created anew at the resurrection.(184) The prevailing view was that the soul continued in a conscious, though disembodied state, by virtue either of inherent or of communicated immortality. The nature of that state depends upon the moral character formed in this life either for weal or woe, without the possibility of a change except in the same direction. The catholic doctrine of the status intermedius was chiefly derived from the Jewish tradition of the Sheol, from the parable of Dives and Lazarus (Luke 16:19 sqq.), and from the passages of Christ’s descent into Hades.(185) The utterances of the ante-Nicene fathers are somewhat vague and confused, but receive light from the more mature statements of the Nicene and post-Nicene fathers, and may be reduced to the following points:(186) The pious who died before Christ from Abel or Adam down to John the Baptist (with rare exceptions, as Enoch, Moses, and Elijah) were detained in a part of Sheol,(187) waiting for the first Advent, and were released by Christ after the crucifixion and transferred to Paradise. This was the chief aim and result of the descensus ad inferos, as understood in the church long before it became an article of the Apostles’ Creed, first in Aquileja (where, however, Rufinus explained it wrongly, as being equivalent to burial), and then in Rome. Hermas of Rome and Clement of Alexandria supposed that the patriarchs and Old Testament saints, before their translation, were baptized by Christ and the apostles. Irenaeus repeatedly refers to the descent of Christ to the spirit-world as the only means by which the benefits of the redemption could be made known and applied to the pious dead of former ages.(188) Christian martyrs and confessors, to whom were afterwards added other eminent saints, pass immediately after death into heaven to the blessed vision of God.(189) The majority of Christian believers, being imperfect, enter for an indefinite period into a preparatory state of rest and happiness, usually called Paradise (comp. Luke 23:41) or Abraham’s Bosom (Luke 16:23). There they are gradually purged of remaining infirmities until they are ripe for heaven, into which nothing is admitted but absolute purity. Origen assumed a constant progression to higher and higher regions of knowledge and bliss. (After the fifth or sixth century, certainly since Pope Gregory I., Purgatory was substituted for Paradise). The locality of Paradise is uncertain: some imagined it to be a higher region of Hades beneath the earth, yet "afar off" from Gehenna, and separated from it by "a great gulf" (comp. Luke 16:23, 26);(190) others transferred it to the lower regions of heaven above the earth, yet clearly distinct from the final home of the blessed.(191) Impenitent Christians and unbelievers go down to the lower regions of Hades (Gehenna, Tartarus, Hell) into a preparatory state of misery and dreadful expectation of the final judgment. From the fourth century Hades came to be identified with Hell, and this confusion passed into many versions of the Bible, including that of King James. The future fate of the heathen and of unbaptized children was left in hopeless darkness, except by Justin and the Alexandrian fathers, who extended the operations of divine grace beyond the limits of the visible church. Justin Martyr must have believed, from his premises, in the salvation of all those heathen who had in this life followed the light of the Divine Logos and died in a state of unconscious Christianity, or preparedness for Christianity. For, he says, "those who lived with the Logos were Christians, although they were esteemed atheists, as Socrates and Heraclitus, and others like them."(192) There are, in the other world, different degrees of happiness and misery according to the degrees of merit and guilt. This is reasonable in itself, and supported by scripture. With the idea of the imperfection of the middle state and the possibility of progressive amelioration, is connected the commemoration of the departed, and prayer in their behalf. No trace of the custom is found in the New Testament nor in the canonical books of the Old, but an isolated example, which seems to imply habit, occurs in the age of the Maccabees, when Judas Maccabaeus and his company offered prayer and sacrifice for those slain in battle," that they might be delivered from sin."(193) In old Jewish service-books there are prayers for the blessedness of the dead.(194) The strong sense of the communion of saints unbroken by death easily accounts for the rise of a similar custom among the early Christians. Tertullian bears clear testimony to its existence at his time. "We offer," he says "oblations for the dead on the anniversary of their birth," i.e. their celestial birthday.(195) He gives it as a mark of a Christian widow, that she prays for the soul of her husband, and requests for him refreshment and fellowship in the first resurrection; and that she offers sacrifice on the anniversaries of his falling asleep.(196) Eusebius narrates that at the tomb of Constantine a vast crowd of people, in company with the priests of God, with tears and great lamentation offered their prayers to God for the emperor’s soul.(197) Augustin calls prayer for the pious dead in the eucharistic sacrifice an observance of the universal church, handed down from the fathers.(198) He himself remembered in prayer his godly mother at her dying request. This is confirmed by the ancient liturgies, which express in substance the devotions of the ante-Nicene age, although they were not committed to writing before the fourth century. The commemoration of the pious dead is an important part in the eucharistic prayers. Take the following from the Liturgy of St. James: "Remember, O Lord God, the spirits of whom we have made mention, and of whom we have not made mention, who are of the true faith,(199) from righteous Abel unto this day; do Thou Thyself give them rest there in the land of the living, in Thy kingdom, in the delight of Paradise,(200)in the Bosom of Abraham and of Isaac and of Jacob, our holy fathers; whence pain and grief and lamentation have fled away: there the light of Thy countenance looks upon them, and gives them light for evermore." The Clementine Liturgy in the eighth book of the "Apostolical Constitutions" has likewise a prayer "for those who rest in faith," in these words: "We make an offering to Thee for all Thy saints who have pleased Thee from the beginning of the world, patriarchs, prophets, just men, apostles, martyrs, confessors, bishops, elders, deacons, subdeacons, singers, virgins, widows, laymen, and all whose names Thou Thyself knowest." These views of the middle state in connection with prayers for the dead show a strong tendency to the Roman Catholic doctrine of Purgatory, which afterwards came to prevail in the West through the great weight of St. Augustin and Pope Gregory I. But there is, after all, a considerable difference. The ante-Nicene idea of the middle state of the pious excludes, or at all events ignores, the idea of penal suffering, which is an essential part of the Catholic conception of purgatory. It represents the condition of the pious as one of comparative happiness, inferior only to the perfect happiness after the resurrection. Whatever and wherever Paradise may be, it belongs to the heavenly world; while purgatory is supposed to be a middle region between heaven and hell, and to border rather on the latter. The sepulchral inscriptions in the catacombs have a prevailingly cheerful tone, and represent the departed souls as being "in peace" and "living in Christ," or "in God."(201) The same view is substantially preserved in the Oriental church, which holds that the souls of the departed believers may be aided by the prayers of the living, but are nevertheless "in light and rest, with a foretaste of eternal happiness."(202) Yet alongside with this prevailing belief, there are traces of the purgatorial idea of suffering the temporal consequences of sin, and a painful struggle after holiness. Origen, following in the path of Plato, used the term "purgatorial fire,"(203) by which the remaining stains of the soul shall be burned away; but he understood it figuratively, and connected it with the consuming fire at the final judgment, while Augustin and Gregory I. transferred it to the middle state. The common people and most of the fathers understood it of a material fire; but this is not a matter of faith, and there are Roman divines(204) who confine the purgatorial sufferings to the mind and the conscience. A material fire would be very harmless without a material body. A still nearer approach to the Roman purgatory was made by Tertullian and Cyprian, who taught that a special satisfaction and penance was required for sins committed after baptism, and that the last farthing must be paid (Matt. 5:20) before the soul can be released from prison and enter into heaven. § 157. After Judgment. Future Punishment. The doctrine of the Fathers on future punishment is discussed by Dr. Edward Beecher, l.c., and in the controversial works called forth by Canon Farrar’s Eternal Hope (Five Sermons preached in Westminster Abbey, Nov. 1877. Lond., 1879.) See especially Dr. Pusey: "What is of Faith as to Everlasting Punishment?" A Reply to Dr. Farrar’s Challenge. Oxf. and Lond., second ed. 1880 (284 pages). Canon F. W. Farrar: Mercy and Judgment: A few last words on Christian Eschatology with reference to Dr. Pusey’s "What is of Faith?" London and N. York, 1881 (485 pages). See chs. II., III., IX.-XII. Farrar opposes with much fervor "the current opinions about Hell," and reduces it to the smallest possible dimensions of time and space, but expressly rejects Universalism. He accepts with Pusey the Romanizing view of "future purification" (instead of "probation"), and thus increases the number of the saved by withdrawing vast multitudes of imperfect Christians from the awful doom. After the general judgment we have nothing revealed but the boundless prospect of aeonian life and aeonian death. This is the ultimate boundary of our knowledge. There never was in the Christian church any difference of opinion concerning the righteous, who shall inherit eternal life and enjoy the blessed communion of God forever and ever. But the final fate of the impenitent who reject the offer of salvation admits of three answers to the reasoning mind: everlasting punishment, annihilation, restoration (after remedial punishment and repentance). I. Everlasting Punishment of the wicked always was, and always will be the orthodox theory. It was held by the Jews at the time of Christ, with the exception of the Sadducces, who denied the resurrection.(205) It is endorsed by the highest authority of the most merciful Being, who sacrificed his own life for the salvation of sinners.(206) Consequently the majority of the fathers who speak plainly on this terrible subject, favor this view. Ignatius speaks of "the unquenchable fire;"(207) Hermas, of some "who will not be saved," but "shall utterly perish," because they will not repent.(208) Justin Martyr teaches that the wicked or hopelessly impenitent will be raised at the judgment to receive eternal punishment. He speaks of it in twelve passages. "Briefly," he says, "what we look for, and have learned from Christ, and what we teach, is as follows. Plato said to the same effect, that Rhadamanthus and Minos would punish the wicked when they came to them; we say that the same thing will take place; but that the judge will be Christ, and that their souls will be united to the same bodies, and will undergo an eternal punishment (aivwnivan kovlasin) and not, as Plato said, a period of only a thousand years (ciliontaeth' perivodon)"(209) In another place: "We believe that all who live wickedly and do not repent, will be punished in eternal fire" (ejn aijwnivw/ puriv).(210) Such language is inconsistent with the annihilation theory for which Justin M. has been claimed.(211) He does, indeed, reject with several other ante-Nicene writers, the Platonic idea that the soul is in itself and independently immortal(212) and hints at the possibility of the final destruction of the wicked,(213) but he puts that possibility countless ages beyond the final judgment, certainly beyond the Platonic millennium of punishment, so that it loses all practical significance and ceases to give relief. Irenaeus has been represented as holding inconsistently all three theories, or at least as hesitating between the orthodox view and the annihilation scheme. He denies, like Justin Martyr, the necessary and intrinsic immortality of the soul, and makes it dependent on God for the continuance in life as well as for life itself.(214) But in paraphrasing the apostolic rule of faith he mentions eternal punishment, and in another place he accepts as certain truth that "eternal fire is prepared for sinners," because "the Lord openly affirms, and the other Scriptures prove" it.(215) Hippolytus approves the eschatology of the Pharisees as regards the resurrection, the immortality of the soul, the judgment and conflagration, everlasting life and "everlasting punishment;" and in another place be speaks of "the rayless scenery of gloomy Tartarus, where never shines a beam from the radiating voice of the Word."(216) According to Tertullian the future punishment "will continue, not for a long time, but forever."(217) It does credit to his feelings when he says that no innocent man can rejoice in the punishment of the guilty, however just, but will grieve rather. Cyprian thinks that the fear of hell is the only ground of the fear of death to any one, and that we should have before our eyes the fear of God and eternal punishment much more than the fear of men and brief suffering.(218) The generality of this belief among Christians is testified by Celsus, who tells them that the heathen priests threaten the same "eternal punishment" as they, and that the only question was which was right, since both claimed the truth with equal confidence.(219) The final Annihilation of the wicked removes all discord from the universe of God at the expense of the natural immortality of the soul, and on the ground that sin will ultimately destroy the sinner, and thus destroy itself. This theory is attributed to Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, and others, who believed only in a conditional immortality which may be forfeited; but, as we have just seen, their utterances in favor of eternal punishment are too clear and strong to justify the inference which they might have drawn from their psychology. Arnobius, however, seems to have believed in actual annihilation; for he speaks of certain souls that "are engulfed and burned up," or "hurled down and having been reduced to nothing, vanish in the frustration of a perpetual destruction."(220) The Apokatastasis or final restoration of all rational beings to holiness and happiness. This seems to be the most satisfactory speculative solution of the problem of sin, and secures perfect harmony in the creation, but does violence to freedom with its power to perpetuate resistance, and Ignores the hardening nature of sin and the ever increasing difficulty of repentance. If conversion and salvation are an ultimate necessity, they lose their moral character, and moral aim. Origen was the first Christian Universalist. He taught a final restoration, but with modesty as a speculation rather than a dogma, in his youthful work De Principiis (written before 231), which was made known in the West by the loose version of Rufinus (398).(221) In his later writings there are only faint traces of it; he seems at least to have modified it, and exempted Satan from final repentance and salvation, but this defeats the end of the theory.(222) He also obscured it by his other theory of the necessary mutability of free will, and the constant succession of fall and redemption.(223) Universal salvation (including Satan) was clearly taught by Gregory of Nyssa, a profound thinker of the school of Origen (d. 395), and, from an exegetical standpoint, by the eminent Antiochian divines Diodorus of Tarsus (d. 394) and Theodore of Mopsuestia (d. 429), and many Nestorian bishops.(224) In the West also at the time of Augustin (d. 430) there were, as he says, "multitudes who did not believe in eternal punishment." But the view of Origen was rejected by Epiphanius, Jerome, and Augustin, and at last condemned as one of the Origenistic errors under the Emperor Justinian (543).(225) Since that time universalism was regarded as a heresy, but is tolerated in Protestant churches as a private speculative opinion or charitable hope.(226) § 158. The most striking point in the eschatology of the ante-Nicene age is the prominent chiliasm, or millennarianism, that is the belief of a visible reign of Christ in glory on earth with the risen saints for a thousand years, before the general resurrection and judgment.(227) It was indeed not the doctrine of the church embodied in any creed or form of devotion, but a widely current opinion of distinguished teachers, such as Barnabas, Papias, Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Methodius, and Lactantius; while Caius, Origen, Dionysius the Great, Eusebius (as afterwards Jerome and Augustin) opposed it. The Jewish chiliasm rested on a carnal misapprehension of the Messianic kingdom, a literal interpretation of prophetic figures, and an overestimate of the importance of the Jewish people and the holy city as the centre of that kingdom. It was developed shortly before and after Christ in the apocalyptic literature, as the Book of Enoch, the Apocalypse of Baruch, 4th Esdras, the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, and the Sibylline Books. It was adopted by the heretical sect of the Ebionites, and the Gnostic Cerinthus.(228) The Christian chiliasm is the Jewish chiliasm spiritualized and fixed upon the second, instead of the first, coming of Christ. It distinguishes, moreover, two resurrections, one before and another after the millennium, and makes the millennial reign of Christ only a prelude to his eternal reign in heaven, from which it is separated by a short interregnum of Satan. The millennium is expected to come not as the legitimate result of a historical process but as a sudden supernatural revelation. The advocates of this theory appeal to the certain promises of the Lord,(229) but particularly to the hieroglyphic passage of the Apocalypse, which teaches a millennial reign of Christ upon this earth after the first resurrection and before the creation of the new heavens and the new earth.(230) In connection with this the general expectation prevailed that the return of the Lord was near, though uncertain and unascertainable as to its day and hour, so that believers may be always ready for it.(231) This hope, through the whole age of persecution, was a copious fountain of encouragement and comfort under the pains of that martyrdom which sowed in blood the seed of a bountiful harvest for the church. Among the Apostolic Fathers Barnabas is the first and the only one who expressly teaches a pre-millennial reign of Christ on earth. He considers the Mosaic history of the creation a type of six ages of labor for the world, each lasting a thousand years, and of a millennium of rest; since with God "one day is as a thousand years." The millennial Sabbath on earth will be followed by an eighth and eternal day in a new world, of which the Lord’s Day (called by Barnabas "the eighth day") is the type.(232) Papias of Hierapolis, a pious but credulous contemporary of Polycarp, entertained quaint and extravagant notions of the happiness of the millennial reign, for which he appealed to apostolic tradition. He put into the mouth of Christ himself a highly figurative description of the more than tropical fertility of that period, which is preserved and approved by Irenaeus, but sounds very apocryphal.(233) Justin Martyr represents the transition from the Jewish Christian to the Gentile Christian chiliasm. He speaks repeatedly of the second parousia of Christ in the clouds of heaven, surrounded by the holy angels. It will be preceded by the near manifestation of the man of sin (a[nqrwpo" th'" ajnomiva") who speaks blasphemies against the most high God, and will rule three and a half years. He is preceded by heresies and false prophets.(234) Christ will then raise the patriarchs, prophets, and pious Jews, establish the millennium, restore Jerusalem, and reign there in the midst of his saints; after which the second and general resurrection and judgment of the world will take place. He regarded this expectation of the earthly perfection of Christ’s kingdom as the key-stone of pure doctrine, but adds that many pure and devout Christians of his day did not share this opinion.(235) After the millennium the world will be annihilated, or transformed.(236) In his two Apologies, Justin teaches the usual view of the general resurrection and judgment, and makes no mention of the millennium, but does not exclude it.(237) The other Greek Apologists are silent on the subject, and cannot be quoted either for or against chiliasm. Irenaeus, on the strength of tradition from St. John and his disciples, taught that after the destruction of the Roman empire, and the brief raging of antichrist (lasting three and a half years or 1260 days), Christ will visibly appear, will bind Satan, will reign at the rebuilt city of Jerusalem with the little band of faithful confessors and the host of risen martyrs over the nations of the earth, and will celebrate the millennial sabbath of preparation for the eternal glory of heaven; then, after a temporary liberation of Satan, follows the final victory, the general resurrection, the judgment of the world, and the consummation in the new heavens and the new earth.(238) Tertullian was an enthusiastic Chiliast, and pointed not only to the Apocalypse, but also to the predictions of the Montanist prophets.(239) But the Montanists substituted Pepuza in Phrygia for Jerusalem, as the centre of Christ’s reign, and ran into fanatical excesses, which brought chiliasm into discredit, and resulted in its condemnation by several synods in Asia Minor.(240) After Tertullian, and independently of Montanism, chiliasm was taught by Commodian towards the close of the third century,(241) Lactantius,(242) and Victorinus of Petau,(243) at the beginning of the fourth. Its last distinguished advocates in the East were Methodius (d., a martyr, 311), the opponent of Origen,(244) and Apollinaris of Laodicea in Syria. We now turn to the anti-Chiliasts. The opposition began during the Montanist movement in Asia Minor. Caius of Rome attacked both Chiliasm and Montanism, and traced the former to the hated heretic Cerinthus.(245) The Roman church seems never to have sympathized with either, and prepared itself for a comfortable settlement and normal development in this world. In Alexandria, Origen opposed chiliasm as a Jewish dream, and spiritualized the symbolical language of the prophets.(246) His distinguished pupil, Dionysius the Great (d. about 264), checked the chiliastic movement when it was revived by Nepos in Egypt, and wrote an elaborate work against it, which is lost. He denied the Apocalypse to the apostle John, and ascribed it to a presbyter of that name.(247) Eusebius inclined to the same view. But the crushing blow came from the great change in the social condition and prospects of the church in the Nicene age. After Christianity, contrary to all expectation, triumphed in the Roman empire, and was embraced by the Caesars themselves, the millennial reign, instead of being anxiously waited and prayed for, began to be dated either from the first appearance of Christ, or from the conversion of Constantine and the downfall of paganism, and to be regarded as realized in the glory of the dominant imperial state-church. Augustin, who himself had formerly entertained chiliastic hopes, framed the new theory which reflected the social change, and was generally accepted. The apocalyptic millennium he understood to be the present reign of Christ in the Catholic church, and the first resurrection, the translation of the martyrs and saints to heaven, where they participate in Christ’s reign.(248) It was consistent with this theory that towards the close of the first millennium of the Christian era there was a wide-spread expectation in Western Europe that the final judgment was at hand. From the time of Constantine and Augustin chiliasm took its place among the heresies, and was rejected subsequently even by the Protestant reformers as a Jewish dream.(249) But it was revived from time to time as an article of faith and hope by pious individuals and whole sects, often in connection with historic pessimism, with distrust in mission work, as carried on by human agencies, with literal interpretations of prophecy, and with peculiar notions about Antichrist, the conversion and restoration of the Jews, their return to the Holy Land, and also with abortive attempts to calculate "the times and seasons" of the Second Advent, which "the Father hath put in his own power" (Acts 1:7), and did not choose to reveal to his own Son in the days of his flesh. In a free spiritual sense, however, millennarianism will always survive as the hope of a golden age of the church on earth, and of a great sabbath of history after its many centuries of labor and strife. The church militant ever longs after the church triumphant, and looks "for new heavens and a new earth, wherein dwelleth righteousness" (2 Pet. 3:13). Engelhardt)，第206页，以及唐纳森 (Donaldson)，II. 321。↩︎ 持此说的有佩塔维乌斯 (Petavius)、比彻 (Beecher，第206页)、法勒（第236页）等人。↩︎ 《与特利弗对话》(Dial. c. Tr.) 4、5；参《护教篇》(Apol.) I. 21。他的门徒塔提安 (Tatian) 在反对柏拉图派 (Platonists) 时说（《驳希腊人》[Adv. Graec.]，第13章）：“希腊人哪，灵魂本身并非不朽，而是有死的（οὐκ ἐστιν ἀθάνατος ἡ ψυχὴ καθ’ ἑαυτήν, θνητὴ δέ*）。然而，它也可能不死。”爱任纽、安提阿的提阿非罗 (Theophilus of Antioch)、阿尔诺比乌斯 (Arnobius) 和拉克坦提乌斯 (Lactantius) 都持同样的见解。见尼奇 (Nitzsch)，I. 351–353。↩︎ 在《与特利弗对话》(Dial.) 第5章中，他借那位使他归信的老人之口说：“那些配得见上帝的人不再死亡；其余的人则要受刑罚，只要他愿意让他们继续存在并受刑罚，就一直如此。”但他在紧前面曾说：“我并不是说一切灵魂都要死亡；因为那对恶人倒是天赐的福分。那么如何呢？敬虔人的灵魂留在较好的地方，不义之人和恶人的灵魂则在较坏的地方，等候审判的时候。”参奥托 (Otto) 对此段的注释，《著作集》(Op.) II. 26。↩︎ 《驳异端》(Adv. Haer.) 11. 34，§ 3：“omnia quae facta sunt ... perseverant quoadusque ea Deus et esse et perseverare voluerit.”（一切受造之物……只要上帝愿意它们存在并持续，它们就持续。）爱任纽推论说，凡受造之物都有开端，因此也可能有终结。它是否继续，取决于人的感恩或忘恩。凡保存生命恩赐、感谢赐予者的人，必得长久的年日，直到永永远远（accipiet et in saeculum saeculi longitudinem dierum）；但那丢弃这恩赐、向造他的主忘恩的人，便“使自己永远失去持续”（ipse se privat in saeculum saeculi perseverantia）。根据这段仅存于不完善的拉丁文译本中的文字，多德韦尔 (Dodwell)、比彻（第260页）和法勒（241页）推断爱任纽教导灭绝说，并将 perseverantia 解释为持续存在；马叙埃 (Massuet，见其载于施蒂伦 [Stieren] 1. 415的注释) 和蒲西（第183页）却将 perseverantia 解释为在上帝里面真实生命的持续，或永恒的幸福。必须承认，这段话并不清楚，因为 longitudo dierum（长久的年日）与 perseverantia（持续）并不相同，而 perseverantia 也不等于 existentia 或 vita（存在或生命）。在第IV卷20，7中，爱任纽说，基督“为人的益处成为父恩典的分赐者……免得人完全离弃上帝，便不复存在”（cessaret esse）；但他又补充说：“人的生命在于瞻仰上帝”（vita autem hominus visio Dei）。在归于他名下的第四篇普法夫残篇 (Pfaffian Fragment) 中（施蒂伦 I. 889），他说基督“将在末时来临，除灭一切恶（εἰς τὸ καταργῆσαι πᾶν τὸ κακὸν*），并使万有和好（εἰς τὸ ἀποκαταλλάξαι τὸ πάντα*，引自《歌罗西书》1:20），使一切不洁都归于终结”。这段文字与《哥林多前书》15:28和《歌罗西书》1:20一样，似乎指向普遍复归，而非灭绝；但它也和这些保罗书信的经文一样，容许作出与永刑相一致的解释。见施蒂伦的长注。↩︎ 《驳异端》(Adv. Haer.) III. 4，1；If. 28，7。见蒲西，第177–181页。齐格勒 (Ziegler)（《爱任纽》[Irenäus]，第312页）说，爱任纽在好几处经文中教导刑罚的永恒性，或以此为前提，并引述III. 23，3；IV. 27，4；28，1；IV. 33，11；39，4；40，1和2。↩︎ 《驳一切异端》(Philos.) IX. 23、30。↩︎ 《护教篇》(Apol.)，第45章。参《论灵魂的见证》(De Test. An.) 4；《论观剧》(De Spect.) 19、30。蒲西，第184页及下页。↩︎ 《论死亡》(De Mortal.) 10；《书信》(Ep.) VIII. 2。蒲西 (Pusey)，第190页。他还引述《克莱门认知录》(Rocognitions of Clement) 和《克莱门讲道集》(Clementine Homilies，XI. 11)，以支持这一方的观点。↩︎ 奥利金 (Origen)，《驳塞尔苏斯》(C. Cels.) VIII. 48。奥利金在答辩中并未否认这一事实，而是力图证明真理在基督徒一方。↩︎ 《驳异教徒》(Adv. Gent.) 11. 14。有条件的不朽及恶人灭绝的理论，近来由一位虔诚的英国作者爱德华·怀特牧师 (Rev. Edward White) 在《在基督里的生命》(Life in Christ) 中重新提出。R. 罗特博士 (Dr. R. Rothe) 也主张灭绝说，但认为只有当恶人的归信在道德上已成为不可能之后，灭绝才会发生。见其身后由申克尔 (Schenkel) 编的《教义学》(Dogmatik)，II. 335。↩︎ 《论首要原理》(De Princ.) I. 6，3。参《耶利米书讲道》(In Jer. Hom.) 19；《驳塞尔苏斯》(C. Cels.) VI. 26。↩︎ 从奥古斯丁 (Augustin) 到尼奇 (Nitzsch，I. 402)，人们通常断言，奥利金将撒但也包括在万有复归（ἀποκατάστασις τῶν πάντων*）之中；然而，他在《罗马书注释》(In Ep. ad Rom.) 第VIII卷9（《著作集》[Opera] IV. 634）中说，撒但不会归信，即使到世界末了也不会；而在《致亚历山大的几位朋友》(Ad quosdam amicos Alex.) 一信中（《著作集》[Opera] I. 5，蒲西引于第125页），他又说：“虽然他们说，那邪恶之父，也是那些将被逐出上帝国度之人的灭亡之父，可以得救——这种话，即使丧失理智的人也说不出来。”↩︎ 他论到复归在若干世代中完成之后，又提及πάλιν ἄλλη ἀρχὴ*。见尼安德 (Neander) 精审的评论，I. 656（美国版）。↩︎ 尼奇 (Nitzsch，I. 403及下页) 也将拿先斯的贵格利 (Gregory Nazianzen)，并且可能还有金口约翰 (Chrysostom)，列入普救论者之中。法勒 (Farrar) 也如此，且更为肯定（第249页及后、271页及后）。但支持相反立场的段落更为有力，见蒲西，第209页及后、244页及后，不能仅以“迁就流行的看法”来解释。不过，金口约翰确实尊崇奥利金的名声，颂扬他的老师、大数的狄奥多鲁 (Diodorus of Tarsus)，而他对《哥林多前书》15:28的解释也似乎指向复归。蒲西将狄奥多鲁和摩普绥提亚的狄奥多若 (Theodore of Mopsuestia) 视为聂斯托利主义 (Nestorianism) 的创始者，对他们过于贬抑，并不公正地断言他们否认道成肉身（第223–226页）。他们与金口约翰乃是健全的文法释经法的奠基者，反对奥利金学派在寓意解释上的种种过度发挥。↩︎ 蒲西 (Pusey) 坚称（第125–137页），奥利金曾被553年的第五次大公会议定罪；但赫费勒 (Hefele) 确凿地证明，那十五条反对奥利金的咒诅条款，是543年在门纳斯 (Mennas) 主持下举行的君士坦丁堡地方会议通过的。见其《大公会议史》(Conciliengesch.)，第2版，II. 859及后。此前杜潘 (Dupin)、瓦尔希 (Walch) 和德林格 (Döllinger) 已主张同一看法。↩︎ 至少在德国的路德宗教会和英格兰教会中是如此。本格尔 (Bengel) 极为谨慎地暗示复归说，符腾堡 (Würtemberg) 的敬虔派则普遍持此说。在近代神学家中，德国的奥利金——施莱尔马赫 (Schleiermacher)——是最杰出的普救论者。他的出发点并非如奥利金那样是自由，而是相反的加尔文主义理论，即对个人和民族的特殊拣选；这种拣选必然包含特殊的弃绝，或更确切地说，越过不选，但这只是暂时的，直到拣选最终临到外邦人的全数和以色列全家。撒但对他并不构成障碍，因为他否认撒但作为位格的存在。近来起源于美国的一个宗派，即普救派 (Universalists)，有一份包含三条的信条，称为《温彻斯特信条》(Winchester Confession，1803年)；其中一条教导“全人类大家庭”最终将恢复“圣洁与幸福”。↩︎ Chiliasm（千禧年说，源于χίλια ἔτη*，意为一千年，《启示录》20:2、3）是这一理论的希腊语名称；millennarianism 或 millennialism（源于拉丁文 mille anni，一千年）则是同一理论的拉丁语名称。其信奉者称为 Chiliasts 或 Millennarians（千禧年论者），也称 Pre-millennarians 或 Pre-millennialists（前千禧年论者，表明他们相信基督将在千禧年之前再来）；但其中也包括许多仅仅相信基督教的黄金时代尚未来到的人。Post-millennarians（后千禧年论者）或 Anti-millennarians（反千禧年论者），则是把基督第二次降临置于千禧年之后的人。↩︎ 见优西比乌 (Eusebius)，《教会史》(H. E.) III. 27、28。↩︎ 《马太福音》5:4；19:28；《路加福音》14:12及下节。↩︎ 《启示录》20:1–6。这是整部圣经中唯一一段严格意义上论及千禧年的经文。对于千禧年应按字面还是象征意义理解，以及它开始于过去还是将来，释经家至今仍有分歧。但另有一些经文也被用来为千禧年理论提供间接支持，尤其是《以赛亚书》11:4–9；《使徒行传》3:21；《罗马书》11:15。现代前千禧年论者还援引旧约中关于犹太人在圣地复兴的预言，称这些是尚未应验的预言。但古代千禧年论者将这些预言应用于基督教会，视其为真正的以色列。↩︎ 参《马太福音》24:33、36；《马可福音》13:32；《使徒行传》1:7；《帖撒罗尼迦前书》5:1、2；《彼得后书》3:10；《启示录》1:3；3:3。↩︎ 《巴拿巴书信》(Barn. Epist.) 第15章。他的观点似乎取自《诗篇》90:4、《彼得后书》3:8，但主要来自犹太传统。他没有引用《启示录》。见奥托 (Otto) 载于希尔根费尔德 (Hilgenfeld) 主编的《科学神学杂志》(Zeitschrift für wissenschaftliche Theologie)，1877年，第525–529页的文章，以及丰克 (Funk) 在《使徒教父集》(Patr. Apost.) I. 46的注释。↩︎ 《驳异端》(Adv. Haer.) V. 33，§ 3（施蒂伦 [Stieren] 编，I. 809），引自《主的圣言》(The Oracles of the Lord) 第四卷：“日子将到，葡萄树生长，每棵有一万条枝，每条枝有一万条细枝，每条真正的细枝有一万根嫩条，每根嫩条有一万串葡萄，每串有一万颗葡萄，每颗葡萄榨后都出二十五量酒。当一位圣徒伸手拿一串葡萄时，另一串就会喊道：‘我是一串更好的葡萄，拿我吧；借着我称颂主。’同样，[他说，]‘一粒麦子将长出一万穗，每穗有一万粒，每粒可出十磅纯净的细面粉；苹果、种子和青草也将按同样的比例出产；一切动物以地上的出产为食，届时都将和平相处，完全顺服于人。’”这些话是由“那些见过主的门徒约翰的长老们”传给帕皮亚 (Papias) 的；他们记得曾从约翰那里听见这些话，说是出自主。在第一世纪末或第二世纪初的《巴录启示录》(Apocalypse of Baruch) 第二十九章，也有类似的弥赛亚时代描述：“大地将出产果实，一结一万；一棵葡萄树上将有一千串，一串将出一千颗葡萄，一颗葡萄将出一千粒浆果，一粒浆果将出一量酒。饥饿的人将欢喜，他们将每日再见奇事。因为诸灵将从我面前出去，每早带来香料的芬芳，到一日将尽时，带来滴下康健甘露的云彩。那时，吗哪的宝藏将再从上头降下，他们在那些年间将以此为食。”拉丁文见弗里切 (Fritzsche) 编《旧约伪经集》(Libri Apoc. V. T.)，第666页。↩︎ 《与特利丰对话》(Dial. c. Tryph.) 第32、51、110章。参《但以理书》7:25及《帖撒罗尼迦后书》2:8。↩︎ 《对话》(Dial.) 第80、81章。他援引《以赛亚书》（65:17及下节）、《以西结书》的预言、《诗篇》90:4，以及“一个名叫约翰、是基督使徒之一的人”所写的《启示录》。在另一段文字，即《对话》(Dial.) 第113章中，游斯丁 (Justin) 说，正如约书亚领以色列人进入圣地，将土地分给各支派，基督也将使散居各地的以色列人归信，并分赐那美地；但不是作为地上的产业，而是赐给我们（ἡμῖν*）永远的基业。他将在耶路撒冷照耀，作永远的光，因为他是照着麦基洗德的等次作撒冷王，也是至高者永远的祭司。但他没有提及千禧年后撒但被释放的事。参M. 冯·恩格尔哈特 (M. von Engelhardt)，《殉道者游斯丁的基督教》(Das Christenthum Justins des Märt.，1878年)，第302–307页，以及唐纳森 (Donaldson)，《基督教文献批判史》(Crit. Hist. of Christ. Lit.) II. 316–322，对游斯丁末世论的讨论。↩︎ 这一点尚有争议。泽米施 (Semisch) 主张灭绝，魏茨泽克 (Weizsäcker) 主张转化。冯·恩格尔哈特 (von Engelhardt，第309页) 则未作定论。在《对话》(Dial.) 第113章，游斯丁说，上帝将借基督更新（καινουργεῖν*）天地；在《护教篇》(Apologies) 中，他则说世界将被焚毁。↩︎ 《护教篇》(Apol.) I. 50、51、52。因此，唐纳森 (Donaldson，11. 263) 和布里格斯博士 (Dr. Briggs，前引书，第21页) 怀疑《对话》中的千禧年论段落（至少第81章）是后人插入的，或文本遭到讹改，但这种怀疑毫无根据。哲罗姆 (Jerome) 的千禧年论者名单中没有游斯丁，并不能推翻所有抄本的见证。↩︎ 《驳异端》(Adv. Haer.) V. 23–36。关于爱任纽 (Irenaeus) 的末世论，见齐格勒 (Ziegler)，《里昂主教爱任纽》(Iren. der B. v. Lyon，柏林 [Berl.]，1871年)，第298–320页；以及基尔希纳 (Kirchner)，《爱任纽的末世论》(Die Eschatol. d. Iren.)，载《研究与评论》(Studien und Kritiken)，1863年，第315–358页。↩︎ 《论肉身的复活》(De Res. Carn.) 25；《驳马吉安》(Adv. Marc.) III. 24；IV. 29等。他曾在一部专著《论信徒的盼望》(De Spe Fidelium) 中讨论此题，该书现已散佚。↩︎ 见§ 111，第424页及下页。↩︎ 《驳外邦诸神训诫》(Instruct. adv. Gentium Deos)，43、44，其中带有犹太人的观念，认为千禧年间的婚姻将多有生育。↩︎ 《神圣教理》(Instit.) VII. 24；《概要》(Epit.) 71、72。他引用西比拉书 (Sibylline books)，并期待世界迅速终结，但认为只要罗马城尚存，末日就不会来到。↩︎ 见其《启示录注释》及残篇《论世界的构造》(De Fabrica Mundi，一部《创世记注释》的一部分)。哲罗姆将他列为千禧年论者。↩︎ 见其《十童女之筵席》(Banquet of the Ten Virgins)，IX. 5，及《论复活》(Discourse on Resurrection)。↩︎ 优西比乌 (Eusebius)，《教会史》(H. E.) II. 25（反对孟他努派的普罗克鲁 [Proclus]），及III. 28（反对千禧年说）。↩︎ 《论首要原理》(De Princ.) II. 11。不过，他所针对的是一种极为感官化的千禧年观念，其中有婚娶和奢华的宴席。↩︎ 优西比乌 (Eusebius)，VII. 24、25。↩︎ 《上帝之城》(De Civit. Dei)，XX. 6–10。↩︎ 《奥格斯堡信条》(Augsburg Confession) 第XVII条谴责重洗派 (Anabaptists) 及其他人，“他们如今散布犹太人的见解，说在死人复活以前，敬虔者将占有世上的国度，恶人则处处受到压制”。克兰麦 (Cranmer) 于1553年拟定的圣公会信条第41条，将千禧年描述为“犹太人老朽昏聩的寓言”；但后来在伊丽莎白 (Elizabeth) 治下修订时（1563年），此条被删除。↩︎

title: 《基督教会史》·第二卷·第十一章 尼西亚会议以前时期的异端
text: Translated from Philip Schaff's History of The Christian Church 第十一章 尼西亚会议以前时期的异端 目录 § 112. 教会内部的犹太教与异教 § 113. 拿撒勒派与伊便派（厄尔克赛派、曼达派） § 114. 伪克莱门文献中的伊便尼主义 § 115. 诺斯替主义：文献 § 116. 诺斯替主义的含义、起源与性质 § 117. 诺斯替主义的体系及其神学 § 118. 诺斯替主义的伦理 § 119. 崇拜与组织 § 120. 诺斯替主义的学派 § 121. 行邪术的西门与西门派 § 122. 尼哥拉党 § 123. 克林妥 § 124. 巴西里得 § 125. 瓦伦廷 (Valentinus) § 126. 瓦伦廷学派：赫拉克利翁、托勒密、马科斯、巴尔德萨尼、哈摩尼乌斯 § 127. 马吉安及其学派 § 128. 俄斐派、塞特派、佩拉特派、该隐派 § 129. 萨图尔尼努斯 (Saturninus，又名 Satornilos) § 130. 卡尔波克拉底 (Carpocrates) § 131. 塔提安与禁欲派 § 132. 诺斯替派的游斯丁 § 133. 赫尔摩根尼 § 134. 其他诺斯替派别 § 135. 摩尼与摩尼教徒 § 136. 摩尼教的体系 § 112. 教会内部的犹太教与异教 前面各章已经叙述了教会在道德与思想上，如何战胜公开表明立场、始终一贯的犹太教与异教；现在我们必须考察教会与这些敌人以隐蔽而更危险的形式所进行的深刻而激烈的斗争：犹太教与异教披上基督教的外衣，潜藏其中，威胁着要使教会犹太教化和异教化。若不认识教父时期的异端，就绝不能透彻理解教父神学与文献。这些异端在古代希腊与拉丁教会的神学运动中所起的作用，与各种形式的理性主义 (Rationalism) 在欧美新教教会现代神学中所起的作用同样重要。 犹太教及其宗教与圣书，希腊罗马异教及其世俗文化、科学与艺术，本应进入基督教之中，得到转化与成圣。然而，即使在使徒时期，许多犹太人和外邦人也只是受了水的洗，并未受福音的圣灵与火的洗，却将自己旧有的宗教观念与习俗偷带进教会。由此产生了《新约》、特别是保罗书信与大公书信所抨击的异端倾向。1 在第二世纪之初，我们又遇见这些同样的异端；此后，它们以更成熟的形式、更广泛的规模，出现在基督教世界几乎所有地区。一方面，它们表明基督教在历史上的普世意义，以及它对当时一切思想较为深刻、态度较为认真的人所具有的不可抗拒的力量。基督教使他们所有的宗教观念都陷入混乱与激荡之中。这新宗教的真理、美与活力如此打动他们，使他们再也不能安然停留在犹太教或异教之中；然而，许多人又不能或不愿从内心舍弃自己旧有的宗教与哲学。于是，基督教与非基督教的成分奇异地混杂起来，处于混沌的酝酿之中。旧宗教并非不作最后的拼死挣扎便走向灭亡，而是试图借挪用基督教观念来挽救自己。另一方面，这又使基督教独有的真理面临极大的危险，迫使教会起来抵御歪曲，并防止自己倒退到犹太教或异教的水平。 基督教进入世界之时，面对另外两种宗教，一种具有相对的真实性，另一种则在本质上是虚假的；异端也同样以伊便主义 (Ebionism) 与诺斯替主义 (Gnosticism) 这两种主要形式出现。如前所述，它们的萌芽已经引起使徒们的注意。赫格西普 (Hegesippus) 说，教会直到哈德良 (Hadrian) 时代，在教义上仍保有童贞般的纯洁；这句话必须理解为仅着眼于第二世纪诺斯替主义的公开扩展，因此也只具有相对的真实性。这位作者本人就明确指出，从行邪术的西门 (Simon Magus) 的日子起，异端便已暗中运行。伊便主义是一种犹太教化、伪托彼得的基督教，或者同样可以称为基督教化的犹太教；诺斯替主义则是一种异教化、伪托保罗的基督教，或是一种伪基督教的异教。 这两大类型的异端，恰好是相对的两极。伊便主义是对基督教的特殊主义式收缩；诺斯替主义则是对它的含混扩张。前者是粗陋的实在论与字面主义；后者是幻想的唯心论与唯灵论。在前者，精神被束缚于外在形式之中；在后者，精神则沉溺于放纵的自由。伊便主义使救恩取决于遵守律法；诺斯替主义则使救恩取决于思辨的知识。在犹太教律法主义的影响下，基督教势必僵化、石化；在诺斯替主义思辨的影响下，它则势必消解为空洞的概念与幻想。伊便主义否认基督的神性，只将福音视为一种新的律法；诺斯替主义否认救赎主真实的人性，使他的位格与工作成为纯粹的幻影，一种幻影说 (Docetism) 式的幻象。 然而，两极却彼此相通；这两种倾向从相反的方向达到同一结果——否认道成肉身，否认神性与人性在基督及其国度中真实而恒久的联合；因此，按照圣约翰判断敌基督谬妄之灵的准则，两者都在其列。在这两种体系中，基督都不再是中保与使人和好的那一位，他的宗教也没有比犹太教与异教取得任何实质性的进展；后两者或者把上帝与人置于抽象的二元对立中，或者只容许二者有短暂而虚幻的联合。 因此，也有一些谬误形式，将伊便主义与诺斯替主义的成分结合起来。我们见到一种诺斯替式或神智学式的伊便主义（即伪克莱门文献中的形式），也见到一种犹太教化的诺斯替主义（见于克林妥 (Cerinthus) 等人）。在使徒时期，我们也发现这些混合形式受到抨击。事实上，甚至在基督教出现以前及其范围以外，我们便已在艾赛尼派 (Essenes)、医治派 (Therapeutae)，以及柏拉图化的犹太哲学家斐洛 (Philo) 那里，遇见类似形式的宗教混合主义。 § 113. 拿撒勒派与伊便派（厄尔克赛派、曼达派） I. 爱任纽 (Irenaeus)：《驳异端》(Adv. Haer.)，I. 26。希波吕托 (Hippolytus)：《驳斥一切异端》(Refut. omnium Haer.)，或《哲学论》(Philosophumena)，卷 IX. 13–17。埃皮法尼乌斯 (Epiphanius)：《异端论》(Haer.)，29、30、53。殉道者游斯丁 (Justin M.)、德尔图良 (Tertullian)、俄利根 (Origen)、赫格西普 (Hegesippus)、优西比乌 (Eusebius) 与哲罗姆 (Jerome) 的著作中，也有零散记载。另有数部伪经福音书，尤其是《希伯来人福音》。这些史料晦暗不明，且彼此矛盾。参见希尔根费尔德 (Hilgenfeld)《正典以外所接受的新约文献》(Novum Test. extra Canonem receptum) 中所收厄尔克赛 (Elxai)、《希伯来人福音》等的残篇。莱比锡 (Lips.)，1866年， 吉泽勒 (Gieseler)：《拿撒勒派与伊便派》(Nazaräer u. Ebioniten)，载施托伊德林 (Stäudlin) 与奇尔施纳 (Tzschirner) 主编的《文库》(Archiv) 第四卷，莱比锡 (Leipz.)，1820年。 克雷德纳 (Credner)：《论艾赛尼派与伊便派及二者的部分关联》(Ueber Essaeer und Ebioniten und einen theitweisen Zusammenhang derselben)，载维纳 (Winer) 主编的《学术神学杂志》(Zeitschrift für wissensch. Theol.)，苏尔茨巴赫 (Sulzbach)，1829年。 鲍尔 (Baur)：《论伊便派的起源与教义应溯源于艾赛尼派》(De Ebionitarum Origine et Doctrina ab Essaeis repetenda.)，图宾根 (Tüb.)，1831年。 施利曼 (Schliemann)：《伪克莱门文献与伊便主义》(Die Clementinen u. der Ebionitismus)，汉堡 (Hamb.)，1844年，第362–552页。 里奇尔 (Ritschl)：《论厄尔克赛教派》(Ueber die Secte der Elkesaiten)，载尼德纳 (Niedner) 主编的《历史神学杂志》(Zeitschr. Hist. Theol.)，1853年，第4期。 D. 赫沃尔松 (D. Chwolsohn)：《萨比人及萨比教》(Die Ssabier und der Ssabismus.)，圣彼得堡 (St. Petersburg)，1856年，·卷。 乌尔霍恩 (Uhlhorn)：《伊便派》(Ebioniten) 与《厄尔克赛派》(Elkesaiten)，载赫尔措格 (Herzog) 编百科全书，新版，第IV卷（1879年），第13页及下页、第184页及下页。 G. 萨蒙 (G. Salmon)：《厄尔克赛、厄尔克赛派》(Elkesai, Elkesaites)，载史密斯与韦斯 (Smith & Wace) 编词典，第II卷（1880年），第95、98页。 M. N. 西乌菲 (M. N. Siouffi)：《苏巴人或萨比人的宗教、教义与风俗研究》(Études sur la religion des Soubbas on Sabéens, leurs dogmes, leurs möurs.)，巴黎，1880年。 K. 凯斯勒 (K. Kessler)：《曼达派》(Mandaeer)，载赫尔措格 (Herzog) 编百科全书，修订版，第IX卷（1881年），第205–222页。 AD. 希尔根费尔德 (AD. Hilgenfeld)：《原始基督教异端史》(Ketzergesch. des Urchristenthums)，莱比锡 (Leip.)，1884年（第421页及下页）。 在使徒教会中由彼得与雅各所代表的犹太基督教，与保罗的外邦基督教结合，形成了一个基督教会；在其中，“受割礼不受割礼都无关紧要，要紧的就是在基督里作新造的人”。 I. 然而，一部分犹太基督徒甚至在耶路撒冷毁灭以后，仍坚守祖先的民族习俗，并以拿撒勒派 (Nazarenes) 之名，在叙利亚的一些教会中延续下来，直到第四世纪末；这个名称起初或许是犹太人对所有基督徒的蔑称，因为他们是拿撒勒人耶稣的追随者。2 他们既遵守摩西的礼仪律法，又相信耶稣的弥赛亚身份与神性；他们使用希伯来文的《马太福音》，为同胞的不信而深深哀恸，盼望他们将来全体归信，并盼望基督在地上作王一千年。但他们对使徒保罗并无反感，也从不因外邦基督徒和异端者不守律法而谴责他们。因此，他们并非异端，而是发育不全的分离主义基督徒；他们停留在狭隘而惶恐的犹太基督教这一已经过时的立场上，萎缩为一个无足轻重的教派。哲罗姆说，他们既想作犹太人，又想作基督徒，结果两者都不是。 我们必须仔细区分这些拿撒勒派与那些异端的犹太基督徒，即人数更多的伊便派 (Ebionites)。他们的名称，并非如德尔图良最先暗示的那样，3 源于一位假定的教派创始人伊便 (Ebion)——我们对这人一无所知——而是源于希伯来词 אֶבְיוֹן*，意为贫穷的。它最初或许像“拿撒勒人”和“加利利人”一样，是对所有基督徒的蔑称，因为他们大多生活贫困；4 但后来便专用于这一教派。至于这名称究竟是贬义的，用来表示他们关于基督与律法的教义之贫乏，如俄利根那颇具巧思却不甚正确的解释；还是褒义的，则以后者更为可能，因为伊便派自视为贫穷的基督及其贫穷门徒的真正追随者，并认为对虚心之人的祝福只适用于他们自己。按照埃皮法尼乌斯的说法，伊便最初在耶路撒冷毁灭以后逃往佩拉 (Pella) 的那群基督徒中传播他的谬误；按照优西比乌所引赫格西普的记载，约在107年，耶路撒冷主教西面 (Symeon) 死后，一个名叫丢布提 (Thebutis) 的人，因自己未被选为主教，便在犹太基督徒中制造分裂，使许多人背道。 我们在巴勒斯坦 (Palestine) 及其邻近地区、塞浦路斯岛 (Cyprus)、小亚细亚，甚至罗马，都能见到伊便派。虽然其成员大多是犹太人，有时也有外邦基督徒加入。它一直延续到第四世纪，但到狄奥多勒 (Theodoret) 的时代，已经完全消亡。它使用一部现已失传的希伯来文福音书，很可能是《马太福音》的窜改本。 各种形式的伊便主义都有以下特征：将基督教贬低到犹太教的水平；主张摩西律法普遍而永久有效；敌视使徒保罗。不过，正如犹太教本身有不同教派一样，我们也必须至少区分伊便主义的两个支派。二者之间的关系，犹如法利赛主义 (Pharisaism) 与艾赛尼主义 (Essenism)；或者借用现代的例子来说，犹如德国较早的自然神论式理性主义与思辨的泛神论式理性主义，又如一位论 (Unitarianism) 中的实践派与思辨派。 普通伊便派的人数远为众多，他们体现了法利赛式的律法主义，正是《加拉太书》所反对的犹太教化者的真正继承人。他们的教义可以归纳为以下命题： (a) 耶稣的确是所应许的弥赛亚、大卫的子孙和至高的立法者，但他不过是一个人，像摩西和大卫一样，由约瑟与马利亚自然生育而来。直到受约翰的洗、有一个更高的灵与他结合之时，他才开始意识到自己蒙召作弥赛亚。因此，俄利根把这一教派比作福音书中的瞎子：他看不见主，却向主呼喊：“大卫的子孙，可怜我吧！” (b) 对所有人而言，受割礼和遵守摩西的全部礼仪律法，都是得救所必需的。 (c) 保罗是背道者和异端者，他的所有书信都应弃绝。这个教派认为，他生来是异教徒，后来出于不纯的动机才改信犹太教。 (d) 基督很快就要再来，开启弥赛亚荣耀的千年统治，以地上的耶路撒冷为其中心。 第二类伊便尼派 (Ebionites) 从爱色尼派 (Essenes) 的观念出发，给自己的犹太教染上了思辨或神智论的色彩，正如《歌罗西书》所斥责的那些谬误者一样。他们构成了通往诺斯替主义 (Gnosticism) 的过渡阶梯。埃尔克赛派 (Elkesaites) 就属于这一类。5 据埃皮法尼乌斯 (Epiphanius) 说，他们兴起于图拉真 (Trajan) 在位时，地点在爱色尼派居住的死海周围地区。他们的名称源于其传说中的创始人埃尔克赛 (Elxai 或 Elkasai)，意为“隐藏的能力”；据吉泽勒 (Gieseler) 的推想，这指的是圣灵。6 这似乎原是一部书的名称；该书如同《摩门经》一样，声称是由天使启示的，在这一教派中备受尊崇。根据俄利根 (Origen) 著作和希波吕托斯 (Hippolytus) 的《哲学论》(Philosophumena) 中所存的片段，这部秘密著作包含了那独特的伪克莱门体系的基础。7（见下一节。）它显然出于犹太教，把耶路撒冷视为宗教世界的中心，把基督视为受造者、天使及其他一切受造物的主，把圣灵视为女性；它要求人受割礼，也受洗，弃绝保罗，并为人在逼迫之时否认信仰辩护。它声称成书于图拉真在位第三年（101年）。这一点，加上它要求受割礼，便使它比克莱门《讲道集》(Homilies) 古老得多。约公元222年，一个名叫阿尔基比亚德 (Alcibiades) 的人从叙利亚将该书的一份抄本带到罗马；该书宣告一种新的赦罪方法，因而引起了注意。 与此相似的一个教派是曼达派 (Mandaeans)，名称源自 Manda，意为知识（γνῶσις*）；他们也称萨比派 (Sabians)，即施洗者（源自 sâbi，意为施洗、洗涤），又称穆格塔西拉 (Mughtasilah)，意思相同。由于他们极其尊崇施洗约翰，故被称为“约翰的基督徒”。8 他们的起源尚不确定。如今在波斯境内、底格里斯河 (Tigris) 东岸，仍有他们的余众。他们的神圣语言是一种亚兰语方言，对于比较语言学颇有价值。9 目前他们说阿拉伯语和波斯语。他们的体系十分复杂，其中异教成分占据优势，最接近摩尼教 (Manichaeism)。10 § 114. 伪克莱门文献中的伊便尼主义 I. 史料 Τὰ Κλημέντια*，更确切地说是 Κλήμεντος τῶν Πέτρου ἐπιδημιῶν κηρυγμάτων ἐπιτομή*，最初由科特利耶 (Cotelier) 刊载于《使徒教父集》(Patres Apost.)，巴黎 (Par.)，1672年（缺第二十篇讲道及第十九篇的一部分）；克莱里库斯 (Clericus) 在其1698、1700和1724年版科特利耶著作中重刊；施韦格勒 (Schwegler) 又于斯图加特 (Stuttg.)，1847年重刊（采用克莱里库斯的文本）。后来，阿尔布. Unfehlbarkeitsdogma)。吉森 (Giessen)，1872年。 伪克莱门《讲道集》(Homilies) 的体系，同时展现了伊便尼主义在神智论上的完备形态及其内部的瓦解。它所代表的与其说是一个教派，不如说是个人的见解，但它与埃尔克赛派可能有某种尚未确切查明的联系；从《哲学论》(Philosophumena) 可知，后者甚至已在罗马发展出支派。就其一神论基础、对保罗的隐蔽敌意，以及主张基督教与犹太教在本质上相同而言，它确实属于伊便尼主义或犹太主义；但它明确拒绝诺斯替派关于造物主 (demiurge) 的基本教义。因此，不能像鲍尔那样，恰当地将它归入诺斯替各派之列。 克莱门《讲道集》二十篇，托名于著名的罗马主教革利免 (Clement)；《腓立比书》4:3提到他是保罗的同工，但在伪克莱门文献中，他显然被混同于图密善皇帝的亲属弗拉维乌斯·革利免 (Flavius Clement)。这些讲道实际上出于第二世纪后半叶一位受过哲学教育、姓名不详的作者，此人可能是一位犹太基督徒。它们是一部哲学宗教小说，以若干历史传统为基础；如今已不可能把这些传统与后来附加的伪托成分区分开来。把西门看作行邪术者的观念，来自《使徒行传》第八章的记载；殉道者游斯丁 (Justin Martyr) 则曾提到他在罗马的活动。书前附有彼得致耶路撒冷主教雅各的一封信，信中彼得将自己的讲道寄给雅各，请他严守秘密；另有伪革利免致同一位雅各的信，叙述彼得如何在临终前不久任命他（革利免）为自己在罗马的继承人，并嘱咐他将一部应彼得要求而撰写的著作送交雅各，书名为《革利免所编彼得巡行讲道摘要》(Clementis Epitome praedicationum Petri in peregrinationibus)。11 这些书信的用意，显然是要把最高的使徒权威赋予这部所谓彼得巡回讲道和辩论的摘录，同时解释它们何以长期秘而不传。12 《讲道集》本身的内容，简述如下：革利免是一位受过教育、出身皇族的罗马人，他不满足于异教，渴慕真理，在提比略 (Tiberius) 在位时听说耶稣已在犹太地出现，便前往那里。他在凯撒利亚遇见使徒彼得，受他的教导而归信，随后陪同他在巴勒斯坦各地传道，前往推罗 (Tyre)、的黎波里 (Tripolis)、老底嘉 (Laodicea) 和安提阿 (Antioch)。他聆听彼得的讲道，以及彼得与行邪术的西门 (Simon Magus) 之间漫长而反复的辩论，并应使徒的要求，将其要旨写下。因此，西门·彼得才是这部小说真正的主角，自始至终代表纯正的原始基督教，与行邪术的西门相对立；后者被描绘为一个“满怀敌意的人”和“骗子”，是一切反犹太异端的创始者，尤其是马吉安派诺斯替主义 (Marcionite Gnosticism) 的创始者。作者熟悉并使用四部正典福音书，其中用《马太福音》最多，用《约翰福音》最少；此外还使用了另一部同类著作，可能带有伊便尼派色彩，但现已不知其为何书。13 鲍尔最先于1831年巧妙地提出一个推测，后为他的学生所采纳：伪克莱门文献中的彼得，借着行邪术者这一面具所攻击的，其实是使徒保罗（《讲道集》从未提及他的名字），把他视为败坏基督教的始作俑者和罪魁。14 这一推测很容易与鲍尔的观点相吻合；他认为，原始教会中彼得主义与保罗主义之间，存在着广泛而不可调和的对立。书中有几处恶意影射保罗，尤其影射安提阿的冲突，也给这一推测提供了某种支持。行邪术的西门被指控声称基督曾在异象中向他显现，召他作使徒，而他却教导与基督相反的教义，憎恨基督的使徒，并谴责作为教会坚固磐石和根基的彼得，说他“自己定了自己的罪”。15 但这一影射可能只是顺带对保罗的一句讥讽。《讲道集》的整个构思，以及其中关于西门的出身、经历和教义的叙述，都不容许将这个异教术士与这位基督徒使徒等同起来。《讲道集》16 把行邪术的西门描绘为一个撒马利亚人，曾在亚历山大 (Alexandria) 学习希腊文，否认上帝的至高地位和死人复活，以基利心山 (Mount Gerizim) 取代耶路撒冷，并宣称自己是真正的基督。他随身带着一个女伴或情妇海伦娜 (Helena)，她从至高的诸天降下，是原初的本质和智慧。倘若作者所指的是保罗，那么这些以及其他特征，便足以将他的意图彻底掩盖，使之归于失败；因为它们在保罗的生平与教义中连最遥远的对应也找不到，反而与保罗书信及《使徒行传》的记载直接相反。 《认亲记》中的反保罗倾向有所缓和，但仍无视保罗的工作，并把彼得写成外邦人的使徒。 伪革利免借彼得之口提出、又极巧妙地穿插在叙事中的教义，是伊便尼派 (Ebionitic) 与诺斯替派 (Gnostic) 的观念和幻想、伦理与形而上学的观念和幻想的混杂。他只把基督教看作纯洁的原始宗教的恢复；17 上帝在创造之时启示了这宗教，但由于罪的蒙蔽力量和鬼魔的诱惑影响，它必须不时得到更新。这宗教的代表人物乃是世界的柱石：亚当、以诺、挪亚、亚伯拉罕、以撒、雅各、摩西和基督。实际上，他们只是同一个亚当或原人的七次不同化身；这原人是上帝真正的先知，无所不知，绝无谬误。凡记载这些圣人过失的文字，如挪亚醉酒、列祖多妻、摩西杀人，尤其是那亵渎性的亚当堕落史，以及一切以不配归于上帝的人类情感来描写上帝的经文，都是魔鬼及其群魔窜入《旧约》的。因此，斐洛 (Philo) 和俄利根 (Origen) 诉诸寓意解释，以消除圣经中似乎令人反感的内容；伪革利免却采用了更为武断的假说，认为这些是魔鬼插入的文字。在上帝的真先知中，他又特别尊崇亚当、摩西和基督，并将基督置于众人之上，却未在本质上把他提升到先知和立法者以上的地位。因此，宗教史并非进步的历史，而只是回归原始启示的历史。基督教与摩西教完全相同，两者又都与亚当的宗教一致。人无论信摩西还是信基督，只要不亵渎其中任何一位，便都一样。但若认识两者，并在两者中发现相同的教义，就是在上帝里面富足，就是认出新的原来是旧的，旧的如今成了新的。基督教的进步，仅在于将福音扩展到外邦人，以及由此而具有的普世性质。 本书作者将独一上帝、即世界创造者的教义，立为这纯洁宗教的根本原则。这完全是伊便尼派的思想，直接反对诺斯替派造物主 (demiurge) 学说的二元论。但随后，他又使受造生命的整个洪流，经过一长串性别与伦理上的对立和配对 (syzygies)，从上帝流出，复又归入上帝，以他为绝对的安息；在这里，他显然触及了诺斯替主义泛神论的流溢说。上帝自身从起初就是一，却把万物分为相对的两方：右与左、天与地、昼与夜、光明与黑暗、生命与死亡。这样，一元便成为二元。较好的先来，较坏的随后；但从人开始，次序便颠倒了。照上帝形象受造的亚当是真先知；他的妻子夏娃则代表假预言。在他们之后，先有邪恶的该隐，后有公义的亚伯。同样，彼得在行邪术的西门之后出现，如同光明在黑暗之后、健康在疾病之后。因此，在末后的时候，敌基督也将先于基督降临而出现。最后，现今的整个秩序都消融于未来；虔诚者进入永生；不敬虔者则因上帝形象的败坏使灵魂成为必死的，在遭受一种被描述为炼净之火的刑罚后，便归于消灭。18 作者说到永远的刑罚时，不过是迁就通俗的观念。按伊便尼派意义遵行律法，以及按半诺斯替派原则获得知识，乃是救恩之路的两个部分。前者包括经常禁食、洁净礼、戒食肉类和自愿贫穷；同时又吩咐人及早结婚，以防淫乱。作者宣称洗礼是罪得赦免绝对必需的条件，在这一点上接近大公教会的体系。他也接受了其中所含的大公教会原则，即只有在外在的教会中才能找到救恩。 在教会组织方面，他完全接受单一主教制的观点。主教在会众中居于基督的地位，有捆绑和释放的权柄。长老与执事则在他之下。但奇特的是，他又以典型的伊便尼派方式，将主的兄弟雅各——基督教世界中心耶路撒冷的主教——立为基督的总代理、全教会有形的元首、众主教之主教。因此，连彼得也必须向他报告自己的工作；也正因如此，按照卷首书信的说法，彼得的讲道以及革利免所作的摘要，都被送交雅各保管，同时说明，彼得已指定革利免为自己在罗马的继承人。 不难看出，《讲道集》的作者诉诸这种伪托彼得的原始基督教，是为了调和基督教世界中当时存在的一切分歧与分裂。他的这一努力当然未能成功，反倒为当时仍存于正统大公教会中的伊便尼派成分的消解铺平了道路。 除了这些《讲道集》(Homilies)——《摘要》(Epitome) 不过是它的一部拙劣节本——之外，还有几部同样托名罗马的革利免的作品，有些已经刊印，有些仍未出版。它们以相同的历史材料为基础，只有无关紧要的差异，但在教义方面，大体上没有犹太教主义和诺斯替主义的成分，与正统的界线也接近得多。 其中最重要的是革利免的《认亲记》(Recognitions)，共十卷；俄利根曾提到此书，但如今只存鲁菲努斯 (Rufinus) 的拉丁文译本。书名来自末后几卷的叙事，讲述革利免一家离散的成员重新团聚，最后都在基督教中相会，并由彼得施洗。 关于这两部作品孰先孰后的问题，批评学者意见不一：有人认为《认亲记》是《讲道集》的正统版本，或至少是较接近正统的版本；19 另有人认为《讲道集》是《认亲记》受到异端篡改的版本。20 但极有可能，这两部作品都以更古老、更简单的犹太基督徒文献为基础，而那些文献则托名彼得和革利免。21 至于成书地点，《讲道集》可能起源于叙利亚东部，《认亲记》则起源于罗马。两者的年代被定在第二世纪后半叶。 从文学角度看，这些作品颇值得注意，因为它们是继《黑马牧人书》(Pastor Hermae) 之后最早的基督教传奇小说。无论在内容上，尤其在道德的严肃性和感情的温柔上，它们都远远超过第四或第五世纪卡里同 (Chariton) 和阿喀琉斯·塔提奥斯 (Achilles Tatios) 等人的异教传奇小说。文风虽稍显冗长，却自有引人入胜之处；其将教诲与历史、哲学与诗意的成分结合起来的手法，显出作者确是一位艺术家。 附注 拉加德 (Lagarde) 在其所编《克莱门文献》(Clementina) 的序言（第22页），以及 G.
