The forty years’ repose was followed by, the last and most violent persecution, a struggle for life and death. "The accession of the Emperor Diocletian is the era from which the Coptic Churches of Egypt and Abyssinia still date, under the name of the ’Era of Martyrs.’ All former persecutions of the faith were forgotten in the horror with which men looked back upon the last and greatest: the tenth wave (as men delighted to count it) of that great storm obliterated all the traces that had been left by others. The fiendish cruelty of Nero, the jealous fears of Domitian, the unimpassioned dislike of Marcus, the sweeping purpose of Decius, the clever devices of Valerian, fell into obscurity when compared with the concentrated terrors of that final grapple, which resulted in the destruction of the old Roman Empire and the establishment of the Cross as the symbol of the world’s hope."(33) Diocletian (284–305) was one of the most judicious and able emperors who, in a trying period, preserved the sinking state from dissolution. He was the son of a slave or of obscure parentage, and worked himself up to supreme power. He converted the Roman republican empire into an Oriental despotism, and prepared the way for Constantine and Constantinople. He associated with himself three subordinate co-regents, Maximian (who committed suicide, 310), Galerius (d. 311), and Constantius Chlorus (d. 306, the father of Constantine the Great), and divided with them the government of the immense empire; thereby quadrupling the personality of the sovereign, and imparting vigor to provincial administration, but also sowing the seed of discord and civil war(34). Gibbon calls him a second Augustus, the founder of a new empire, rather than the restorer of the old. He also compares him to Charles V., whom he somewhat resembled in his talents, temporary success and ultimate failure, and voluntary retirement from the cares of government. In the first twenty years of his reign Diocletian respected the toleration edict of Gallienus. His own wife Prisca his daughter Valeria, and most of his eunuchs and court officers, besides many of the most prominent public functionaries, were Christians, or at least favorable to the Christian religion. He himself was a superstitious heathen and an oriental despot. Like Aurelian and Domitian before him, he claimed divine honors, as the vicar of Jupiter Capitolinus. He was called, as the Lord and Master of the world, Sacratissimus Dominus Noster; he guarded his Sacred Majesty with many circles of soldiers and eunuchs, and allowed no one to approach him except on bended knees, and with the forehead touching the ground, while he was seated on the throne in rich vestments from the far East. "Ostentation," says Gibbon, "was the first principle of the new system instituted by Diocletian." As a practical statesman, he must have seen that his work of the political restoration and consolidation of the empire would lack a firm and permanent basis without the restoration of the old religion of the state. Although he long postponed the religious question, he had to meet it at last. It could not be expected, in the nature of the case, that paganism should surrender to its dangerous rival without a last desperate effort to save itself. But the chief instigator of the renewal of hostility, according to the account of Lactantius, was Diocletian’s co-regent and son-in-law, Galerius, a cruel and fanatical heathen.(35) He prevailed at last on Diocletian in his old age to authorize the persecution which gave to his glorious reign a disgraceful end. In 303 Diocletian issued in rapid succession three edicts, each more severe than its predecessor. Maximian issued the fourth, the worst of all, April 30, 304. Christian churches were to be destroyed; all copies of the Bible were to be burned; all Christians were to be deprived of public office and civil rights; and at last all, without exception, were to sacrifice to the gods upon pain of death. Pretext for this severity was afforded by the occurrence of fire twice in the palace of Nicomedia in Bithynia, where Diocletian resided (36). It was strengthened by the tearing down of the first edict by an imprudent Christian (celebrated in the Greek church under the name of John), who vented in that way his abhorrence of such "godless and tyrannical rulers," and was gradually roasted to death with every species of cruelty. But the conjecture that the edicts were occasioned by a conspiracy of the Christians who, feeling their rising power, were for putting the government at once into Christian hands, by a stroke of state, is without any foundation in history. It is inconsistent with the political passivity of the church during the first three centuries, which furnish no example of rebellion and revolution. At best such a conspiracy could only have been the work of a few fanatics; and they, like the one who tore down the first edict, would have gloried in the deed and sought the crown of martyrdom.(37) The persecution began on the twenty-third day of February, 303, the feast of the Terminalia (as if to make an end of the Christian sect), with the destruction of the magnificent church in Nicomedia, and soon spread over the whole Roman empire, except Gaul, Britain, and Spain, where the co-regent Constantius Chlorus, and especially his son, Constantine the Great (from 306), were disposed, as far as possible, to spare the Christians. But even here the churches were destroyed, and many martyrs of Spain (St. Vincentius, Eulalia, and others celebrated by Prudentins), and of Britain (St. Alban) are assigned by later tradition to this age. The persecution raged longest and most fiercely in the East under the rule of Galerius and his barbarous nephew Maximin Daza, who was intrusted by Diocletian before his retirement with the dignity of Caesar and the extreme command of Egypt and Syria(38). He issued in autumn, 308, a fifth edict of persecution, which commanded that all males with their wives and servants, and even their children, should sacrifice and actually taste the accursed offerings, and that all provisions in the markets should be sprinkled with sacrificial wine. This monstrous law introduced a reign of terror for two years, and left(39) the Christians no alternative but apostasy or starvation. All the pains, which iron and steel, fire and sword, rack and cross, wild beasts and beastly men could inflict, were employed to gain the useless end. Eusebius was a witness of this persecution in Caesura, Tyre, and Egypt, and saw, with his own eyes, as he tells us, the houses of prayer razed to the ground, the Holy Scriptures committed to the flames on the market places, the pastors hunted, tortured, and torn to pieces in the amphitheatre. Even the wild beasts, he says, not without rhetorical exaggeration, at last refused to attack the Christians, as if they had assumed the part of men in place of the heathen Romans; the bloody swords became dull and shattered; the executioners grew weary, and had to relieve each other; but the Christians sang hymns of praise and thanksgiving in honor of Almighty God, even to their latest breath. He describes the heroic sufferings and death of several martyrs, including his friend, "the holy and blessed Pamphilus," who after two years of imprisonment won the crown of life (309), with eleven others—a typical company that seemed to him to be "a perfect representation of the church." Eusebius himself was imprisoned, but released. The charge of having escaped martyrdom by offering sacrifice is without foundation.(40) In this, as in former persecutions, the number of apostates who preferred the earthly life to the heavenly, was very great. To these was now added also the new class of the traditores, who delivered the holy Scriptures to the heathen authorities, to be burned. But as the persecution raged, the zeal and fidelity of the Christians increased, and martyrdom spread as by contagion. Even boys and girls showed amazing firmness. In many the heroism of faith degenerated to a fanatical courting of death; confessors were almost worshipped, while yet alive; and the hatred towards apostates distracted many congregations, and produced the Meletian and Donatist schisms. The number of martyrs cannot be estimated with any degree of certainty. The seven episcopal and the ninety-two Palestinian martyrs of Eusebius are only a select list bearing a similar relation to the whole number of victims as the military lists its of distinguished fallen officers to the large mass of common soldiers, and form therefore no fair basis for the calculation of Gibbon, who would reduce the whole number to less than two thousand. During the eight years(41) of this persecution the number of victims, without including the many confessors who were barbarously mutilated and condemned to a lingering death in the prisons and mines, must have been much larger. But there is no truth in the tradition (which figures in older church histories) that the tyrants erected trophies in Spain and elsewhere with such inscriptions as announce the suppression of the Christian sect.(42) The martyrologies date from this period several legends, the germs of which, however, cannot now be clearly sifted from the additions of later poesy. The story of the destruction of the legio Thebaica is probably an exaggeration of the martyrdom of St. Mauritius, who was executed in Syria, as tribunus militum, with seventy soldiers, at the order of Maximin. The martyrdom of Barlaam, a plain, rustic Christian of remarkable constancy, and of Gordius, a centurion (who, however, was tortured and executed a few years later under Licinius, 314) has been eulogized by St. Basil. A maiden of thirteen years, St. Agnes, whose memory the Latin church has celebrated ever since the fourth century, was, according to tradition, brought in chains before the judgment-seat in Rome; was publicly exposed, and upon her steadfast confession put to the sword; but afterwards appeared to her grieving parents at her grave with a white lamb and a host of shining virgins from heaven, and said: "Mourn me no longer as dead, for ye see that I live. Rejoice with me, that I am forever united in heaven with the Saviour, whom on earth I loved with all my heart." Hence the lamb in the paintings of this saint; and hence the consecration of lambs in her church at Rome at her festival (Jan. 21), from whose wool the pallium of the archbishop is made. Agricola and Vitalis at Bologna, Gervasius and Protasius at Milan, whose bones were discovered in the time of Ambrose Janurius, bishop of Benevent, who became the patron saint of Naples, and astonishes the faithful by the annual miracle of the liquefaction of his blood, and the British St. Alban, who delivered himself to the authorities in the place of the priest he had concealed in his house, and converted his executioner, are said to have attained martyrdom under Diocletian.(43) § 25. The Edicts of Toleration. a.d. 311–313. See Lit. in § 24, especially Keim, and Mason (Persecution of Diocletian, pp. 299 and 326 sqq.) This persecution was the last desperate struggle of Roman heathenism for its life. It was the crisis of utter extinction or absolute supremacy for each of the two religions. At the close of the contest the old Roman state religion was exhausted. Diocletian retired into private life in 305, under the curse of the Christians; he found greater pleasure in planting cabbages at Salona in his native Dalmatia, than in governing a vast empire, but his peace was disturbed by the tragical misfortunes of his wife and daughter, and in 313, when all the achievements of his reign were destroyed, he destroyed himself. Galerius, the real author of the persecution, brought to reflection by a terrible disease, put an end to the slaughter shortly before his death, by a remarkable edict of toleration, which he issued from Nicomedia in 311, in connexion with Constantine and Licinius. In that document he declared, that the purpose of reclaiming the Christians from their wilful innovation and the multitude of their sects to the laws and discipline of the, Roman state, was not accomplished; and that he would now grant them permission to hold their religious assemblies provided they disturbed not the order of the state. To this he added in conclusion the significant instruction that the Christians, "after this manifestation of grace, should pray to their God for the welfare of the emperors, of the state, and of themselves, that the state might prosper in every respect, and that they might live quietly in their homes."(44) This edict virtually closes the period of persecution in the Roman empire. For a short time Maximin, whom Eusebius calls "the chief of tyrants," continued in every way to oppress and vex the church in the East, and the cruel pagan Maxentius (a son of Maximian and son-in-law of Galerius) did the same in Italy. But the young Constantine, who hailed from the far West, had already, in 306, become emperor of Gaul, Spain, and Britain. He had been brought up at the court of Diocletian at Nicomedia (like Moses at the court of Pharaoh) and destined for his successor, but fled from the intrigues of Galerius to Britain, and was appointed by his father and proclaimed by the army as his successor. He crossed the Alps, and under the banner of the cross, he conquered Maxentius at the Milvian bridge near Rome, and the heathen tyrant perished with his army of veterans in the waters of the Tiber, Oct. 27, 312. A few months afterwards Constantine met at Milan with his co-regent and brother-in-law, Licinius, and issued a new edict of toleration (313), to which Maximin also, shortly before his suicide (313), was compelled to give his consent at Nicomedia.(45) The second edict went beyond the first of 311; it was a decisive step from hostile neutrality to friendly neutrality and protection, and prepared the way for the legal recognition of Christianity, as the religion of the empire. It ordered the full restoration of all confiscated church property to the Corpus Christianorum, at the expense of the imperial treasury, and directed the provincial magistrates to execute this order at once with all energy, so that peace may be fully established and the continuance of the Divine favor secured to the emperors and their subjects. This was the first proclamation of the great principle that every man had a right to choose his religion according to the dictates of his own conscience and honest conviction, without compulsion and interference from the government.(46) Religion is worth nothing except as an act of freedom. A forced religion is no religion at all. Unfortunately, the successors of Constantine from the time of Theodosius the Great (383–395) enforced the Christian religion to the exclusion of every other; and not only so, but they enforced orthodoxy to the exclusion of every form of dissent, which was punished as a crime against the state. Paganism made another spasmodic effort. Licinius fell out with Constantine and renewed the persecution for a short time in the East, but he was defeated in 323, and Constantine became sole ruler of the empire. He openly protected and favored the church, without forbidding idolatry, and upon the whole remained true to his policy of protective toleration till his death (337). This was enough for the success of the church, which had all the vitality and energy of a victorious power; while heathenism was fast decaying at its root. With Constantine, therefore, the last of the heathen, the first of the Christian, emperors, a new period begins. The church ascends the throne of the Caesars under the banner of the once despised, now honored and triumphant cross, and gives new vigor and lustre to the hoary empire of Rome. This sudden political and social revolution seems marvellous; and yet it was only the legitimate result of the intellectual and moral revolution which Christianity, since the second century, had silently and imperceptibly wrought in public opinion. The very violence of the Diocletian persecution betrayed the inner weakness of heathenism. The Christian minority with its ideas already controlled the deeper current of history. Constantine, as a sagacious statesman, saw the signs of the times and followed them. The motto of his policy is well symbolized in his military standard with the inscription: "Hoc signo vinces."(47) What a contrast between Nero, the first imperial persecutor, riding in a chariot among Christian martyrs as burning torches in his gardens, and Constantine, seated in the Council of Nicaea among three hundred and eighteen bishops (some of whom—as the blinded Confessor Paphnutius, Paul of Neocaesarea, and the ascetics from Upper Egypt clothed in wild raiment—wore the insignia of torture on their maimed and crippled bodies), and giving the highest sanction of civil authority to the decree of the eternal deity of the once crucified Jesus of Nazareth! Such a revolution the world has never seen before or since, except the silent, spiritual, and moral reformation wrought by Christianity itself at its introduction in the first, and at its revival in the sixteenth century. § 26. Lond. 1848. 2 vols. To these protracted and cruel persecutions the church opposed no revolutionary violence, no carnal resistance, but the moral heroism of suffering and dying for the truth. But this very heroism was her fairest ornament and staunchest weapon. In this very heroism she proved herself worthy of her divine founder, who submitted to the death of the cross for the salvation of the world, and even prayed that his murderers might be forgiven. The patriotic virtues of Greek and Roman antiquity reproduced themselves here in exalted form, in self-denial for the sake of a heavenly country, and for a crown that fadeth not away. Even boys and girls became heroes, and rushed with a holy enthusiasm to death. In those hard times men had to make earnest of the words of the Lord: "Whosoever doth not bear his cross and come after me, cannot be my disciple." "He, that loveth father and mother more than me, is not worthy of me." But then also the promise daily proved itself true: "Blessed are they, who are persecuted for righteousness’ sake; for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." "He, that loseth his life for my sake, shall find it." And it applied not only to the martyrs themselves, who exchanged the troubled life of earth for the blessedness of heaven, but also to the church as a whole, which came forth purer and stronger from every persecution, and thus attested her indestructible vitality. These suffering virtues are among the sweetest and noblest fruits of the Christian religion. It is not so much the amount of suffering which challenges our admiration, although it was terrible enough, as the spirit with which the early Christians bore it. Men and women of all classes, noble senators and learned bishops, illiterate artisans and poor slaves, loving mothers and delicate virgins, hoary-headed pastors and innocent children approached their tortures in no temper of unfeeling indifference and obstinate defiance, but, like their divine Master, with calm self-possession, humble resignation, gentle meekness, cheerful faith, triumphant hope, and forgiving charity. Such spectacles must have often overcome even the inhuman murderer. "Go on," says Tertullian tauntingly to the heathen governors, "rack, torture, grind us to powder: our numbers increase in proportion as ye mow us down. The blood of Christians is their harvest seed. Your very obstinacy is a teacher. For who is not incited by the contemplation of it to inquire what there is in the core of the matter? And who, after having joined us, does not long to suffer?"(48) Unquestionably there were also during this period, especially after considerable seasons of quiet, many superficial or hypocritical Christians, who, the moment the storm of persecution broke forth, flew like chaff from the wheat, and either offered incense to the gods (thurificati, sacrificati), or procured false witness of their return to paganism (libellatici, from libellum), or gave up the sacred books (traditores). Tertullian relates with righteous indignation that whole congregations, with the clergy at the head, would at times resort to dishonorable bribes in order to avert the persecution of heathen magistrates.(49) But these were certainly cases of rare exception. Generally speaking the three sorts of apostates (lapsi) were at once excommunicated, and in many churches, through excessive rigor, were even refused restoration. Those who cheerfully confessed Christ before the heathen magistrate at the peril of life, but were not executed, were honored as confessors.(50) Those who suffered abuse of all kind and death itself, for their faith, were called martyrs or bloodwitnesses.(51) Among these confessors and martyrs were not wanting those in whom the pure, quiet flame of enthusiasm rose into the wild fire of fanaticism, and whose zeal was corrupted with impatient haste, heaven-tempting presumption, and pious ambition; to whom that word could be applied: "Though I give my body to be burned, and have not love, it profiteth me nothing." They delivered themselves up to the heathen officers, and in every way sought the martyr’s crown, that they might merit heaven and be venerated on earth as saints. Thus Tertullian tells of a company of Christians in Ephesus, who begged martyrdom from the heathen governor, but after a few had been executed, the rest were sent away by him with the words: "Miserable creatures, if you really wish to die, you have precipices and halters enough." Though this error was far less discreditable than the opposite extreme of the cowardly fear of man, yet it was contrary to the instruction and the example of Christ and the apostles,(52) and to the spirit of true martyrdom, which consists in the union of sincere humility and power, and possesses divine strength in the very consciousness of human weakness. And accordingly intelligent church teachers censured this stormy, morbid zeal. The church of Smyrna speaks thus: "We do not commend those who expose themselves; for the gospel teaches not so." Clement of Alexandria says: "The Lord himself has commanded us to flee to another city when we are persecuted; not as if the persecution were an evil; not as if we feared death; but that we may not lead or help any to evil doing." In Tertullian’s view martyrdom perfects itself in divine patience; and with Cyprian it is a gift of divine grace, which one cannot hastily grasp, but must patiently wait for. But after all due allowance for such adulteration and degeneracy, the martyrdom of the first three centuries still remains one of the grandest phenomena of history, and an evidence of the indestructible divine nature of Christianity. No other religion could have stood for so long a period the combined opposition of Jewish bigotry, Greek philosophy, and Roman policy and power; no other could have triumphed at last over so many foes by purely moral and spiritual force, without calling any carnal weapons to its aid. This comprehensive and long-continued martyrdom is the peculiar crown and glory of the early church; it pervaded its entire literature and gave it a predominantly apologetic character; it entered deeply into its organization and discipline and the development of Christian doctrine; it affected the public worship and private devotions; it produced a legendary poetry; but it gave rise also, innocently, to a great deal of superstition, and undue exaltation of human merit; and it lies at the foundation of the Catholic worship of saints and relics. Sceptical writers have endeavored to diminish its moral effect by pointing to the fiendish and hellish scenes of the papal crusades against the Albigenses and Waldenses, the Parisian massacre of the Huguenots, the Spanish Inquisition, and other persecutions of more recent date. Dodwell expressed the opinion, which has been recently confirmed by the high authority of the learned and impartial Niebuhr, that the Diocletian persecution was a mere shadow as compared with the persecution of the Protestants in the Netherlands by the Duke of Alva in the service of Spanish bigotry and despotism. Gibbon goes even further, and boldly asserts that "the number of Protestants who were executed by the Spaniards in a single province and a single reign, far exceeded that of the primitive martyrs in the space of three centuries and of the Roman empire." The victims of the Spanish Inquisition also are said to outnumber those of the Roman emperors.(53) Admitting these sad facts, they do not justify any sceptical conclusion. For Christianity is no more responsible for the crimes and cruelties perpetrated in its name by unworthy professors and under the sanction of an unholy alliance of politics and religion, than the Bible for all the nonsense men have put into it, or God for the abuse daily and hourly practised with his best gifts. But the number of martyrs must be judged by the total number of Christians who were a minority of the population. The want of particular statements by contemporary writers leaves it impossible to ascertain, even approximately, the number of martyrs. Dodwell and Gibbon have certainly underrated it, as far as Eusebius, the popular tradition since Constantine, and the legendary poesy of the middle age, have erred the other way. This is the result of recent discovery and investigation, and fully admitted by such writers as Renan. Origen, it is true, wrote in the middle of the third century, that the number of Christian martyrs was small and easy to be counted; God not permitting that all this class of men should be exterminated.(54) But this language must be understood as referring chiefly to the reigns of Caracalla, Heliogabalus, Alexander Severus and Philippus Arabs, who did not persecute the Christians. Soon afterwards the fearful persecution of Decius broke out, in which Origen himself was thrown into prison and cruelly treated. Concerning the preceding ages, his statement must be qualified by the equally valid testimonies of Tertullian, Clement of Alexandria (Origen’s teacher), and the still older Irenaeus, who says expressly, that the church, for her love to God, "sends in all places and at all times a multitude of martyrs to the Father."(55) Even the heathen Tacitus speaks of an "immense multitude" (ingens multitudo) of Christians, who were murdered in the city of Rome alone during the Neronian persecution in 64. To this must be added the silent, yet most eloquent testimony of the Roman catacombs, which, according to the calculation of Marchi and Northcote, extended over nine hundred English miles, and are said to contain nearly seven millions of graves, a large proportion of these including the relics of martyrs, as the innumerable inscriptions and instruments of death testify. The sufferings, moreover, of the church during this period are of course not to be measured merely by the number of actual executions, but by the far more numerous insults, slanders, vexatious, and tortures, which the cruelty of heartless heathens and barbarians could devise, or any sort of instrument could inflict on the human body, and which were in a thousand cases worse than death. Finally, while the Christian religion has at all times suffered more or less persecution, bloody or unbloody, from the ungodly world, and always had its witnesses ready for any sacrifice; yet at no period since the first three centuries was the whole church denied the right of a peaceful legal existence, and the profession of Christianity itself universally declared and punished as a political crime. Before Constantine the Christians were a helpless and proscribed minority in an essentially heathen world, and under a heathen government. Then they died not simply for particular doctrines, but for the facts of Christianity. Then it was a conflict, not for a denomination or sect, but for Christianity itself. The importance of ancient martyrdom does not rest so much on the number of victims and the cruelty of their sufferings as on the great antithesis and the ultimate result in saving the Christian religion for all time to come. Hence the first three centuries are the classical period of heathen persecution and of Christian martyrdom. The martyrs and confessors of the ante-Nicene age suffered for the common cause of all Christian denominations and sects, and hence are justly held in reverence and gratitude by all. Notes. Dr. Thomas Arnold, who had no leaning to superstitious and idolatrous saint-worship, in speaking of a visit to the church of San Stefano at Rome, remarks: "No doubt many of the particular stories thus painted will bear no critical examination; it is likely enough, too, that Gibbon has truly accused the general statements of exaggeration. But this is a thankless labor. Divide the sum total of the reported martyrs by twenty—by fifty, if you will; after all you have a number of persons of all ages and sexes suffering cruel torment and death for conscience’ sake, and for Christ’s; and by their sufferings manifestly with God’s blessing ensuring the triumph of Christ’s gospel. Neither do I think that we consider the excellence of this martyr spirit half enough. I do not think that pleasure is a sin; but though pleasure is not a sin, yet surely the contemplation of suffering for Christ’s sake is a thing most needful for us in our days, from whom in our daily life suffering seems so far removed. And as God’s grace enabled rich and delicate persons, women and even children, to endure all extremities of pain and reproach, in times past; so there is the same grace no less mighty now; and if we do not close ourselves against it, it might be in us no less glorious in a time of trial." Lecky, a very able and impartial historian, justly censures the unfeeling chapter of Gibbon on persecution. "The complete absence," he says (History of European Morals, I. 494 sqq.), "of all sympathy with the heroic courage manifested by the martyrs, and the frigid, and in truth most unphilosophical severity with which the historian has weighed the words and actions of men engaged in the agonies of a deadly, struggle, must repel every generous nature, while the persistence with which he estimates persecutions by the number of deaths rather than the amount of suffering, diverts the mind from the really distinctive atrocities of the Pagan persecutions .... It is true that in one Catholic country they introduced the atrocious custom of making the spectacle of men burnt alive for their religious opinions an element in the public festivities. It is true, too, that the immense majority of the acts of the martyrs are the transparent forgeries of lying monks; but it is also true that among the authentic records of Pagan persecutions there are histories, which display, perhaps more vividly than any other, both the depth of cruelty to which human nature may sink, and the heroism of resistance it may attain. There was a time when it was the just boast of the Romans, that no refinement of cruelty, no prolongations of torture, were admitted in their stern but simple penal code. But all this was changed. Those hateful games, which made the spectacle of human suffering and death the delight of all classes, had spread their brutalising influence wherever the Roman name was known, had rendered millions absolutely indifferent to the sight of human suffering, had produced in many, in the very centre of an advanced civilisation, a relish and a passion for torture, a rapture and an exultation in watching the spasms of extreme agony, such as an African or an American savage alone can equal. The most horrible recorded instances of torture were usually inflicted, either by the populace, or in their presence, in the arena. We read of Christians bound in chains of red-hot iron, while the stench of their half-consumed flesh rose in a suffocating cloud to heaven; of others who were torn to the very bone by, shells or hooks of iron; of holy virgins given over to the lust of the gladiator or to the mercies of the pander; of two hundred and twenty-seven converts sent on one occasion to the mines, each with the sinews of one leg severed by a red-hot iron, and with an eye scooped from its socket; of fires so slow that the victims writhed for hours in their agonies; of bodies torn limb from limb, or sprinkled with burning lead; of mingled salt and vinegar poured over the flesh that was bleeding from the rack; of tortures prolonged and varied through entire days. For the love of their Divine Master, for the cause they believed to be true, men, and even weak girls, endured these things without flinching, when one word would have freed them from their sufferings, No opinion we may form of the proceedings of priests in a later age should impair the reverence with which we bend before the martyr’s tomb. § 27. In thankful remembrance of the fidelity of this "noble army of martyrs," in recognition of the unbroken communion of saints, and in prospect of the resurrection of the body, the church paid to the martyrs, and even to their mortal remains, a veneration, which was in itself well-deserved and altogether natural, but which early exceeded the scriptural limit, and afterwards degenerated into the worship of saints and relics. The heathen hero-worship silently continued in the church and was baptized with Christian names. In the church of Smyrna, according to its letter of the year 155, we find this veneration still in its innocent, childlike form: "They [the Jews] know not, that we can neither ever forsake Christ, who has suffered for the salvation of the whole world of the redeemed, nor worship another. Him indeed we adore (proskunou'men) as the Son of God; but the martyrs we love as they deserve (ajgapw'men ajxivw") for their surpassing love to their King and Master, as we wish also to be their companions and fellow-disciples."(56) The day of the death of a martyr was called his heavenly birth-day,(57) and was celebrated annually at his grave (mostly in a cave or catacomb), by prayer, reading of a history of his suffering and victory, oblations, and celebration of the holy supper. But the early church did not stop with this. Martyrdom was taken, after the end of the second century, not only as a higher grade of Christian virtue, but at the same time as a baptism of fire and blood,(58) an ample substitution for the baptism of water, as purifying from sin, and as securing an entrance into heaven. Origen even went so far as to ascribe to the sufferings of the martyrs an atoning virtue for others, an efficacy like that of the sufferings of Christ, on the authority of such passages as 2 Cor. 12:15; Col. 1:24; 2 Tim. 4:6. According to Tertullian, the martyrs entered immediately into the blessedness of heaven, and were not required, like ordinary Christians, to pass through the intermediate state. Thus was applied the benediction on those who are persecuted for righteousness’ sake, Matt. 5:10–12. Hence, according to Origen and Cyprian, their prayers before the throne of God came to be thought peculiarly efficacious for the church militant on earth, and, according to an example related by Eusebius, their future intercessions were bespoken shortly before their death. In the Roman Catacombs we find inscriptions where the departed are requested to pray for their living relatives and friends. The veneration thus shown for the persons of the martyrs was transferred in smaller measure to their remains. The church of Smyrna counted the bones of Polycarp more precious than gold or diamonds.(59) The remains of Ignatius were held in equal veneration by the Christians at Antioch. The friends of Cyprian gathered his blood in handkerchiefs, and built a chapel over his tomb. A veneration frequently excessive was paid, not only to the deceased martyrs, but also the surviving confessors. It was made the special duty of the deacons to visit and minister to them in prison. The heathen Lucian in his satire, "De morte Peregrini," describes the unwearied care of the Christians for their imprisoned brethren; the heaps of presents brought to them; and the testimonies of sympathy even by messengers from great distances; but all, of course, in Lucian’s view, out of mere good-natured enthusiasm. Tertullian the Montanist censures the excessive attention of the Catholics to their confessors. The libelli pacis, as they were called—intercessions of the confessors for the fallen—commonly procured restoration to the fellowship of the church. Their voice had peculiar weight in the choice of bishops, and their sanction not rarely overbalanced the authority of the clergy. Cyprian is nowhere more eloquent than in the praise of their heroism. His letters to the imprisoned confessors in Carthage are full of glorification, in a style somewhat offensive to our evangelical ideas. Yet after all, he protests against the abuse of their privileges, from which he had himself to suffer, and earnestly exhorts them to a holy walk; that the honor they have gained may not prove a snare to them, and through pride and carelessness be lost. He always represents the crown of the confessor and the martyr as a free gift of the grace of God, and sees the real essence of it rather in the inward disposition than in the outward act. Commodian conceived the whole idea of martyrdom in its true breadth, when he extended it to all those who, without shedding their blood, endured to the end in love, humility, and patience, and in all Christian virtue. XLVIII，tit.19，1.13，莱基 (Lecky)《欧洲道德史》(Hist. of Europ. Morals) I.448引。9↩︎ Legio fulminatrix, κεραυνοφόρος*（雷霆军团）。第十二军团早在图拉真时代便已名为 Fulminata，因此这个名称不可能源于此次事件。↩︎ φιλόθεος παλλακή*↩︎ 除非我们宁愿认为它源于 אֵל* 和 גְּבָל*↩︎ 然而，他的意思不过是宽容而已，正如兰普里狄乌斯 (Lampridius) 在22（21）所说：Judaeis privilegia reservavit, Christianos esse passus est.（他保留犹太人的特权，容许基督徒存在。）↩︎ 居普良说：“Maximus fratrum numerus”（极多的弟兄）。↩︎ 见弗朗茨·格雷斯 (Franz Görres)，前引书。↩︎ 优西比乌，《教会史》(H. E.)，VIII.1。↩︎ 阿瑟·詹姆斯·梅森 (Arthur James Mason) 的《戴克里先的逼迫》(Persecution of Diocletian) 一书，就是这样开篇的。↩︎ 马克西米安 (Maximian，别号赫库利乌斯〔Herculius〕) 统治意大利和非洲；伽列里乌斯 (Galerius，阿尔门塔里乌斯〔Armentarius〕) 统治多瑙河沿岸地区，后来又统治东方；君士坦提乌斯 (Constantius，克洛鲁斯〔Chlorus〕) 统治高卢、西班牙和不列颠；戴克里先则将亚细亚、埃及和色雷斯 (Thrace) 留归自己，驻居尼科米底亚。伽列里乌斯和君士坦提乌斯休弃原配之后，前者娶了戴克里先的女儿（不幸的瓦莱里娅〔Valeria〕），后者娶了马克西米安名义上的女儿（狄奥多拉〔Theodora〕）。被休弃的海伦娜 (Helena) 之子君士坦丁 (Constantine)，娶马克西米安的女儿法乌斯塔 (Fausta) 为继室（父子二人娶了两姐妹）。他于306年7月25日被擢升为凯撒。见吉本 (Gibbon)，第XIII、XIV章。↩︎ 拉克坦提乌（《逼迫者之死》，De Morte. Persec.，第9章）称他为“一头野兽”，其中怀有“天生的野蛮，以及罗马血统所无的凶残”。他最终死于一种可怕的疾病，拉克坦提乌对此有详细记述（第33章）。↩︎ 拉克坦提乌指控伽列里乌斯纵火，说他如同第二个尼禄，为要惩罚无辜的基督徒，竟使皇宫陷入危险。当时住在宫廷的君士坦丁，后来在一个庄严的场合，将这场火灾归因于雷击（《致圣徒的演说》，Orat. ad Sanct.，第25章）；但火灾一再发生，却加强了拉克坦提乌的怀疑。↩︎ 吉本在第XVI章暗示，这可能是一场政治阴谋。他谈到尼科米底亚皇宫的火灾时说：“嫌疑自然落到了基督徒身上；有人提出一种颇有几分可能的说法，认为这些亡命的狂热者，受当前的苦难激怒，又担忧迫在眉睫的灾祸，便与他们忠实的弟兄——宫中的宦官——结成阴谋，图谋杀害两位皇帝；他们憎恨这两位皇帝，视他们为上帝教会不共戴天的仇敌。”布克哈特 (Burkhardt) 在论君士坦丁的著作中，第332页及后，再次提出吉本的猜测，却没有任何证据。鲍尔斥之为牵强附会，极不可信（《教会史》，Kirchengesch.，I.452，注）。梅森（第97页及下页）驳斥了此说。↩︎ 见拉克坦提乌 (Lactantius)，《逼迫者之死》(De Morte Persec.)，第18、19、32章；吉本 (Gibbon)，第XIV、V章（史密斯版，第II卷，第16页）。马克西明 (Maximin) 原名达扎 (Daza)。不可将他与马克西米安 (Maximian) 混淆（后者年纪较大，比他早死三年）。他是个粗野、无知而迷信的暴君，残酷不亚于伽列里乌斯，荒淫之不可思议更有过之（见拉克坦提乌，前引书，第37章及后）。313年，他被李锡尼 (Licinius) 击败后，服毒而死。↩︎ 关于马克西明的这道敕令，见优西比乌 (Eusebius)，《巴勒斯坦殉道者》(Mart. Pal.)，IX.2；博兰德派文献 (Boll.) 中的《殉道者行传》，5月8日，第291页，及10月19日，第428页；梅森 (Mason)，前引书，第284页及后。↩︎ 莱特福特 (Lightfoot) 在其博学的“优西比乌”条目中为他辩护，见史密斯与韦斯 (Smith and Wace) 编《基督教传记辞典》(Dict. of Christ. Biogr.)，II.311。↩︎ 若将第一道宽容敕令之后（311—313年）马克西明和李锡尼所施行的地方性逼迫也计算在内，则为十年。↩︎ 例如：“Nomine Christianorum deleto; superstitione Christiana ubique deleta, et cultu Deorum propagato.”（基督徒之名已被抹去；基督教的迷信已处处铲除，诸神的崇拜得以推广。）铭文全文见巴罗尼乌斯 (Baronius)（ad. ann.，304年，第8、9条）；然而，这些铭文与宽容敕令承认逼迫失败的说法相矛盾，连加姆斯 (Gams) 也承认它们毫无价值（《西班牙教会史》，K. Gesch. v. Spanien，I.387）。↩︎ 详情见各部《殉道录》及《圣徒传》，亦见巴罗尼乌斯 (Baronius) 的《编年史》(Annal.)。这位历史学家对“insigne et perpetuum miraculum sanguinis S. Januarii”（圣雅努阿里乌斯之血那显著而长存的神迹）深信不疑，以致认为不必举出任何见证人，因为“tota Italia, et totus Christianus orbis testis est locupletissimus!”（整个意大利以及整个基督教世界，都是最充分的见证！）Ad ann.，305年，第6条。↩︎ 德布罗意先生 (M. de Broglie)（《教会与帝国》，L’Église et l’Empire，I.182）对这份宣言的描述十分贴切：“Singulier document, moitié insolent, moitié suppliant, qui commence par insulter chrétiens et finit par leur demander de prier leur maÎ tre pour lui.”（这是一份奇特的文告，半是傲慢，半是哀求；开头辱骂基督徒，结尾却请求他们向自己的主为他祈祷。）梅森 (Mason)（前引书，第299页）说：“这位垂死的皇帝毫无悔意；除了承认自己无能为力，别无认罪。他假装自己不是逼迫者，而是改革者，想以此蒙骗那发怒的基督，胜过他的智慧。他带着咒骂，把宽容敕令掷在教会脸上，却又迷信地盼望借此免受惩罚。”↩︎ 通常的说法是（凯姆〔Keim〕，前引书；吉泽勒〔Gieseler〕；鲍尔〔Baur〕，第I卷，第454页及后，亦如此说），君士坦丁 (Constantine) 和李锡尼 (Licinius) 颁布过两道宽容敕令，一道在312年，另一道于313年在米兰颁布，因为后一道提及先前的一道敕令。但这里所指似乎是随伽列里乌斯311年敕令一同发给官员、如今已经佚失的指示；君士坦丁也是该敕令的联署者。312年并没有敕令。见察恩 (Zahn)，尤其见梅森 (Mason)（第328页及下页）；亦见乌尔霍恩 (Uhlhorn)（《冲突》等，Conflict, etc.，英译本，第497页）。↩︎ “Ut daremus et Christianis et omnibus liberam potestatem sequendi religionem, quam quiscunque voluisset.”（使基督徒以及所有人，都有自由的权利，信奉各自所愿信奉的宗教。）见优西比乌 (Eusebius)，H.，X.5；拉克坦提乌 (Lactantius)，《逼迫者之死》(De Mort. Pers.)，第48章。梅森 (Mason)（第327页）论《米兰敕令》说：“这是第一次宣告这样一种学说：如今人们视之为文明的标志与原则、稳固自由的基础、现代政治的特征。它以有力而鲜明的语句，阐明了完全的良心自由，以及不受束缚的宗教选择。”↩︎ 关于君士坦丁及其与教会的关系，更详尽的叙述见下一卷。↩︎ 参较匿名的《致丢格那妥书》(Ep. ad Diognetum) 第6、7章末尾的类似段落，以及殉道者游斯丁 (Justin M.) 的《与犹太人特利丰对话》(Dial. c. Tryph. Jud.)，第110章。↩︎ 《论逼迫中的逃避》(De fuga in persec.)，第13章：“Massaliter totae ecclesiae tributum sibi irrogaverunt.”（整个教会集体给自己摊派贡金。）↩︎ Ὁμολογηταί*，confessores（认信者）；《马太福音》10:32；《提摩太前书》6:12。↩︎ Μάρτυρες*（见证人、殉道者）；《使徒行传》22:20；《希伯来书》12:1；《彼得前书》5:1；《启示录》17:6。↩︎ 参较《马太福音》10:23；24:15—20；《腓立比书》1:20—25；《提摩太后书》4:6—8。↩︎ 在阿尔瓦公爵 (Duke of Alva) 统治下，荷兰殉道者的人数，据格劳秀斯 (Grotius) 说，超过100,000人；据罗马天主教历史学家P. 萨尔皮 (P. Sarpi) 说，则为50,000人。莫特利 (Motley) 在其《荷兰共和国兴起史》(History of the Rim of the Dutch Republic) 第II卷第504页中，论到阿尔瓦的恐怖统治时说：“那些城市陷于火海与饥荒，遭到洗劫和摧毁，其间所行的暴虐几乎令人难以置信；未出生的婴儿从活着的母亲腹中被撕扯出来；成千上万的妇女和儿童遭到强暴；整城居民被士兵烧死、砍碎，残酷之人恣意挖空心思所能想出的各种手段，无不施用。”巴克尔 (Buckle) 和弗里德兰德 (Friedländer)（III.586）断言，在托尔克马达 (Torquemada) 掌权的十八年间，西班牙宗教裁判所按最低估计也惩处了105,000人，其中8,800人被烧死。在安达卢西亚 (Andalusia)，仅一年内就有2,000名犹太人被处死，17,000人受惩处。↩︎ Ὀλίγοι κατὰ καιροὺς καὶ σφόδρα εὐαρίθμητοι τεθνήκασι.*. 《驳塞尔苏斯》(Adv. Cels.)，III.8。撒狄的米利都 (Melito of Sardis) 那篇由优西比乌 (Eusebius) 保存的著名《护教辞》残篇（IV.26），提供了更早的见证；但它所说的，只是马可·奥勒留 (Marcus Aurelius) 以前施行逼迫的皇帝为数不多。↩︎ 《驳异端》(Adv. Haer.)，IV，第33章，§ 9：Ecclesia omni in loco ob eam, quam habet erga Deum dilectionem, multitudinem martyrum in omni tempore praemittit ad Patrem.（教会因着对上帝的爱，在各处、在一切时候，都将大批殉道者先行送到父那里。）↩︎ 《坡旅甲殉道记》(Martyrium Polycarpi)，第17章；参较优西比乌 (Eusebius)，《教会史》(H. E.)，IV.15。↩︎ Ἡμέρα γενέθλιος, γενέθλια*，natales, natalitia martyrum（殉道者的诞辰、诞辰纪念日）。↩︎ Lavacrum sanguinis（血的洗濯），βάπτισμα διὰ πυρός*（火的洗礼）；参较《马太福音》20:22；《路加福音》12:50；《马可福音》10:39。↩︎ 不过，值得注意的是，士每拿 (Smyrna) 会众在《坡旅甲殉道记》(Martyrium Polycarpi) 中记述的一些惊人现象，在优西比乌 (Eusebius) 的叙述（IV.15）中并未出现，可能是后来插入的。↩︎

title: 《基督教会史》·第二卷·第一章 基督教的传播
text: Translated from Philip Schaff's History of The Christian Church 第一章 基督教的传播 目录 § 3. 文献 § 4. 阻碍与助力 § 5. 基督教成功的原因 § 6. 传播的途径 § 7. 基督教在罗马帝国的分布范围 § 8. 亚洲的基督教 § 9. 埃及的基督教 § 10. 北非的基督教 § 11. 欧洲的基督教 § 3. 文献 I. 史料 没有统计资料或确切的记述，只有散见于下列文献中的零星线索： 普林尼 (Pliny，107年)：《书信》(Ep.) x. 96及下篇（致图拉真的信）。伊格那丢 (Ignatius，约110年)：《致马格尼西亚人书》(Ad Magnes.)，第10章。《致丢格那妥书》(Ep. ad Diogn.，约120年)，第6章。 殉道者游斯丁 (Justin Martyr，约140年)：《对话录》(Dial.) 117；《护教辞》(Apol.) I. 53。 爱任纽 (Irenaeus，约170年)：《驳异端》(Adv. Haer.) I. 10；III. 3、4；v. 20等。 德尔图良 (Tertullian，约200年)：《护教辞》(Apol.) I. 21、37、41、42；《致异教徒》(Ad Nat.) I. 7；《致斯卡普拉》(Ad Scap.)，第2、5章；《驳犹太人》(Adv. Jud.) 7、12、13。 奥利金 (Origen，卒于254年)：《驳塞尔苏斯》(Contr. Cels.) I. 7、27；II. 13、46；III. 10、30；《论原理》(De Princ.)，第IV卷，第1章，§ 2；《马太福音注释》(Com. in Matth.)，第857页，德拉吕 (Delarue) 编。 优西比乌 (Eusebius，卒于340年)：《教会史》(Hist. Eccl) III. 1；v. 1；vii. 1；viii. 1，另参第ix、x卷。鲁菲努斯 (RUFINUS)：《教会史》(Hist. Eccles.) ix. 6。 奥古斯丁 (Augustin，卒于430年)：《上帝之城》(De Civitate Dei)。M. 多兹 (M. Dods) 英译，爱丁堡，1871年；新版（收入沙弗的《尼西亚及后尼西亚教父文库》），纽约，1887年。 II. 著作 米歇尔·勒基安 (Mich. Le Quien，一位博学的多明我会士，卒于1733年)：《基督教东方》(Oriens Christianus)。巴黎，1740年。3卷，对开本。这是一部完备的东方教会地理著作，按君士坦丁堡、亚历山大、安提阿和耶路撒冷四大牧首辖区编排。 莫斯海姆 (Mosheim)：《历史评注》(Historical Commentaries) 等（默多克〔Murdock〕编），I. 第259–290页。 吉本 (Gibbon)：《罗马帝国衰亡史》(The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire)，第xv章。 A. 伯尼奥 (A. Beugnot)：《西方异教消亡史》(Histoire de la destruction du paganisme en Occident)。巴黎，1835年，2卷。获铭文与美文学学院 (Académie des inscriptions et belles-letters) 奖。 艾蒂安·沙斯泰尔 (Etienne Chastel)：《东罗马帝国异教消亡史》(Histoire de la destruction du paganisme dans I’ empire d’ Orient)。巴黎，1850年。该学院 (Académie) 的获奖论文。 尼安德 (Neander)：《基督教宗教与教会史》(History of the Christian Relig. and Church)（托里〔Torrey〕译），I. 第68–79页。 维尔奇 (Wiltsch)：《教会地理与统计手册》(Handbuch der kirchl. Geographie u. Statistik)。柏林，1846年。I. 第32页及后。 Chs. 梅里韦尔 (Chs. Merivale)：《罗马帝国的归信》(Conversion of the Roman Empire)（1864年度波义耳讲座），纽约，1865年重印。另参其《帝国统治下的罗马人史》(History of the Romans under the Empire)，记述自尤利乌斯·凯撒 (Julius Caesar) 至马可·奥勒留 (Marcus Aurelius) 的历史，伦敦及纽约，7卷。 爱德华·A. 弗里曼 (Edward A. Freeman)：《欧洲历史地理》(The Historical Geography of Europe)。伦敦及纽约，1881年。2卷（第I卷，第II、III章，第18–71页）。 参弗里德兰德 (Friedländer)：《罗马风俗史》(Sittengesch. Roms)，III. 第517页及后；以及勒南 (Renan)：《马可·奥勒留》(Marc-Aurèle)，巴黎，1882年，第xxv章，第447–464页（“基督教的统计与地理扩展”〔Statistique et extension géographique du Christianisme〕）。 V. 舒尔策 (V. Schultze)：《希腊罗马异教衰亡史》(Geschichte des Untergangs des griech-römischen. Heidenthums)。耶拿，1887年。 § 4. 阻碍与助力 在最初三个世纪中，基督教被置于最不利的环境之下，为要使它彰显自身的道德力量，并且单凭属灵的兵器战胜世界。直到君士坦丁 (Constantine) 统治之时，它在罗马帝国内甚至不具有合法地位；起初被当作犹太教的一个派别而受到漠视，后来又被视为叛逆性的新事物，遭到诽谤、禁止和逼迫，信奉它的人要受到没收财产和处死的刑罚。此外，它不像后来的伊斯兰教那样，对人心败坏的倾向稍有迁就，反而与犹太人和异教徒的流行观念相对立，坚持要求人悔改归信、舍弃自我与世界，毫不宽贷；以致照德尔图良所说，因贪恋享乐而不肯加入这个新教派的人，比因贪生而不肯加入的人还多。基督教的犹太渊源，以及大多数信奉者的贫穷与卑微，也尤其触犯了希腊人和罗马人的骄傲。塞尔苏斯 (Celsus) 夸大了这个事实，无视许多例外，讥讽地说，传讲这种“非理性信仰”的，都是“织工、鞋匠和漂洗工，这些最没有学问的人”，而他们尤其懂得怎样把它推荐给“妇女和儿童”。 然而，尽管有这些异乎寻常的困难，基督教仍不断发展，为其神圣的起源及其适合人类更深层需要的特性提供了鲜明的证据；当时的爱任纽、游斯丁、德尔图良及其他教父，也确实以此作为论据。不仅如此，这些阻碍本身，在上帝护理的手中，反成了促进发展的工具。逼迫导致殉道，而殉道不仅令人恐惧，也具有吸引力，激发了最高尚、最无私的志向。每一位真正的殉道者，都是基督教真实与圣洁的活见证。德尔图良能够向异教徒高呼：“你们精心设计的一切残酷手段，都不能有所成就；它们不过是吸引人归入这个教派的诱饵。你们越是残害我们，我们的人数就越增加。基督徒的血就是他们的种子。”基督徒在道德上的认真，与当时普遍的腐败形成强烈对照；它虽使轻浮纵欲的人退避，却必然给心灵最深邃、最高尚的人留下极深的印象。贫穷和受压迫者对福音的偏爱，证明了福音安慰与救赎的能力。不过，从一开始，上层社会和有教养的阶层中，也有人受到这个新宗教的吸引，人数虽不多，却包括尼哥底母、亚利马太的约瑟、使徒保罗、方伯士求·保罗、雅典的丢尼修、哥林多的以拉都，以及一些皇室成员。在图密善 (Domitian) 的逼迫中受难的，包括他自己的近亲弗拉维娅·多米提拉 (Flavia Domitilla) 及其丈夫弗拉维乌斯·克莱门斯 (Flavius Clemens)。在卡利斯图斯地下墓窟 (Catacomb of Callistus) 最古老、以圣卢基娜 (St. Lucina) 命名的部分，葬有显赫的庞波尼乌斯氏族 (gens Pomponia) 的成员，或许还有弗拉维王朝家族的成员。元老和骑士阶层也产生了若干公开或隐蔽的归信者。普林尼哀叹，小亚细亚各个阶层的人（omnis ordinis）都转而归向基督徒。德尔图良断言，迦太基 (Carthage) 有十分之一的人信奉基督教，其中包括元老、出身最高贵的妇女，以及阿非利加方伯的至亲。从第二世纪中叶起，众多教父，如殉道者游斯丁、爱任纽、希波吕托斯 (Hippolytus)、革利免 (Clement)、奥利金、德尔图良、居普良 (Cyprian)，在才智与修养上，超过了或至少不逊于同时代最杰出的异教徒。 这种进展也不限于某些特定地区，而是同样遍及帝国各处。德尔图良在《护教辞》中说：“我们不过是昨日才出现的一个群体，却已遍布你们的一切地方——城市、岛屿、堡垒、市镇、集会，甚至你们的军营、部族、团体、宫廷、元老院、广场！我们只把神庙留给你们。你们的军队，我们数得清；而我们仅在一个行省中的人数，就比他们更多。”这一切事实，都揭露了塞尔苏斯那种可憎指控的不公；一位近代怀疑论者又重述了这一指控，说这个新教派几乎全由民众中的渣滓组成——农民和工匠、男孩和妇女、乞丐和奴隶。 § 5. 基督教成功的原因 基督教迅速传播并最终得胜，其首要的积极原因，在于它作为普世救恩之宗教所具有的绝对内在价值，也在于其兼具神人二性的创立者那完美的教训和榜样；他向每一颗相信的心证明，自己是救人脱离罪恶的救主，是永生的赐予者。基督教适合人类一切阶层、境况和关系，适合一切民族和种族、一切文化程度，适合每一个渴望从罪中得赎、渴望圣洁生活的灵魂。它的价值，显明在其教义的真理及自证之力中；显明在其训诫的纯洁与崇高中；显明在它使人心灵和生活重生、成圣的果效中；显明在妇女及其所主持的家庭生活地位的提升中；显明在穷苦患难者处境的改善中；也显明在信仰告白者的信心、弟兄之爱、善行以及得胜的死亡中。 除了这些内在的道德与属灵见证，又有强有力的外在证据证明基督教的神圣起源，就是旧约的预言与预表，在新约中如此鲜明地得到应验；最后还有神迹的见证。按照夸德拉图斯 (Quadratus)、殉道者游斯丁、爱任纽、德尔图良、奥利金及其他人的明确记述，在这一时期，神迹仍不时伴随着传教士的宣讲，使异教徒归信。 特别有利的外在环境，是罗马帝国的广大疆域、秩序与统一，以及希腊语言和文化的普及。 除了这些积极原因，犹太教与异教世界毫无希望的处境，也从反面给基督教带来了有力的优势。自耶路撒冷毁灭这一可怕的审判之后，犹太教便在咒诅之下漂泊不安，不再有自己的国家。异教在外表上仍占统治地位，内里却已腐烂，正走向不可避免的衰亡。民间宗教与公共道德，受到怀疑主义和唯物主义哲学的侵蚀；希腊的学术与艺术丧失了创造力；罗马帝国仅靠刀剑的力量和现世利益来维系；社会的道德纽带已经断裂；无边的贪婪和各样罪恶，从王座到陋室，横行于罗马及各行省，连塞涅卡 (Seneca) 和塔西佗 (Tacitus) 这样的人也承认这一点。像安敦宁·庇护 (Antoninus Pius) 和马可·奥勒留这样有德行的皇帝，只是例外而非常例，也无法阻止道德的日趋败坏。古典时代在其最辉煌的岁月所产生的一切，没有一样能够医治这个时代的致命创伤，甚至不能给予暂时的缓解。在渐浓的黑夜中，唯一的希望之星，就是耶稣那年轻、清新、无畏的宗教；它不惧死亡，信心坚强，爱火炽烈，注定要日益获得一切有思想者的认同，被视为现今与未来唯一有生命的宗教。当世界不断受到战争、革命和公共灾难的震荡，当种种哲学体系和王朝兴起又消逝之时，这个新宗教尽管遭遇外部可怕的反对和内部的危险，却以真理不可抗拒的力量，默默而稳步地前进，逐渐渗入人类的骨髓与血脉。 伟大的奥古斯丁说：“基督向这个衰老、败坏世界中的人显现，使他们在周围万物日渐凋零之际，能够借着他得到崭新、青春的生命。” 附注 吉本在他那著名的第十五章中，把基督教在罗马帝国内的迅速发展归因于五点：早期基督徒的热忱，对来世赏罚的信仰，神迹的能力，基督徒严谨（纯洁）的道德，以及紧密的教会组织。然而，这些原因本身，都是吉本所忽略的一个原因所产生的结果，即基督教的神圣真理，以及基督教训与榜样的完美。参约翰·亨利·纽曼博士 (Dr. John Henry Newman)《赞同的文法》(Grammar of Assent)，第445页及下页；乔治·P. 费舍尔博士 (Dr. George P. Fisher)《基督教的开端》(The Beginnings of Christianity)，第543页及后。费舍尔说：“〔早期基督徒的〕‘热忱’，是对一个人的热忱，也是对与他不可分的事业的热忱；对来世生命的信仰，源于对那位曾死而复活、升入高天者的信心；早期门徒也自觉地把行神迹的能力与同一源头联系起来；道德的洁净，以及作为早期基督徒教会团契之基础的弟兄合一，同样是他们与基督的关系、以及他们共同爱他的结果。基督教在罗马世界的胜利，就是基督的胜利；他被举起来，为要吸引万人来归向他。” 莱基 (Lecky)（《欧洲道德史》Hist. of Europ. Morals，I. 412）比吉本探究得更深，将早期基督教的成功归因于其内在的卓越，以及它对古罗马帝国时代需求的非凡适应性。他说：“基督教正是在这场运动中取得了优势；我们不难发现它获胜的原因。在这样的环境中，从来没有别的宗教兼具如此众多而各不相同的力量和吸引力。它不像犹太教，不受地域纽带的束缚，同样适合每一个民族、每一个阶层。它不像斯多葛主义 (Stoicism)，而是以最强烈的方式诉诸人的情感，并提供一种富有同情之心的敬拜所具有的一切魅力。它不像埃及宗教，而是将其独特的教训与一种纯洁高尚的伦理体系结合起来，并证明自己能够在行动中将其实现。在社会与民族大规模融合的运动中，它宣告全人类普遍的弟兄关系。在哲学与文明使人心日渐柔和的影响下，它教导爱的至高神圣性。对于奴隶而言——他们在罗马宗教生活中从未发挥过如此重大的影响——它是受苦者和受压迫者的宗教。对于哲学家而言，它既是后期斯多葛派最高伦理的回响，也是柏拉图 (Plato) 学派最优良教训的扩展。对于一个渴求奇事的世界，它提供了一部充满奇迹的历史，其中的奇事比阿波罗尼乌斯 (Apollonius) 的还要奇异；犹太人和迦勒底人 (Chaldean) 的赶鬼者几乎无法与它的赶鬼者匹敌，而神迹不断发生的传说则在其信徒中流传。对于一个深感政治秩序正在瓦解、热切而焦虑地窥探未来的世界，它以震撼人心的力量宣告世界即将毁灭——它的一切朋友将得荣耀，它的一切仇敌将受永刑。对于一个已经厌倦凝视加图 (Cato) 所体现、卢坎 (Lucan) 所歌颂的那种冷峻而不动情感的伟大形象的世界，它呈现了一个怜悯与爱的理想——这个理想注定在此后许多世纪里，把世上一切最伟大、最高尚者吸引到它周围——一位能够在朋友坟前流泪、能够体恤我们软弱的教师。最后，对于一个被敌对的信条和相冲突的哲学搅扰得纷乱不安的世界，它传授自己的教义，不是将其作为人的思辨，而是作为神的启示；这启示的确证，与其说凭借理性，不如说凭借信心。‘人心里相信，就可以称义；’‘人若立志遵着我父的旨意行，就必晓得这教训或是出于上帝；’‘你们若不信，就不能明白；’‘天生属于基督的心；’‘心造就神学家’——这些话最能表达基督教起初对世界所产生的作用。它与一切伟大的宗教一样，更关切情感的方式，而非思想的方式。它成功的主要原因，是其教训与人类属灵本性的契合。正因为它忠实于那个时代的道德情操，忠实地体现了当时人们所趋向的至高完善典范，契合了他们的宗教需求、目标和情感，使人的整个属灵生命都能在其影响下舒展畅游，它才如此深深地扎根于人心之中。” 梅里韦尔 (Merivale)（《罗马帝国的归信》Convers. of the Rom. Emp.，序言）将罗马帝国的归信主要归于四个原因：1）所记载的预言显然应验，以及神迹为基督教真理提供的外在证据；2）基督教满足了人所承认的对救赎者与成圣者的需要，由此提供的内在证据；3）早期信徒在生与死中所彰显的良善与圣洁；4）基督教在君士坦丁 (Constantine) 治下所取得的现世成功，这成功“如同一场席卷一切的革命，使广大人类转向那在基督耶稣里启示出来、如旭日般升起的真理”。 勒南 (Renan) 在其《马可·奥勒留》(Marc-Aurèle，巴黎，1882年)第31章，第561–588页，讨论了基督教获胜的原因。他主要将其归因于世界所需要的“新的生活规范”和“道德改革”，而这些是哲学或任何既有宗教都不能给予的。犹太人确实远远超越了当时的败坏。“Glorie éternelle et unique, qui doit faire oublier bien des folies et des violence! Les Juifs sont les révolutionnaires du 1er et du 2e siècle de notre ère.”（“这是永恒而独一无二的荣耀，足以使人忘却许多愚妄和暴行！犹太人是公元第一、第二世纪的革命者。”）他们将基督教给予了世界。“Les populations se précipitèrent, par une sorte du mouvement instinctif, dans une secte qui satisfaisait leur aspirations les plus intimes et ouvrait des ésperances infinies.”（“民众出于一种本能的冲动，蜂拥进入一个满足他们内心最深切渴望、为他们开启无限希望的教派。”）勒南十分看重不朽的信仰以及向每一个罪人提供完全赦免的应许，认为这些是基督教吸引人的因素；但他与吉本一样，忽略了基督教作为救恩宗教的真正力量。正是这种力量，说明了它不仅在古罗马帝国，而且在每一个扎下根来的国家和民族中取得成功的原因。 § 6. 传播的途径 一个值得注意的事实是：使徒时期之后，直到中世纪开始，才再有伟大宣教士的名字见诸记载；那时，各民族的归信是由少数人促成或开创的，如爱尔兰 (Ireland) 的圣帕特里克 (St. Patrick)、苏格兰 (Scotland) 的圣哥伦巴 (St. Columba)、英格兰 (England) 的圣奥古斯丁 (St. Augustine)、德国的圣卜尼法斯 (St. Boniface)、斯堪的纳维亚 (Scandinavia) 的圣安斯加尔 (St. Ansgar)，以及斯拉夫 (Slavonic) 各族中的圣西里尔 (St. Cyril) 和美多迪乌斯 (Methodius)。尼西亚会议前时期 (ante-Nicene age)，没有差会，没有宣教机构，也没有有组织的宣教活动；然而，自圣约翰去世以后不到300年，当时代表文明世界的罗马帝国，其全体人口在名义上都已基督教化。 要理解这个惊人的事实，我们必须记住，使徒们亲自奠定的根基既坚固又深厚。他们从耶路撒冷直到罗马撒下的种子，经他们的鲜血滋润，长成了丰盛的庄稼。我们主的话又在更大的范围内应验了：“那人撒种，这人收割。我差你们去收你们所没有劳苦的；别人劳苦，你们享受他们所劳苦的”（《约翰福音》4:38）。 基督教一经建立，便成了自身最好的宣教士。它从内部自然生长。它仅凭自身的存在就吸引了人。它是照在黑暗中、照亮黑暗的光。虽然没有终身专门从事这项工作的职业宣教士，但每一个会众群体都是一个差会，每一位基督徒都是一位宣教士，受基督之爱的激励，热切地使同胞归信。耶路撒冷和安提阿 (Antioch) 的教会，以及司提反 (Stephen) 殉道后那些“分散各处，往各处去传道”的弟兄，已经树立了榜样。1殉道者游斯丁 (Justin Martyr) 的归信，是由于他“在海边散步”时遇见的一位可敬老人。德尔图良 (Tertullian) 说，每一个基督徒工人“既寻见上帝，又将他显明出来，尽管柏拉图断言，发现创造主并不容易，即使寻见了，要使众人认识他也很困难”。塞尔苏斯 (Celsus) 嘲讽地说，漂布工、毛织工和皮革工人，以及乡野无知之辈，是传播基督教最热心的人，最先把它带给妇女和儿童。妇女和奴隶将它带进家庭；福音传给穷人，又借着穷人传扬，使他们富足，这正是福音的荣耀。奥利金 (Origen) 告诉我们，城市教会派遣宣教士前往乡村。人睡觉的时候，种子仍在生长，结出果实来，先发苗，后长穗，再后穗上结成饱满的子粒。每一个基督徒都向邻舍述说自己归信的故事，工人向工友述说，奴隶向同为奴隶的人述说，仆人向男女主人述说，正如水手讲述自己从海难中获救的故事一样。 福音主要通过活生生的讲道和个人交往而传播；圣经也在相当大的程度上发挥了作用，它很早就流传开来，并译成多种语言，包括拉丁文（北非和意大利的译本）、叙利亚文（库里顿译本〔Curetonian〕和别西大译本〔Peshito〕），以及埃及文（采用孟斐斯〔Memphitic〕、底比斯〔Thebaic〕和巴什穆尔〔Bashmuric〕三种方言）。从大马士革 (Damascus) 到不列颠 (Britain)，罗马帝国各地之间的往来相当便利而安全。为商业和罗马军团修筑的大道，也供和平的使者通行，为十字架无声的征服效力。商业本身在当时与现今一样，是一种强有力的媒介，将福音和基督教文明的种子带到罗马帝国最偏远的地方。 在这一时期，基督教传入各国的具体方式和确切时间，大多不能确定；我们所知道的，除了它确已传入这一事实之外，并无多少。毫无疑问，使徒及其亲传门徒所做的工作，远比《新约》告诉我们的多。但另一方面，中世纪的传统将许多国家教会和地方教会的起源追溯到使徒，而这些教会不可能在第二或第三世纪以前就已兴起。甚至亚利马太的约瑟 (Joseph of Arimathaea)、尼哥底母 (Nicodemus)、亚略巴古的丢尼修 (Dionysius the Areopagite)、拉撒路 (Lazarus)、马大 (Martha) 和马利亚 (Mary)，也都被传说变成了前往异国的宣教士。 § 7. 基督教在罗马帝国的分布范围 殉道者游斯丁约在第二世纪中叶说：“无论希腊人、蛮族，还是任何其他种族，无论他们以何种名称或风俗区别于人，无论他们对技艺或农业多么无知，无论住在帐棚里，还是乘着有篷的车辆四处漂泊——没有一个民族不奉被钉十字架的耶稣之名，向万有之父、万物的创造主献上祈祷和感谢。”半个世纪以后，德尔图良以挑战的口吻对异教徒说：“我们不过是昨日才出现的，却已遍满你们的城市、岛屿、军营、宫殿、元老院和广场；我们留给你们的，只有你们的庙宇。”2这些话，以及爱任纽 (Irenaeus) 和阿诺比乌斯 (Arnobius) 的类似说法，显然都是修辞上的夸张。奥利金的陈述较为谨慎而适度。不过，可以合理地断言，约在第三世纪末，帝国的每一个行省、每一座城市都已知道基督的名，这名既受尊崇，也遭逼迫。马克西米安 (Maximian) 在一道敕令中说，“几乎所有人”都已放弃祖先的崇拜，转而归附这个新教派。 由于缺乏统计资料，基督徒的人数只能凭推测。在第三世纪末、第四世纪初，他们的人数极可能接近罗马臣民的十分之一或十二分之一，即约一千万人。 然而，基督徒是一个紧密团结的群体，朝气蓬勃，充满活力与希望，人数日增；异教徒则大多是一盘散沙，人数日减。这一事实使教会实际蕴藏的未来力量大为增强。 基督教在罗马帝国境外的亚洲各地区和欧洲西北部蛮族中的传播，起初自然远离历史的主流，尚不足以立即产生重大影响。但它为那些地区的文明发展及其日后在世界上的地位预备了道路。 附注 吉本 (Gibbon) 和弗里德兰德 (Friedländer，III. 531) 估计，君士坦丁 (Constantine) 即位时（306年），基督徒约占其臣民的二十分之一，这一估计可能过低；马特 (Matter) 和罗伯逊 (Robertson) 估计为五分之一，则又过高。一些较早的作者受早期护教士夸张言辞的误导，甚至认为帝国境内的基督徒人数即使不超过异教崇拜者，也至少与之相等。若果真如此，单凭通常的审慎考虑，也早在君士坦丁以前就该采取宽容政策了。莫斯海姆 (Mosheim) 在其《历史评注》等著作（Hist. 所说，他那个时代（380年）安提阿 (Antioch) 的基督徒人口约有十万，即全城人口的一半。 § 8. 亚洲的基督教 亚洲是基督教的摇篮，正如它也是人类与文明的摇篮。使徒们亲自将这新宗教传遍巴勒斯坦 (Palestine)、叙利亚 (Syria) 和小亚细亚 (Asia Minor)。据小普林尼 (Pliny) 所说，在图拉真 (Trajan) 治下，小亚细亚诸神的庙宇几乎无人问津，献祭用的牲畜也几乎找不到买主。第二世纪，基督教传入美索不达米亚 (Mesopotamia) 的埃德萨 (Edessa)，并深入波斯 (Persia)、米底亚 (Media)、巴克特里亚 (Bactria) 和帕提亚 (Parthia) 的一些地区；第三世纪，又传入亚美尼亚 (Armenia) 和阿拉伯 (Arabia)。诚然，保罗本人曾在阿拉伯度过三年，但可能是在退隐默想中，为他的使徒职事作准备。有一个传说说，使徒多马和巴多罗买曾将福音传到印度。但更为可信的说法是，亚历山大 (Alexandria) 的基督教教师潘代乌斯 (Pantaeus) 约于190年前往该国，而到第四世纪，那里已有教会。 权力中心由罗马迁往君士坦丁堡 (Constantinople)，以及君士坦丁一世治下东罗马帝国的建立，使小亚细亚，尤其是君士坦丁堡，在此后数世纪的教会史上占据了举足轻重的地位。从325年至787年的七次大公会议，全都在该城或其附近举行；有关三位一体和基督位格的教义争论，也主要在小亚细亚、叙利亚和埃及展开。 在上帝奥秘的护理之下，这些圣经与早期教会之地已被麦加 (Mecca) 的先知征服，圣经被《古兰经》取代，希腊教会也沦于受奴役与停滞的境地；但东方因基督教不朽的精神而获得新生的日子，已不遥远。献身的传教士宣讲纯正的福音，过圣洁的生活，他们所进行的和平十字军东征，将重新征服圣地，并解决东方问题。 § 9. 埃及的基督教 在非洲，基督教最先在埃及站稳脚跟，时间可能早至使徒时期。这片有法老、金字塔与狮身人面像、神庙与陵墓、象形文字与木乃伊、圣牛与鳄鱼、专制与奴役的土地，自族长时代起，便与神圣历史紧密交织，甚至以“为奴之家”的名称嵌入十诫之中。这里曾是约瑟及其弟兄的家，也是以色列的摇篮。早在公元前二百多年，犹太人的圣经便在埃及译成希腊文；这部连基督和使徒们也使用的希腊文译本，将希伯来思想传遍罗马世界，并孕育了新约特有的语言风格。亚历山大城聚居着众多犹太人，既是东方的文学中心，也是商业中心，还是连接东西方的纽带。最宏大的藏书汇集于此；犹太思想在这里与希腊思想密切接触，摩西的宗教也在这里与柏拉图 (Plato) 和亚里士多德 (Aristotle) 的哲学相遇。当基督在耶路撒冷和加利利教导人时，斐洛 (Philo) 正在这里著书；他的著作注定要通过亚历山大学派的教父，对基督教释经产生重大影响。 据古老传统，传福音的马可奠定了亚历山大教会的根基。旧开罗 (Cairo)，即埃及的巴比伦，其科普特人 (Copts) 声称，彼得是在这里写下第一封书信的（《彼得前书》5:13）；但他所指的必是幼发拉底河畔的巴比伦，或是奥秘意义上的巴比伦——罗马。优西比乌 (Eusebius) 列举亚历山大最早的几位主教为安尼亚诺斯 (Annianos，公元62—85年)、阿比利奥斯 (Abilios，至98年) 和克尔东 (Kerdon，至110年)。这一主教座自然逐渐获得了都主教及牧首的地位与尊荣。早在第二世纪，亚历山大便已有一所兴盛的神学院，革利免 (Clement) 和俄利根 (Origen) 在那里任教，成为圣经学术与基督教哲学的先驱。福音从下埃及传到中埃及、上埃及及邻近各省，或许在第四世纪已远达努比亚 (Nubia)、埃塞俄比亚 (Ethiopia) 和阿比西尼亚 (Abyssinia)。235年在亚历山大举行的一次会议上，有来自尼罗河之地各处的二十位主教出席。 第四世纪，埃及给教会带来了阿里乌派 (Arian) 异端、亚他那修 (Athanasius) 的正统信仰，以及圣安东尼 (St. Antony) 和圣帕科米乌斯 (St. Pachomius) 的修道敬虔；这种敬虔以不可抗拒之势传遍了基督教世界。 埃及的神学文献主要用希腊文写成。早期希腊文圣经抄本大多抄写于亚历山大，其中可能也包括价值无可估量的《西奈抄本》(Sinaitic MSS.) 和《梵蒂冈抄本》(Vatican MSS.)。但早在第二世纪，圣经就已用三种不同的方言译成本地语言。这些译本的残存部分，对于确定希腊文新约最早的文本，具有相当重要的分量。 信奉基督教的埃及人是法老时代埃及人的后裔，但已大量混有黑人和阿拉伯人的血统。基督教从未完全深入这个民族，而在哈里发欧麦尔 (Omar) 治下穆罕默德教徒征服埃及时（640年），几乎被一扫而空。欧麦尔焚毁了亚历山大宏伟的图书馆，借口是：书中的内容若与《古兰经》一致，便属无用；若不一致，便是有害，理当毁灭。自那时起，埃及几乎从教会史中消失，至今仍在新主人的统治下呻吟，依然是一个为奴之家。人民绝大多数是穆斯林，但科普特人——在五百五十万人中约占五十万——仍延续着祖先名义上的基督教，并成为西方较为活跃的各教会的传教工场。 § 10. Africa)，具体何时、如何传入，我们并不知道。这里与意大利之间往来不断。基督教迅速传遍毛里塔尼亚 (Mauritania) 和努米底亚 (Numidia) 的沃野与灼热的沙地。居普良 (Cyprian) 在258年能够召集八十七位主教举行会议，而在308年，造成分裂的多纳徒派 (Donatists) 在迦太基召开了一次有二百七十位主教参加的会议。当然，那时的教区都很小。 最古老的拉丁文圣经译本被误称为“意大利译本”(Itala)，是哲罗姆“武加大译本”(Vulgata) 的基础；它很可能是在非洲为非洲人译成的，而不是在罗马为罗马人译成的，因为当时罗马的基督徒通用希腊语。拉丁神学也不是诞生于罗马，而是诞生于迦太基。德尔图良是其创始者。米努基乌斯·费利克斯 (Minutius Felix)、阿尔诺比乌斯 (Arnobius) 和居普良，见证了第三世纪非洲基督教与神学的活跃和兴盛。第五世纪的第一个四分之一世纪中，它在诸教父中最伟大的圣奥古斯丁 (St. Augustin) 崇高的智慧与火热的心灵里，臻于最高的完善；但在他去世（430年）后不久，它先被汪达尔人的野蛮势力埋没，到第七世纪，又被穆罕默德教徒的征服所掩埋。然而，他的著作在整个黑暗时代引领着拉丁教会的基督教思想，激励了宗教改革者，直到今日仍是一股充满生命力的力量。 § 11. 欧洲的基督教 “帝国的进程一路向西。” 这一历史规律，也是基督教的规律。使徒教会的行程，是从耶路撒冷走向罗马。自此以后，宣教的进程便不断向西，越走越远。 对于整个西方，罗马教会远比其他教会重要。据优西比乌所说，第三世纪中叶，罗马教会有一位主教、四十六位长老、七位执事和同样数目的副执事、四十二位辅祭员，以及共五十位读经员、驱魔员和守门员；此外还有一千五百名寡妇和穷人由教会照管。由此我们或可估计，其信徒人数约有五六万，即全城人口的二十分之一左右；该城人口固然无法确切判定，但在安敦尼诸帝 (Antonines) 统治时期，必已超过一百万。6 基督徒埋葬死者的地下墓窟规模极其庞大，也证实了基督教在罗马的力量。 教会从罗马传播到意大利的各个城市。据我们所知，第一次罗马教省会议由特勒斯福鲁斯 (Telesphorus，142–154年) 主持，共有十二位主教参加。第三世纪中叶（255年），罗马的哥尼流 (Cornelius) 召开了一次有六十位主教参加的会议。 177年的逼迫表明，第二世纪时，教会已经在高卢 (Gaul)
